summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, visited the premises of the respondent on a complaint made by him against the respondent and his brother in law, alleging that the respondent was guilty of an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the . The respondent pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. The trial court acquitted the respondent holding that the Food Inspector had not proved that the Lal Chand was unfit for human consumption. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 3 of the Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect infested, it would be deemed to be unfit for such human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2(1)(f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was clearly wrong in its inter pretation of section2(1) (f). [475C] 2. Section 2(ia) (b) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia (supra), and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfitfor human consumption is a correct statement of law. [476D E] 3. The expression "unfitness" includes infestation even by dead insects, but does not include infested pieces of food which are capable of being consumed as a result of any other cause '. [473F G] 4. In the instant case, the Public Analyst had reported that the lal mirchi powder was either worm. infested or insectinfested. The certificate of the Public analyst does not support the case that thelal mirchi was either sieve or insects infested. [474G H] 5. The mere proof of whole or any part of the articles being "filthy, putrid", the mere proof that on account of the presence of the meal worms the sample was unfit to human consumption, is a must for bringing the case within its purview. If the phrase is to be read disjunctively, the more proof of the whole or some part of it being "Filthy for human" or " vegetable substance" or being " insect frailty" or that on due account of presence of meal woks the samples were unfit for consumption. [476C D] 6. The fact that the nine worm were found by the Public Laboratory in the sample are considered to be insects and not sieves, does not make any difference to the question whether the article of food was unfit or for human health. [477D E; 478A] 7. The Food Inspector has reported that he had examined the quantity of the milk purchased from the respondent. He has not expressed his opinion that the jar is either wain for insectu tutions or for consumption as a consequence of any cause.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. He was convicted by the Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court summarily dismissed his revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that he was an agriculturist and that the presumption in his case cannot be drawn against him. HELD : (i) The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds were not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn. [901 D E] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was an agricultural dealer. He had produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he purchased 80 90 odd of land from various parties. No other evidence was produced to show that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. [991 F G] (iii) The presumption under para 3(3) could only be drawn if there is something intrinsically wrong with that evidence. In the present case, the appellant produced receipts showing that he had been in possession of 80 90 sq. of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains were grown. No such receipts were produced by him. [981 F] (iv) The contention that he could not produce a series of transactions by him of sale was not tenable because the presumption against him under paragraph 4(2), could not therefore be drawn, because, in the present matter, the evidence of the next door neighbour should be rejected.

The appellant was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit land. He continued to be a monthly tenancy from month to month under section 106 Transfer of Property Act, but on the expiry of the second year his tenancy became a tenant from month 'to month under him and the tenan cy was determined by a notice to quit. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had been a monthly lessee in respect Of the same land and that the tenancy was determined without notice to him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court, on appeal, reversed the decree holding that the defendant was a statutory tenant from year to month and therefore the tenancy from year lo month under the Transfer of property Act could not be created by the two payments of rent. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent had no right to the tenancy in question because he was a permanent tenant under section 116 of the Transfer Of Property Act; (ii) the suit was barred by limitation as the defendant had not acquired any permanent right in the land by prescription or otherwise and (iii) the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 116 Transfer of the Property Act. HELD: (i)(a) The respondent was a contractual tenant from months to month. He was not entitled to claim protection under section 117 of the Act because he had no permanent right to possession in respect thereof. [278 D] (b) The appellant was entitled to recover possession of the land from the respondent on the basis that he was an ordinary tenant and not as a statutory lessee. [279 F] (c) The mere fact that the rent was paid by the appellant did not make him a tenant of the property in suit. The payment of rent was made by the respondent in 1937 and after 1926, the defendant became a monthly licensee under section 108 Transfer of Goods Act. [280 B C] (d) The High Court was right in holding that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold that the appellant had acquired permanent rights in the property by prescription and as the new tenancy was for building purposes, it was a tenancy from monthly to month, under section 107 Transfer of Contract Act. The suit was therefore barred by time.

The appellant assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on April 1, 1964 calling upon him to show cause why he should not be called upon to produce the production of documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax officer after April 1. 1964 in respect of assessment years 1965 65 onwards and for the subsequent years. The assessee contended that after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 Act, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production and the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) had no relationship to the power of the Court to summon that record. The High Court held that the omission of section 137 did not make any difference and that the ban on the courts as contained in the repealed Section 137 continued to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of Section 138 (1) and after 1967 by Section 138 of the Act even in respect to the documents filed before the income tax authorities, even though they were not filed in the assessment proceeding. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after repeal of section 145(1) by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1960, there is no longer anything in the provisions which would affect the power or jurisdiction of the courts to summon a production of document from the income Tax authorities after April l, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finality attached under Section 137(1), has been attached to the order of Commissioner under Section 13(1). [562D] 2. The legislature intended that no document from an assessment record of an assessee should be produced in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the commissioner of Income Tax, and that such finality attached thereto would not affect the powers of the court to require the production thereof. [562F] 3. Section 138 is a special provision which confers power on the Commissioner to summon any document from his income tax office after April I, 1964 in cases pending before him. The power to summon an assessee under section 13(2) is limited to cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the section is called for by any person, other than a court of law by a judicial order. [563G] 4. Section 139 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act 1961 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any judgment, decree or order of any Court, all proceedings under the Act pending before such Court after April 30, 1964 for the recovery of any amount due to the assessee shall be deemed to have been commenced by the Commissioner on April I.

The appellant was married to a minor daughter of one Mammotty, the first respondent. The father of Mammottty died in 1947 without leaving an issue. On February 25, 1947, the husband made a gift of his properties including immovable property to his minor daughter. The appellant 's mother died on May 3, 1946. The question was whether possession could be given to the wife 's father when the donor was himself the guardian or the de facto guardian or if he had been sent from her father 's house to his mother. HELD: (i) The intention to make the gift was clear and manifest because it was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammots, and as the gift is by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. Possession was not delivered to the minor 's guardian or de facto manager but to her mother, the second appellant, and she accepted the gift on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living. [552 F G] (ii) The question is whether possession can be given under section 6(1)(a) to the appellant when the gift has been made by the husband to his wife and accepted by any person in whose control the minor is at the time.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu religious institutions and endowments in the State. Section 76(1) provides that the Commissioner may, after determining the fee for audit of accounts of a religious institution, by notice, determine the fee payable by the institution. The appellant who was the Mahant of the temple filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand for payment of contribution which was disallowed by the Commissioner on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand was not valid. The High Court held that the demand made by the commissioner was without determination under section 76(2) of the Madras Act, and that the assessment fee was not a fee within the meaning of section 76 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no rule had been issued under section 101 of the Indian , authorising the Commissioner to make under section 75(1), for imposing liability for payment. of contribution as required by section 76, and since the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 77(2), he could not have made a demand for contribution under its provisions and that no Rules had been made under section 97(2). HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the appellant had failed to determine the question whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services were to be rendered. [924 D] (ii) The Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed), for meeting the cost of audit of the institution, and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. The Commissioner had to determine such fee (not exceeding 11/5% of the total income) as was levied by him.

The appellant, a contemner under the Punjab High Court (Disciplinary and Appeal) Rules, 1975, was dismissed from service by an order dated 2nd April 1975. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by a Single Judge of the High court directing issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt of the Court. The Division Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the order of dismissal was not an appealable one under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner asking the High Courts to drop the proceeding. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right from any order or decision of a High Court if the order has been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt; and (2) that initiation of proceedings by the High. Court will be without jurisdiction if it is in violation of section 20. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a matters of right. [512E] 2.1 A writ petition can lie to this High Court under article 226 of the Constitution from an interlocutory order passed in the proceedings for contempt, if the orders have been made by the same Judge or the decision is that of a single judge to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the court; (2)(a) The proceeding was initiated under Section 17 by issuing a notice and thereafter there may be many interlocutory orders passed in such proceeding. [511B C] 2(b) The order or the decisions must be such as it decides some bone of contention raised before the High ' Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [506D E] 2.(c) The proceedings are initiated under s.17 by issuance, of a show cause notice and then again by the decision of the Single Judge to initiate proceeding for contempt. It is neither possible nor advisable to make an exhaustive list of the typo of orders which may be appealable under section19. [525D E; 526F] 2 (d) The High Court has no power to issue a writ in respect of any order passed by it merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appeal against as a rule of law.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the fine to Rs. 2,000/ . On appeal by special leave, Held, that the amending Act of 1949 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the Amending Act of 1948, and the words " in section 6(1 A) were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphy transmitter " this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only. The word " wireless Telegraphy" used in section 4 of the Act was not a textual amendment but a substantial one. The intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was to expurgate section 6 (1 A), from the statute as it was redundant and unnecessary. The words "in any other case" were comprehensive sufficient to take within their sweep the intention of Parliament in passing them, namely, that it was necessary for the Legislature to make a different situation, namely. expelling the intention by the enactment so repealed. The section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The language of an enactment, the argument proceeds, is the phraseology or the words used therein and not the content of that Act. The text of an Act, the interpretation of which is more consistent with the object of the statute, must be construed in its ordinary sense and as such it cannot be said that the earlier Act applied to a case of a later amending Act.

The appellant was the owner of a property which was sold in execution of a decree passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Burdwan. The judgment debtors filed applications under section 36(6) (a)(ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for restoration of possession to them on the ground that they had not been made parties to the suit and that the properties were purchased in execution from the purchaser who was a benamidar for her husband Aghore Nath Roy, a son of Adwaita, the former managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The applications were dismissed by the Subordinate Judge but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had not bona fide acquired any right which could be protected under clause (c) of section 36 (2). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that in a proceeding under section36(6)(a)(iii) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act, it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decree holder was in fact a benamidars for another person. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the order for restoration made by the courts below was a fictitious transaction. The order for restoring possession made by both the courts was not one of mere benamidars but only a device to defeat the rights of the parties and to defeat them. The court could at all enter into the question as to what the decreeholder had done in the course of his action or proceeding and it could not be said that the court acted mala fide in passing the order.

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, instituted a suit against the appellant for specific performance of an agreement to sell the same. The appellant contended that the agreement was not executed by the respondent and that the respondent had no right to execute the decree. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it with costs. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that expression does not mean a person who in law is entitled to execute a decree. [705 D] (ii) The word "decreeholder" in Order XXI, rule 16 means a person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 16 permits a transferee of the decree by assignment in writing or by operation of law to transfer the decree to be passed in future. [700 E F] (iii) The expression "decree" is used in Order 21, Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure to mean a decree holder who has been assigned in writing as required by Order XXI rule 16. It does not include a party which in equity might subsequently become entitled under the provisions of Order XXI. [601 G] (iv) The respondent cannot claim to be transferees of the judgment debtor by assignment of the execution decree passed in favour of Habib & Sons, as that would amount to transfer of the suit property.

The respondent, a manufacturer of glass doors and windows, entered into an agreement with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, for providing and fixing "S.H.W. type" and "Sashes", to the appellant, who was the owner of the furniture, fittings and other goods. The contract provided that the contractor would pay to the Executive Engineers a sum of Rs. 2,000/ per month as price of the materials supplied but not the charge for service. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engi neer, Ajmer, to the Superintending Engineer, who after considering the tender submitted by the appellant accepted the tender and gave his approval for the contract. The Superintending Engineer accepted the offer and fixed the date of completion of the building as "SW.3, type". The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs, 2,00,000. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling glass doors, windows, sashes etc., and entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and that the price of goods supplied was not taxable. HELD: (i) The contract was a works contract and not a contract of sale. [505 B] (ii) The respondent had agreed to supply the windows and the fittings in question and the appellant had made no separate charge for the service. [506 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the contracts were not one of "sale" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Sales Tax Act, because the contract between the respondent and the Executive engineer was a composite and independent contract. [511 D E] (iv) The question whether the contract is one for sale or work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution of the works for a price, depends on the facts of each case. [500 C] In the present case the specifications of the windows were set out in the contract and the primary undertaking of the respondent was not merely to supply those parts of the walls, fittings, etc., but to "fix" the windows. The main object of the contract being to provide for the sale of windows, and for rendering service in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution thereof of the work of sale, the property in the goods passed under the terms of the con tract. [525 C D] (v) The finding that the appellant was not liable to pay sales tax is correct.

The appellant State filed a revision petition against the order of the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court quashed the charges framed by the Presidency Magis trate against the appellant and allowed the revision petition on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought the said goods. [280 F] (2) The charge under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. was framed against all the three accused. The report was lodged in the same manner as the complaint filed by Ram Avatar. [281 B C] (3) The fact that the case was registered at the instance of Ram Avtar is not a sufficient ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. [282 D E] (4) The evidence led by the prosecution does not disclose any cogent ground for interfering with the Judgment of the trial court as it has been shown that the report which had been lodged was no mention in the report. [283 G H] (5) The finding of the Magistrate that the complaint was lodged at the behest of Ram Avar is not correct. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he is present along alongwith Shanker Lal, when the former brought washer plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plate from Ram Avtar.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Bihar, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of motor vehicles. He had alleged that the Railways in this country were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional obligation by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The petitioner alleged that he had been denied the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. The Railways contended that no compensation was paid to the petitioner as it had not been established by any evidence that no loss had taken place. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. It is true that the petitioner has maintained that he may every citizen of this country for the matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. [334C D] 2. It was not correct to say that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The quality of the service should improve. [330D E] 3. It may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations, if any. But in the instant case, it is clear that it was the duty of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this Country. [ 330F G] 4. It has been pointed out by the respondents that the Railway Administration has limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet they have failed to implement in a phased manner the improvements referred to in the Counter affidavit and in our decision. The respondents have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ peti tion. [332F G; 331A] 5. It would be wrong to say, that it is this class of passengers which is a menace to the system. Security both to the travelling public as also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and this means that accidents have to be avoided attack on the persons of the passengers. [333B C] 6. The nature of service should be maintained in order to ensure that the safety and order of the Railway is not interfered with, attack on persons of passengers and prying on their property has to stop. [328D E; 331E F] 7. It will be wrong for the petitioner to contend that no dispute had been generally raise to the stands taken in this case. The Railway Administration should have raised it as a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources has a material bearing, policy regarding priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore propose to issue directions. [320F G H] 8. It cannot be said that the public utility should ever be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the state but there is no evidence on record to show that any dispute has actually been generally or mainly in issue for the same. The fact that the petitioners have maintained that they may every citizens of this Country for the matters of that.

The appellants were holders of land revenue and were assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49, 1949 50 and 1953 51. The appellants filed appeals before the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal against the orders of assessment on the ground that they had not been served with a notice of demand under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The Tribunal dismissed the appeals holding that the applications were barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within time as prescribed by Regulation 21 and in view of section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act which states that every award made under section 13 or 14 shall be in the form prescribed in section 26 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the provisions of the said Act shall apply to the making of such award. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there was default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. [143 C] (ii) The expression "decide it on merits" in Regulation 19(1) is used in a wide sense and includes within its scope an application for restoration of an appeal dismissed for non Prosecution as also an application under Regulation 20. [144 E] (iii) The word "decides" has been defined in section 2(g) to mean "anything done or omitted to be done before such thing was done or made". In the context of section 20 and in the context in which it occurs, it is clear that the Tribunal has no power under Regulation 19 to dismiss a appeal for default. [145 G] (iv) The words "deciding it on merit" in regulation 19(2) are wide enough to include within its ambit an application to the present case for restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases.

The appellant 's father was the Mahant of a temple in Madhya Pradesh. The Mahant of that temple was appointed as the manager on behalf of the deities in the village. He had been paying rent to the deity for the period from 1st April, 1948 to 31st March, 1949. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to be paid the income from Telibandha to the deities and that the income derived therefrom should be allowed to him as a deduction under section 10(2)(vi) of the Madhya Pradesh Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the dedication by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was made in favour of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple and not in favour Of the deity. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf for the appellant that the use of the words "from the profits and income" as out weighing or neutralising the several other provisions which point to an intention that Ramsaran Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the village, did not in any way affect the character and force of the dedication made by the Panchayat. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff 's case of absolute dedication had not been established. [426 B] (ii) The fact that Ram Saran Lal used to credit the income of Teli Dasi did not make an absolute dedication of the Village to the temple. It may well be that Ram saran Lal was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the expenses of the temple and did not made an absolute gift of the villages to the appellant. [420 C] (iii) The mere fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi Award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion the award suffered from any infirmity would not be affected by the Baggi Award.

The appellants were the President of a High Court Bar Association and Chairman, Action Committee of the Avadh Bar Association. The High Court discharged them on the ground that they had committed contempt of court. The appellants filed an appeal to this Court against the judgment and order of the High Court discharging the notices. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly discharged the notices under section 13(2) of the Contempt of Courts Act. [603B] 1.2 The High court was not right in discharging the notice issued to the appellants. The contempt proceedings are therefore quashed and set aside. [ 603D] 2.1 In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the direction that the appellants shall pay the costs of the respondents. [600F] 2:2 The contempt proceeding is accordingly quashed. [ 602C D] 2 2.3 The High COurt has not considered the contumacious conduct of the appellants individually and has given reasons for discharging them. It is true that the High court referred to the contumaious conduct of appellants but the High Courts did not wish to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contuma dominant conduct of which they individually was considered only "indiscreet" by it. The judgment of the Court does not suffer from any infirmity. [599F] 3.1 It is a matter of regret that the members of the Bar do not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The language used by them was unfortunate.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother respondent No. 5 were brothers. Respondent No. 1 was a minor. The appellants Nos 2, 3 and 4 were minors at the time of filing of the award. On or about November 28, 1977 the arbitrators made an application before the Sub Registrar, Arambagh for return of the Award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On February 14, 1978 the arbitrators gave a notice to the appellants Nos 1 to 5 and their younger brother respondent Nos. 6 and 7 calling upon them to appear before the said arbitrators on the date fixed for filing the award, but they did not do so. The arbitrators filed an application under section 16 of the . The Sub Registrar passed an order on February 24, 1978 directing return of award to the arbitrators holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting it for registration and that the limitation for filing such a petition had already expired. On appeal by the appellants, the Sub Judge held that during subsistence of interim injunction on the appellants ' part, the arbitrators were entitled to have their name registered as the law required. The High Court also ordered return of all the award to them. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the order made by the Sub judge directing the arbitrators not to keep the award in the custody of the court was wrong and without jurisdiction, but no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the Court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction, he could not have presented the award within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th January 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down by section 15 of the , (2) the period for registration of the awards had already been expired and therefore the award was in court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Application No. 14/78 dated 25th November 1983. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order made on 28th of January, 1978 is set aside and the order passed by the sub judge directing return to the arbitrator holding that he was presented within time is correct and without Jurisdiction. [693F] 2. The award as it has been made on the 30th of December, 1982 and before the expiry of four months from 28th November 1977, the award is filed in the court pursuant to the order dated 24th June, 1985. It is therefore not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M.V. V.S. Rao vs M/s. P.Veeraswami Naidu & Co., [1985] Supp. 1 SCR 890. [613H; 614A B] 3. The expression "the Registrar" occurring in section 15(1) of the is not to be read as meaning the Registrar who has been appointed under the Act and who has no power to determine the question of limitation for registration, but it does not mean that he can act as a Judge or a person who has become functus officio. [625H; 621A B]. 4. The word "Court" in section 16(1)(c) is used in contradistinction to the expression "court". In the context of section 15, the words "the Court" and "the parties" are not defined. They have been defined in the Act as including the Registrar and the parties to the arbitration proceedings. [650C D] 5.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's premises. The respondent gave notice to the appellant terminating the tenancy and called upon him to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises; (2) that the tenant had not sub let or sublet the premises to the sub tenants and (3) that he had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub letting. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the tenancy by the letter of June 7, 1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and therefore the respondent could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the agreement between the parties was void because of the provisions of section 15 of the Act; (ii) the sub tenancy by which the tenant was permitted to sub letting was a fresh tenancy and therefore, the sub lease was not a continuance of the original tenancy; and (iii) the appellant had waived the right in respect of the prohibition imposed by section 13 (1)(a). HELD : (i ) The agreement between parties was a contract for the benefit of an individual and not for his benefit. [227 D] (ii)(a) The terms of a lease are not to be read as a whole but as a part of it, so that the mere fact that the lessee has waived his rights in regard thereto would not make him liable for eviction under section 15(1). The words "is bound to let" in the clause mean that the landlord must have the right of sub letting and the tenant must be deemed to have waived it. [228 D] In the present case, the respondent had waived its right to sublet the suit premises. [229 E] (b) The agreement was not one for the protection of a tenant who could waive it as he had allowed the tenant to sub lease and consequently he could not eject the appellant. [230 F] (c) The clause in the lease deed did not expressly or by necessary implication exclude the right conferred on the respondent under section 14(1) (e). The clause was intended to be a continuation for the purpose of giving protection to the tenant against eviction. [231 G] (d) The words 'is bound ' and 'is deemed ' to mean that he must have been in possession of the premises. If the landlord had waived it, he would not have been entitled to waive it. The clause merely provided that the rent payable by the tenant shall be paid by him to the landlord. [232 G] In re: H. C. Bhari and Ors., ; , referred to. (e) The respondent 's suit for eviction was not brought within section 13 of the Rent Act, but was a suit under section 23 of the Contract Act. [234 B] (f) The appellant had no right to sue for ejectment on the basis of the agreement which was void as being in contravention of section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act. The suit was therefore time barred.

The respondent Board issued a notification under section 4 of the Bombay Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Act, 1958, directing that all the candidates appointed in the S.S.C. examination shall be deemed to have been duly selected for appointment as Junior Engineers. The appellant Board was constituted by the State Government under article 323 A of the Constitution. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that the provisions of section 3(1) and (2) of the Act were violative of articles 14, 19(1)(g), 31(1), 32 and 33 of the constitution as it was passed by the Board without giving any opportunity to the respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification issued under section 3 of the said Act was valid and did not suffer from any infirmity. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 When the procedure for selection is prescribed in the statute, it is incumbent on the employer to give an opportunity to all the eligible candidates to participate in the process of selection. The procedure prescribed under section 33(2) and the decision of the Board in turn is not vitiated by any error or irregularity. [799C D] 1.2 When the evidence justified the examination Standing Committee to record the finding that the examinees, parents or guardians were parties to the fabrication, it was not open to the High court under article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence and to interfere with the finding and to quash the impugned notification. [789D E] 1:3 The conclusion reached by the Education Standing Committee that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the examinee or their parents or guardian is amply borne out from the record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [788E F] 1 :4 In dealing with question as to whether the committee was justified in arriving at its conclusion against the respondent it would not be reasonable to exclude from consideration the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. The fabrication of counterfeit mark sheets was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before the ragging is done. [781F G] 1 5. When the Evidence Act provides for the procedure to be followed in dealing with questions relating to the conduct of examinations, it would be open to a Court under article 225 to interfere where the statute requires that the examination should be conducted by an officer authorised by the statute. The examination of the witnesses and the result of the examination is not necessarily confined to the examination of witnesses alone but also to the evidence of the examina tioners or their parent or guardian. [783G H] 1 6. When a witness is examined in the presence of the concerned official, it cannot be said that he has been won over by the accused or his parents or the guardians. It is not necessary to go into the question of quantum of punishment. But if the evidence adduced by the prosecution is found to be false and the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of law or in violation of the principles of natural justice, the court has no jurisdiction to quash it merely on the grounds that different view could possibly be taken on the evidence available on the record [783A B] 1 7. When evidence justified a examination Standing committee to record finding that there, parents and guardians are parties to fabrication, the same is not open for the High Courts under article 227 to itself examine the evidence in question and interfere with such finding and quashing the impugned order.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants and Madan Lal entered into a conspiracy with Madan Lal to commit the offence. The appellants were tried by the Special Judge for offences under sections 120 B and 409 read with section 34 of the Penal Code. The Special judge acquitted Madan Lal but convicted Madan Lal under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the intention of the Act was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that the words "any public servant" in section 161 did not include a person who had been convicted under section 4(2). HELD : The appellants could not be convicted under the provisions of section 5 (1) (d). The intention was to make a bribe out of an unwilling person. The object of the section is to create a public servant by means which he may have been interested in or related to the person so concerned and that before a charge under section 6(2), sub clause (4) must be satisfied that there was threat or inducement, or promise proceeding from the public servant or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain pecuniary advantage. The words "public servant" are not defined in the Act. They are used in the sense of a person 's own ' and they have reference to a person whose conduct is such as to make him liable for punishment under section 3(1) of that Act. [187 H; 188 A B] In the present case, the appellants were not charged with having committed an offence under section 420 I. P.C., but were charged with offences under section 409 read along with section 5 of the . The charge was therefore clearly one of conspiracy to commit criminal misconduct and it could not therefore be said that they were interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case.

The appellant Bank, a bank, had advanced certain loans to the respondent Bank. The respondent Bank issued a letter of guarantee in favour of the appellant Bank which was accepted by the Bank and endorsed by the surety to the Bank. In view of the said agreement between the parties, the Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368044 with interest at 6% per annum from the date of the suit till realisation. The trial Court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to safe custody of the pledged oil tins but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the appellant with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods, the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the respondent bank was discharged. The High Court held that the two promissory notes, one executed by the principal debtor in favour the Bank, and the other by the Principal debtor in his favour were independent transactions and they evidence that the principal creditor had offered two securities, one the pledge and the personal guarantee of the surety. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of Guarantee, the appellant was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the specific condition that the Principal creditor shall offer two securities one the security the pledgee of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the bank to be supervised by the bank 's employee and secondly, the personal guarantees of the sureties. [83F] 2. The appellant Bank was discharged by the trial Court, i.e., the court of first instance, and this decree has been reversed by the High Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [84G] 3. In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal debtors at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the respondent, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the bailor parts with the other security the surety would be discharged to his extent to the value Of the security. [85H; 86A] 4. The Bank in good sense has been treated as a separate entity and it is not possible to entertain a contention that section 141 would not be attracted and the surety will not be discharged even if it is found that a creditor has taken morethan one security on the basis of which advance was made and the sureties gave personal guarantee for the advance. [86C] 5.

The appellant was the holder of a village in Bombay. He was granted remuneration for services rendered by him from the Rokade family. The respondent No. 1, who was the Ruler of the former State of Nagpur, was appointed as the sovereign authority to collect the "patelki inam" lands and to grant them to the appellant. The appellant claimed that he had a right to hold the "Patelki Inam" lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the date of his appointment. The claim was rejected by the Government, but the appellant filed a suit for possession of the " patelki inams" lands on the ground that they constituted a grant by way of remuneration or emoluments for services to be rendered by the working Patel from Rokades family. Held, that the appellant could not succeed in his suit as he had no right to claim any share in the emoluments of office. The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authorities. The order of Government dated August 28, 1922 did not confer any new right or rights on a member of the family of the patel. The grants were not service grant, but were service grant and no question of title arose against Government, even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Amritrao was entitled to his share in "patels" lands as a member thereof irrespective of whether he performs the service or not. Amrit Rao vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , followed.

The appellant was the sole surviving male member of a Hindu family. He died in 1945 leaving behind his widow, two sons and a daughter. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties and for mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rules of Hindu law applicable to the case were not in matters of succession and inheritance, and (ii) the rule of Hindu Law applicable to a case of adoption governed matters of property, inheritance and succession, including rules as to joint family property, was not in the matter of property. HELD: (1) The rule of law applicable in the present case is not in respect of properties which are governed by Hindu law but only in matters relating to property. [234 B] (2) The High Court had rightly held that the rule applied to the facts of the case. [235 C D] (3) The rules of the Hindu Law relating to Hindu law were accepted as customary law in matters like the present, and the rules applicable to all kinds of adoptions, including the rules as regards joint family estate, were accepted by them as customary laws in matters not only in matter of succession but also concepts, such as the joint Hindu family property and its devolution by survivorship. [236 D] The rule that a rule of family law applicable generally to all persons governed by it is not inconsistent with what he has held earlier, was correct. [237 E] (4) The general trend of judicial opinion in Bombay was that both the Khoias and the Cutchi Memons retained their rules of joint family as customary Law in matters Of succession and succession including rules relating to joint families.

The appellant No. 1, a manufacturer of fabrics, was manufacturing fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of excise duty on the yarn which was produced at an intermediary stage in their mill. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The language of rule 9(1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant thereto. [707C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The explanation to rule 9 states that commodity obtained at a intermediate stage of manufacture in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) of Rule 9. [077D] 1:3. The Explanation to rule9(1), however, does not contain any definition of "place of removal" but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or premise at an end of which the excisable goods are manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods were used in the manufacture of another commodity in a different place. [087E] 1 :4. The expression "place" is not defined in the Act and therefore, it has to receive its ordinary meaning from the context in which it occurs. [807F] 1 Whether a commodity which is manufactured in such a place or not, is consumed or utilised in the manufacturing process of another entity, then it will be a case of removal for the purpose of payment of excise duties. [908G H] 2.1 In the present case, there can be no doubt that if a commodity is taken outside the factory it will fall under the definition of 'place of manufacture ' and consequently, the goods manufactured in the factory are liable for payment of duty. The words "any premises appurtenant to such place" in Rule 9(i) do not contain an definition of `place of '. [1008H; 1009A] 2:2. The language is clear and unambiguous. It has been given retrospective effect by virtue of section S of the Finance Act, 1982. Under the definition "place or premises of production" may be a factory or any other place or part thereof in the same place. In the absence of any definition, it cannot be said that the goods which are obtained at the intermediate stage and consumed or used in a manufacture of the excisable good, are not removed from the factory premises. [1109C D] 2 :3. If a commodity has been taken outside an factory it would be removal but rule 9 does not, in any manner, indicate that it is only when the goods are removed from one plant to another it will not be a 'place ' of manufacture. The use of the words "place".

The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for stay of the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court. The Civil Judge stayed the hearing and disposed of the application on merits. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, who dismissed it. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining the respondent from proceeding with the hearing. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A suit is not maintainable for an injunc tion restraining the hearing authority under section 68 D of the Act from proceeding further with the trial or approving the scheme either with or without modification. [145C] 1.2 The procedure laid down for preparation and approval of a scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D. Section 68 D provides that where any State Transport Undertaking is of opinion that for the purpose of providing an efficient, adequate, economical and properly co ordinate road transport services it is necessary in the public interest that road transport service in general or any particular class of such service in relation to any area or route or portion thereof should be run and operated by the State Transport Undertakings whether to the exclusion, complete or partial of other persons or other vise, the State Government may frame a scheme giving particulars of the nature of the service proposed to be rendered, the area or routes proposed to he covered and such other particulars respecting thereto as may be prescribed. [146D E] 1:3 The procedure for preparation of the scheme is provided in sections 69 C and 69 D of Act.

The appellant was a public servant. He had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child. The appellant asked for bribe from the girl, but she refused. The girl went to the house of her sister 's husband and told him that he never asked for money. The police searched the room and found the girl in the room. The statement of the girl was recorded by the Magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Magistrate accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel, it cannot be said that the appellant obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act. HELD : The order of sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. [184 D] (i) The order was not excessive and the High court was right in holding that the conviction under section 5(2) of the Act was not justified. [185 F G] (ii) The appellant had no intention to commit any offence. He was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer within the meaning of section 5 (1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The appellant contended that the sanction granted by the Magistrate was not a valid sanction as it was not in accordance with law and that the prosecution had failed to prove the case against him beyond reasonable doubt. Held, that the order granting the certificate did not suffer from any infirmity and the High Court was right in holding that the sanctioning authority acted without jurisdiction and that it was open to the appellant to raise a contention before the High court which was not raised before it. The sanction clearly stated that the case was pending before the Magistrate for trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. Held further, that there was no substance in the contention that the appellant had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice he should be prosecuted. The order granting a certificate did state all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance of Rs. Bokil had applied its mind and was of the opinion that in view of the fact that the question whether or not there was a proper sanction in the case, it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction. The sanctioning authority was competent to grant the certificate under section 6(c) of Act 1 of 1947.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. He had only a life interest and he had only one life interest. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The appellate authority allowed the appeal holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. In second appeal the High Court held that the appellant had no right to evict the respondents under section14(1) (b) as grounds for eviction were not bona fide. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the landlord had only an life interest or right in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life interests that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1)(a) as ground for eviction of his tenants by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own account or on behalf Of another or on account of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or be entitled to receives the rent if the building were let to a tenant". The expression "landlord" is defined in section 2 (6) to mean any person who was receiving or was entitled to received the rent whether on behalf or for himself and other remainder man. [275F H] 2.1 A landlord who holds a life estate in the land and who admittedly has been on his personal right under the deed of settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants, is outside the ken of this Act. The term "landlord ' is defined by section 2 sub section (6). [275H; 276A] 2(a) A tenant with life interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se be not bona bonafide. [276B] 2.(b) A person who holds an estate in a land and whose life interest is affected by the deed or settlement as such will not be entitled for eviction under section 15(1). Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenants are irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and tenants when a suit for eviction is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act. [277C D] 2 (c) A single petition with regard to two different tenancies, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purposes, is not maintainable. [278D E] 3. The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenant as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others who are not his tenants under the provisions of the Act is outside this Act, is irrelevant in the litigation between them. [279E F] 4. The question whether a tenant with a lifeinterest cannot be evicted from the premises in orderto reconstruct it is a mixed question of fact and law. It is settled law that a controversy which may arise in a suit between a person who held a life Interest in the building and who, admittedly has not been on the file of the landlord, can be agitated by an application under section 25 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (lease and Rent) Control Act, 1961. [280F G] 5. The High Court was right in holding that there is no possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder person.

The respondent decree holder filed execution proceedings against the appellant decree holder for recovery of certain amount due from him on account of arrears of rent. The executing court held that after vesting all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh free from all encumbrances. The respondent decree holders appealed to the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that after the vesting of all the right mentioned in s.6(a) (i) the land vests in the intermediary. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that the trees, said to be part of a grove were included in the definition of ' intermediary ' under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari Act, and as such the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section6(h) of that Act read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was not justified in holding on the basis of previous definition or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of groves, and grove land. [717G] 2.1 In view of the definition or the rule made under the Act, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to give effect to previous definitions nor to make any distinction between standing unwanted or unwantled trees which are part of 'land '. [818A B] 2:2 The position taken by the executing court in the instant case, was that after coming into force of the Act what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of grove land as these contin ued to vest in the intermediaries. This means that 'grove land ' and an "intermediary"s groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut tree is always included in bhumidhari rights. After these clear words of the enactment, it was not necessary that even after vesting ofall the rights covered by section 6 (a)(1) the lands vest in intermediary. [862E F] 2 :3 The proposition is well settled under the general law, that trees, before they are cut, form parts of ' land '. And an inseparable part is always excluded from the whole. In view Of this very clear legal position, it cannot be accepted that previous definitions and to make a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari right, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by t he executing court, that there is a distinction between trees and a grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench).

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was that on the night of occurrence when the deceased and his wife were sleeping in a room, the accused persons armed with deadly weapons attacked them with chopper and those injuries were caused by blunt weapon. The deceased succumbed to the injury sustained by him at the hospital. The trial court convicted all the four appellants under Section 326 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted the first appellant Subran, but confirmed the conviction of the second appellant under Section 324 IPC. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove the case against all the accused beyond reasonable doubt; (ii) the evidence of PW 1, the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination, did not establish the presence of any injuries on the body of the deceased; and (iii) the medical evidence also showed that the injuries caused by the chopper were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of Suku. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution has failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubts. [89G] 2.1 In the instant case, the evidence on record clearly established that the appellants were guilty of an offence punishable under Section 304 Part I IPC. They had shared common intention of causing such bodily injury as were likely to cause the death of the first deceased. The injuries attributed to them were not sufficient in ordinary course to cause their death. [90G] 3.2 In the absence of any evidence to show that all the three appellants shared the common intention, the conviction and sentence under Section 325 IPC cannot be sustained and the same would be the position with regard to the conviction under Section 307 IPC. [91H; 92A B] 4.1 The injuries on deceased had been caused by all the five accused persons and that the death had occurred due to receipt of multiple injuries. According to the medical opinion, none of the injuries was sufficient in a ordinary course for causing death of suku. The intention to cause such bodily injuries on any person could not be attributed to him and the medical report also shows that the injury caused by him was not sufficient to cause his death. Therefore, the appellants 2 to 4 were rightly convicted under Section 323 IPC. Accordingly, they are sentenced to suffer imprisonment for seven years each.

The assessee, a non resident assessee, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer included the amount of Rs. 1,960/ as income from undisclosed sources in his books of account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70 and that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under Section 5(2)(a) of the Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The assessee could be said to have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. In this view of the matter, it must be held that in the circumstances of the case, the method of accounting regularly adopted by an assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it was argued that if the assessee is proved to have maintained its accounts with respect to royalty amount on cash receipt basis, then there is no receipt until it is received by it in U,K. [103B C] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the method adopted by the assessee for all its income was really irrelevant. [102C D] 3. In the circumstances, the mode of accounting adopted by assessee for the relevant years is really irrelevant and that Section 5 (2)(b) cannot apply. [ 103D] 4. The amount of royalty paid to the assessee in the books of the Indian Company does not amount to receipt of income by the asses see. It is immaterial when did it actually receive it in the U. K. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that there was any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(1) and section 145 of the .

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (1) the evidence of an accomplice could not be a corroboration of the approver 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 who had prepared the knife alleged to have been used for the murder and his statement was not corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused, the High Court should not have interfered with the conviction; (2) the statement of an approver could not operate as a corroboration in material details and qua the appellant, the conviction was unsustainable. HELD : (1)(a) The evidence of the accomplice is no corroboration of his story because he has been declared hostile by the prosecution. [834 B] (b) The High court was right in holding that the statement made to accused No 1 was corroborated in materials particulars and against him. [ 835 C D] (c) The conviction of the appellant on the testimony of an independent witness is unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of a approver 'S ' who is competent to give evidence and according to the latter which is a rule of practice it is almost always unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [873 F] (2)(a). The statement of the accused under section 342 Cr. P.C., was not sufficient for the conviction of him on the evidence given by an accomplice. [872 G] (3) The fact that the approver had made a confessional statement before the Magistrate did not affect his veracity and it could not affect the credibility of the witness. [878 F] In re: A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 946, followed. (b). The law is that there must be corroboration in the evidence against an accused person, but so far as the appellant is concerned, the court will, as a matter of practice, not accept his testimony without corroboration in materials particular.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961, a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the appellant was convicted by the Special Judge for an offence. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (1 ) the appellant could not be deemed to be a public officer within the definition of section 2(g) of that Act in view of the language of section 81 of the . (2) the words "public servant" include every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of an Government company as defined in section 617 of the , and therefore a public servants within the scope of section 3(1) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act or section 21, Indian Penal code. HELD : (i) The appellant was not an officer in a civil service. He could be said to be an officer within section 21(9), Indian Penal C.P.C. and therefore he was a "public Servant" within the mischief of section 5 of the prevention of Corruption. [693 D] (ii) The words " public servant" includes every officer, in the employ or pay or of Government, within the terms of section21, Penal Code, is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. [689 E] (iii) The word "public servants" in section 21 means a person who is employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was an officer of the Government and not of a Corporation or Corporation as defined by section 617 Of the . [694 G H] (iv) The expression "public service" includes all services which are rendered to any person. Therefore, a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was appointed to certain office for performance of certain public duty is one such person who can be said not to be "public". [689 A B] (v) The definition of "public officer" in the section includes every person who was employed as metal examiner or a metal Examiner in the railway Carriage Workshop. [687 E F] (vi) The High Court has found that the appellant is an officer performing duties at the relevant time and therefore, a public Servant within the term of 21, cl. (12), Indian penal Code. [688 G H; 689 A B].

The appellant was convicted for contravention of r. 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order 1964. In appeal by special leave it was contended that r.141(2), which is within the powers conferred by section 3(1 ) of the Act, does not contain any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juar 's right to make a complaint under cl. (3) of that order and that r, 141(1) is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The High court was not justified in holding that r., 141(a) is within its powers. Rule 141(ii) is outside the powers under section 3 (1 ) and therefore, the order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture is ultra vivos. [272 G] In the instant case, the High court had set aside the conviction for contravention under cl 3 of that Order and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced the accused to imprisonment already undergone. The High 'Court was therefore justified in modifying the sentence passed on the appellant. [273 A B] The fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the , provides that the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Sia was not in any manner concerned with the deep seated enmity between the appellant and the deceased, and that he had been falsely implicated by the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court, in favour of Siya Ram and his companions. [475E] (2) The circumstances show that the appellant was a colleague of the deceased and his associates. There is nothing on record to show that he was aware of the nefarious design of S iichani. It is not enough if he had known that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [775G] (3) The fact that the deceased was a fleeting holes, that he did not know the neces sary design of the Sia. It was also not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happened to facilitate the commission of the crime. [771B C] (4) The circumstance that the High Court had relied on the evidence of Om Prakash Dubey in order to hold that Shri Ram had played an important role in the murderous design, is insufficient to sustain the conviction of Siolet and ViOlet.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that it was doubtful whether any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 304 Part I, Part II, Penal Code. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were not identified but only named persons, they did not take part in the murder. The evidence was adduced to prove that the said persons along with others named or unnamed, participated jointly in the crime. The fact that the other three accused were acquitted by the trial court did not lead to any conclusion that the appellant had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unidentified persons for committing the said offence. (ii)The High Court found that although accused 1 3 and four others were acquitted, they were convicted under s. 302 readwith section 34, of the Penal Code, though the other two accused were convicted only under section 307 read with s.34, of that Code. The appellant was therefore guilty under section 324 read with Section 34 of that Penal Code for having committed the murder of the deceased in furtherance of their common intention. (iii)The evidence was not sufficient to convict him under s 302 read along with section 149, of Indian Penal code. The conviction of accused 2 under section 326 read withs.34 of the Code was bad in law.
