The petitioner, a citizen of India, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights. The respondents, however, did not take any action against the petitioner. The petitioner filed an appeal before the Customs and Excise Authorities under Section 128 of the . The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on the ground that there was breach of fundamental right. The High Court held that the petitioner had no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that (i) the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse; and (ii) the respondents had not taken any action under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The customs authorities are right in holding that no question of the enforcement of a fundamental right arises in article 32 of India. [626C] 1.2 In view of the aforesaid, it is clear that relief under Article 226 of the Constitu tion is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [625D] 1:3. The remedy under Article32 is wholly inapplicable to the facts of this instant case. It has further to be reiterated that for enforcement Of fundamental right which is dependent upon adjudication or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it will not automatically involve breach of the fundamental right for the enforcement thereof. [650E F] 1 :4. The relief under article 32 is wholly unnecessary in view of section 15(1)(b) of the , which provides that the rates of duty and tariff valuation if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the dates on which goods are actually removed or removed from such warehouse. [656F G] 1 5. The provisions of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot be said that there is breach of a right. Whenever a person complains and claims that there has been a violation of law, it does not automatically involved breach of any fundamental right, for the enforce ment of such rights depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a statute for whom elaborate procedure was pre scribed. [646G H] 1 6. The Court is clearly of the opinion that relief contemplated by Article 32 is entirely inappropriate in this case and the application does not lie under Article 12 of the Consti tution.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of a bungalow. The sale was confirmed by the Court of Wards and the sale was set aside on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability of the sons to discharge the debts of their father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on pious obligation of the son who has been receiving a monthly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in execution of the payment order. [44 C] (ii) The debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the share of the appellants did not pass to the auction purchasers. [45 D] (iii) The High Court erred in holding that what could legally be sold under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code was the right, title and interest of the defaulter i.e. of the father alone which could not include the share in the other members of the joint family. [46 E F] (iv) The obligation of a son to discharge debts of his father does not cease merely because he has received a monthly salary or remuneration from a bank and the property is sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end. [47 F G] (v) The legal position is that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and (1) A.I.R. (2) (1878) L.R 14 I.A. i. (3) A,I. R. (4) All. 953, followed. (vi) The right, ownership or interest of a judgment debtor is based upon the pious duty of the children to discharge their debts and that the property was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the decree holder which were characterised as "perfectly" in the hands of the judgment debtor.

The petitioners, who were the police officers of Delhi Administration and the police officials, were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420, 468, 471 read with section 34 I.P.C., for having committed various offences punishable under sections 109/109/109 I. P.C. The prosecution alleged that the petitioners along with others had entered into a conspiracy to cheat the Government of India and to cheat them in respect of certain properties. The petitioners were charged under section 120B read with Section 34 I P. C. for having caused wrongful gain to themselves by using forged documents, forged documents etc., and also for causing wrongful loss to the Government. The Committee found that the accused had committed offences punishable u/s 109/10/109 of I.p.C.; that they were not guilty of any offence under section 8 B of the Act; that they had failed to account for the loss caused to the government by using the forged documents and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 178 I.PC. The committee, therefore, recommended the transfer of the petitioners in these cases to the Delhi Administration. The Delhi Administration filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order of the Committee. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Committee had not properly considered the case of the accused and that it was not competent for the Committee to pass any orders on the complaint. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 before asking them to get into witness box for being cross examined; and (ii) the action of the committee in asking them not to be cross examined at the end of the inquiry was discriminatory. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Committee should not have in the circumstances of the case directed the filing of a complaint against either of the Petitioners for an offence under sections 178 I P C.

The petitioners, who were seven in number, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8(i) of the Rules, by which they were exempted from payment of lump sum in lieu of tax on fares and freights. The petitioners contended that the Act was unconstitutional as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on their fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19 (1)(g) of Constitution and that the impugned Act infringed articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31(2) and 301 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of R.8(i), which are in conflict with the provisions contained in section 3 of the Act, are unconstitutional as offending article 19(6) of our Constitution. The Act and the Rules framed thereunder are not ultra vires the State Legislature. The tax is still on passengers and goods, though what it is to be is deter mined by the amount of fare or freight. The levy is therefore without authority of law. The provisions of the R. and the notification are valid. The State of Rajasthan vs Sri Ram Narain, ; , followed. The Punjab Passengers and goods Taxation Act, 1959 and the Notification issued thereunder were challenged as unconstitutional on the ground that it was discriminatory and ultra vires. The contention that the tax is without authority, because, under the Act it is optional, and involves payment of tax even when no passengers or goods are transported, cannot be accepted. The proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax payable on fares or freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The notification does not cease to be a tax on passengers but only terminates the journey from one point to another. The word "tax" is used in the context of the provisions relating to taxation and it cannot be said that the Legislature intended to make a distinction between the tax on goods and the tax which is imposed on passengers, though the amount is measured by the fares and the freights, and therefore, the tax was beyond the Act by making the lump sum payment compulsory. The expression "taxes" in section 2(1) of that Act includes taxes on passengers. The words "tax on passengers" are not defined in the Act but only those which are imposed as a tax or as a fee for the purpose of taxation. The definition of "taxation" in the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act is wide enough to include all taxes levied under the State Acts and the rules made thereunder. The fact that the word "fee" is not defined by the Act does not mean that it is not a tax. The Legislature has not used the expression "fee". The tax, however, is still a tax in respect of passengers and Goods. The distinction between a tax and a fee is not admissible because the tax may be optional but involves payment for services rendered. The difference between the two is not an essential element of taxation but is one of fact depending on the circumstances of each case. The question whether a tax is imposed under the Entry, and if so, what is the nature of the tax, does not arise. The power to levy taxes is derived from the Constitution and it is the duty of the Court to interpret the provisions in the light of the principles laid down by this Court in State of Madras vs Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt. [1954] S.C.R. 1069, followed.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The workmen were retrenched from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour Court directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The appellant challenged the award in this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective on the date when they were sought to be retrenched. [567F] (2) The Labour Court has awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to he raised. [568F G] (3) The award shall stand modified accordingly. [569G H] (4) The direction for reinstatement is not a regular court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. [570A B] (5) The only limited question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back Wages to the respondents workmen. [571C D] (6) The High Court has not exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 but has exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with the Award. [573F G; 571A B, E] (7) The question whether the workmen should be awarded full or partial back wages is no more open to challenge. It is no longer open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. [574F G, 571A] (8) The Award shall stand accordingly modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the sacrifice on management 's part too.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the conviction and death sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the deceased was last seen in the company of the accused at the time when he went to the house of the deceased; (ii) the evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination of the dead body could not be put in evidence under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the prosecution case was highly improbable and that the High Court had erred in holding that the accused and none else who was responsible for the murder were guilty of the offence of committing the death of the wife of the first appellant; (iii) the High court had wrongly relied on the evidence given by the doctor to convict the accused under section 201 Indian Penal Cods. The prosecution case is that the dead bodies of the daughter of the second appellant were recovered from the house and the deceased died after the commission of the murder, as a result of her adulterous conduct; (iv) the statement of the mother of the child recorded by the Magistrate was recorded during the investigation of the case and as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 Cr. P.C., the same is inadmissible in evidence; (v) the accused had no motive to commit the murder and that he had been falsely implicated; (vi) the recovery of the clothes of the son of the third appellant from the place where the dead dead body was recovered, was not admissible in evidence as it did not relate to the commission by him of the crime. The trial court acquitted the accused on the ground that the statement recorded during investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specifically empowered was inadmissible in Evidence; (vii) the dying declaration made by the deceased before her husband could not have been used against her as evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act, and (viii) the fact that the relations of the two accused with the deceased were shown to be strained would not affect the prosecution story. The State appealed to this court. HELD : (i)(a) The High court was right in holding the appellant guilty of offence under section 304 Part I I.P.C. [11 D] (b) The statement recorded by a magistrate under section 161 Cr.P C. is not admissible under section 162 Cr. It is also the case of the prosecution itself that the appellant had gone to see film show at Kotkbai on that day and talked to him. The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that it was the accused who committed the murder. [12 E] (c) The fact that a person who was not in a position to make a statement under section161 Cr. is made an accomplice does not affect his conviction unless he is corroborated by some other evidence. [13 G H] (d) The evidence of doctor who examined the deceased and recorded her dying declaration, is admissible in terms of section 164 I. P C. [14 F] (e) The accused was not responsible for murder of Churi deceased as a consequence of which she died. It was the case that none else had insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. The fact of the matter is that there was nothing to show that the police was aware of the death. [15 G] (f) The prosecution has failed to establish beyond any doubt that Churi had been born to her as a outcome of her husking and that it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon the accused to make an untrue statement.

The plaintiff sued for recovery of a sum of Rs. 80,507 7 8 being the aggregate amount due and payable by him under the mortgage deed dated 12th June 1936. The defendants pleaded that each of them was liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed the decree holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove a contract to the contrary, and that the defendants were entitled to recover only Rs. 20,000 as the aggregate sum due and not Rs. 40,253 11 10 8 being interest due on that amount at the contract rate in the mortgage from the date of payment to the date on which the decree was passed. The plaintiff appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The suit was barred by section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the Contract Act, and the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for sale of the mortgaged property. The suit must be dismissed as not maintainable because it was not based on any contract to which the provisions of the Specific Relief Act applied. (ii)The suit was not barred by limitation under section 92. The question whether the suit was within time or not was one of fact and in law. The words "subrogation" were used in order to give a right to redeem the whole of the balance of the property mortgaged. In the present case, the plaintiff 's father had not used the word "subjective" he had asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs,. 20,006 7 8 with interest against either defendant I would direct that his liability be reduced to Rs. 2,500 and that his liabilities be reduced accordingly. (iii)The plaintiff 'S 's suit was therefore barred by time. The relief in the present suit was for recovery only Rs 20,020 7 8 and not the aggregate value of Rs 40,255 11 10 with interest.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The appointments were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment by Selection) Rules, 1973. The appellants applied for the posts of Assistant Engineers, and they were selected in the open competition. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C., 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, [1988) Suppl. SCC, 657, relied on. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violationof the decisions rendered by this Court. [497C] 1.2 The Rules were clearly in contravention of the ratio laid down by this court in Ashok Yadav & Anr. vs state of Haryana and Ors., ; , and Mohinder Singh Garg vs Union of India & Ors,, J.T. on 4th September, 1991. [498F G] 1:3. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [500G H] 1 :4. The Rules have been clearly in breach of the dictum laid down in Ashok Kumari Yadav & ors. vs Union Of India & Anr., ; and Mohinder Sharma Garg vs Delhi Administration & Ors , J. T. on April, 1990, referred to.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the prosecution has failed to prove conspiracy; (ii) the evidence of conspiracy is exculpatory in nature and, therefore, would not be admissible against the co accused; (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [415C] 2.1 In the instant case, the prosecution witnesses have not spoken about any confession. They have also stated that they were meeting Sadanand at the jail. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadhanand on the night of occurrence following the incident, the Collector was not found there. It is well settled that the confession of co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In the present case, Sadanand had continuously been detained for meeting Sadarayan and his brother, P.W.4 on 11th April, 1983. The defence has also led evidence that after arrival of the deceased, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they had been meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [413D E] 2:2 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ques tion in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. The conclusion drawn by the High court, therefore cannot be sustained. [414F G] 3.1 The prosecution case has been corroborated by the evidence led by the prosecution and the defence witnesses. It has further come out that during the course of investigation, the story of bribing the jail officials was introduced. The State should also have taken some more care to see that everywhere in the police station is plugged. This kind of evidence cannot be accepted. [416H; 415A] 3:2. In a criminal case involving murder of a District Magistrate, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a person who was not present when the crime was committed following the raid on the Ashram. The trial court has failed in not properly appreciate the evidence and has not given any reasons for holding that it had no jurisdiction to take a view different from what has been stated about him by the trial court. [ 415C D] 3 :3. In such circumstances, the conviction of the appellant is not sustainable. [ 416D E; 417A] 4:1. The evidence of the prosecution witness on this score should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand was taken into custody following the search of the Ashram, better investigation had been expected and he had taken great pains to ensure the same. This is a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accept.

The appellant company was a textile mill and its workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. The company had to pay dearness allowance in addition to dearness allowance for the period during which it was paying the same. The Tribunal found that the company was not engaged in the same line of business and therefore comparison could not be made with as similar concerns. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal has gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula for fixing wage scales. It has also been urged on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal should have taken into account comparable concerns in the matter of fixation of wages and dearness allowance. The principle is that in applying industry cum area formula for fixation of wage scales, the Tribunal must first take into account the total wage packet (i.e. basic wage and dearness allowances) and then compare it with the total pay packet of comparable concerns. If there are a large number of concerns in different regions, the tribunal should adopt the same pattern as in other comparable concerns for fixing wages and Dearness allowance. In doing so the Tribunal has put the subordinate staff in the similar scale of dearness allowance as clerical staff. The fact that some exemplars were filed before it was not sufficient to show that the total number of workmen in the case of the appellant company would be more than the lowest, it cannot be said that the entire industry part of the formula is different from the basic wage packet of the comparable concerns and therefore the Tribunal had committed an error in applying its own method. (ii) The principle of fixing wages for subordinate staff has been evolved by this Court in the cases of Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , followed.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Bombay. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants for redemption of the mortgage and possession of the lands on the ground that they were agriculturists, that the appellants had no right to redeem them as the mortgagors had not been made parties to the suit; that the suit was barred by limitation under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal held that the Rajinama was a complete relinquishment of his interest and that the respondents were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 74 was not applicable to the present case as the appellants were agriculturists and the respondents could not claim redemption of Shiddappa 's one half share in the suit land. The Rajinma was the registered occupant and the Rajinspec tively did not purport to transfer the interest of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that is, the appellants ' right to get possession by adverse possession was extinguished and that as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse Possession. Held, further, that under section 73 of the Act the Rajenama was only a complete relinquish ment of his rights and did not create any relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers. The appellants had not merely an interest in the land but also a right to have it partitioned. The suit was therefore barred by time.

The respondent, a manufacturer of stencil paper, was assessed to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 on the ground that carbon paper was not "paper" as defined in the Act and was liable to sales Tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to the end of March 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal which held that the carbon paper did not lost its character because it was not a paper as defined by the Act. On further appeal, the High Court held that it was a paper which was used for printing, writing or printing, or for packing, or in any other manner, and that the respondent was entitled to claim that carbon Paper should be taxed at the rates specified in Schedule I to the notification and that it could not be said that ribbons were "paper other than hand made paper". The High Court also held that there was no force in the contention of the appellant that carbon copy was not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter. In appeal by certificate, the appellant contended: (1) that carbon copies were not " Paper other than Hand made paper" as used in Notification No. Sales tax Act, 1947; (2) that ribban was not paper within the meaning of Entry 2 of the Notification and therefore the turnover could not he subjected to salestax at the time and at 6%. HELD: (i) The mere fact that the word "paper " forms part of an denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838C] (ii) The word " paper" in the common parlance or in the com plaints, is not determinative of the questions whether the articles are paper as ordinarily understood. It is only when it is used for bearing, writing, or printing or for making packing that the words "popular sense" that sense which people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [ 838E] (iii) The use of the word 'paper ' in Notification Nos. 1/66 and 2/68, dated July 1 1967, shows that the expression "paper as generally known" means paper which is used in the same way, ribbon is not a part or a part thereof. [873F] (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that carbon sheets are not paper as envisaged by Entry 2, of the notification.

The appellant was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. It had its head office at Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh and it had its branches at Hapur. The respondents were employed by the owners of the appellant Mills at Hapur and they were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10/ per month. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents from service on the ground that they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thereby contravened the provisions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal but the High court dismissed it holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. On appeal by special leave, Held:(i) It is well settled that an employer can transfer his employee from one concern to another if he has the right to do so under the contract of service or under any statutory provisions. The essential distinction between a case where there is no express agreement between the parties and the other in which the employer has the power to transfer the employee is really to make a new contract between them. (ii) It was not necessary for an employer to have the right of transfer transferred by an employer from one establishment to another, because, as in the present case, the appellant had no such right. The question whether the appellant has the rights to transfer an employee under the terms of his employment or under a statutory provision is really a matter of fact to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. (iii) It would not be correct to say that the employer in the instant case has no such power. The employer in this case had no right to transfer his employees from one branch to another. The respondent was employed by him as a concern with the appellant at Hapur, and he was running only one factory at Hapur at a time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Bulandshahr. (iv) It could not be said that the respondent had knowledge of the same. The fact that the two factories are distinct entities, situated at different places and to import a term conferring a right on the employer to transfer them to another place does not prevent the employer from transferring an employee if he had the right under the agreement of service.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948 as a limited company. The respondent, the principal employer of the appellant company, was incorporated on July 1, 1948 under the . It had its registered office at Bombay and its branches at Ahmedabad. The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V were in force. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended and it includes among other items, (i) payment of contributions and provision of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and (ii) . . . The appellant company claimed that the contribution payable under Chapter V A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or the conferment of any benefit to the employees. The High Court held that the payment of special contribution under Chapter IV A by the appellant for the period May 31, 1969 to March 26, 1973 was illegal and directed the payment by an employer 's special contribution in accordance with the provisions contained in Chapter VA. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contributions payable under Ch. V A were fee and not a tax; that the Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service, or conferment of an benefit to a company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contribution payable by the employer under Chapter VI A is a fee. It is not sufficient if it has sufficient constitutional protection. [1089G] 2. The expression "fee" in Ch.V A is used to denote the amount of fees and not the tax. The word "fee ' is used in connection with the payment or non payment of the general revenue. The words "taxes on the wages of the employees" are not defined in the Act. They are not intended to be exhaustive. [1189B] 3. The definition of "fee", as given in Ch V A, makes it clear that the expression "taxation fee" is used only for the purpose of levying and collecting contributions under Ch VA and not for conferring any benefit on the appellant. [1289C D] 4. The object of the Act is to provide a fund for the benefit of employees in the case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provision for certain other matters in relation thereto. It does not require that the fund should be paid out of the fund. [1390D E] 5. The appellant 's argument proceeds on the fundamental misconception that the payments are made by the employers under ChV A. [1589E F] 6. The Act does provide for the rendering and payment of any benefits to the employee. It provides for the making of contributions of the nature of those contemplated by the for the benefits to be given to the workers under the Act, and the cost of these benefits will not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the said fund only. [1689G H] 7. The scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they are, in the cases of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the other case, its connection with levy. Corporation(4) have upheld the levy of special contributions as a tax. [1789G; 1090A] 8. The question whether special contribution should be indirect and remote has to be decided on the facts of each case. It cannot be said that the legislature intended to make any law with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II. [1889B C] 9. The purpose for which a Fund may not be expended is to be gathered from the scheme itself, only the employers ' contribution under the , constitutes only a fee, and not tax. It has sufficient Constitutional protection.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services as daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands were of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management, however, did not give them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. The petitioners filed writ petition in this Court challenging the order of their absorption and the management contended that since there was no work available for them, there is no question of regularising them and giving them the same pay as the regularly appointed workers. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the Regular workmen and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [610G H] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This Court has held in several cases that regularisation of daily rated workers and payment of equal pay to them under the Scheme is purely on humanitarian grounds so far as the requirement of the Project, they cannot be absorbed against the same or not. [625H; 625A] 3. The doctrine of regularisation is not applicable to the case of a casual worker and payment for regularisation is purely in the nature of deferred wages. [650B C] 4. The concept of regularisation has been evolved by this Court in several decisions, including the decision in State of Orissa vs Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei & Ors., ; , followed. 5. In view of the clear findings that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work for them the Court directed their absorption. [651B C, G] 6. The Court has not found any ground to interfere with the High Court 's decision in view of clear findings supported by evidence that there were no vacancies nor work available at all for absorption. On these facts, the question of directing their absorption or regu larisation does not arise.

The appellants were the plaintiffs in a suit for possession of certain properties. The respondents contended that the sale was not real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh, but only to the extent of 2 1/2 as share belonging to them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants had failed to prove their right to the property and that the mortgage in favour of the plaintiffs was a mere device to defeat the claim of the appellants. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0. r. 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in view of the provisions of section 8 of the Bengal Money Lenders (Regulation) Act, 1932, the appellants could not be estopped from challenging the validity or otherwise of the said mortgage. On a further appeal to this Court, HELD : The suit was maintainable. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the conviction and sentence on the ground that the omission to comply with the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with by the police officer in charge of the investigation. Held, that the failure to comply the provisions Of section 173(1) of Code of criminal Procedure was fatal to the trial. The omission to do so did not affect the validity of the trial unless it was shown that the accused had been prejudiced in his defence. The defect in the trial was curable by reference to section 537 of the code, as no case of prejudice had been made out against the accused. The provisions of section 537(3), Cr. P.C., were not mandatory but only directory and did not require compliance with the requirements of section 173. The fact that the appellant got the necessary copies of the depositions of the witnesses in the Sessions Court before the statements of the prosecution witnesses were recorded by that court, could not affect his trial unless he succeeded in showing that they had been prejudice in their defence. Gurbachan Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. The word "shall" used in section 537, Cr.P.C. is not mandatory and only directory, because an omission by a police officer to fully comply with certain provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. The irregularity in the procedure for inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial is curable under section 537 Cr.p.C.; it has not been shown that any prejudice had taken place in the defence of the accused by reason of his non compliance with those provisions. Gurbyn vs State of Bombay, ; and Gurbachan vs The state of Punjab (A.I.R. 1956 S.C, 415), referred to.

The appellant Municipality, which was constituted under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, had been directed to stop the discharge of effluents in the manner specified in the notice issued by it. The respondent Municipality filed a petition for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the appellant not to take any action against the respondent Municipality for failure to comply with the requisition made by it under section 153A(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the provisions of section 153 A were ultra vires and void as it would be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right conferred on the citizens by article 19(1)(C) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of sections 153A and 153A are not intended for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. They are designed to achieve the purpose of preventing a nuisance which may be caused by the discharge or otherwise of the effluent. [395 D] (ii) The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective opinion of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge and the discharge. The purpose of the section is to enable the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists, to issue a notice requiring the person to whom the notice is given to show causes why he shall not be ordered to arrange the discharge thereof in the way specified in sub section. [397 D E] (iii) The purpose for which the notice has been issued is to give an opportunity to the person concerned to show that the nuisance in question exists and to agree to comply therewith, and it is open to the Municipality to require a special judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire into the matter.

The appellant was found in possession of certain goods. The police recovered from him a large number of parts of railway machinery and kept them in 11 bags. The appellant 's explanation that the goods were being used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway was not accepted by the trial court as correct. The High Court dismissed his bail bond but on appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution must prove that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise. HELD: (i) The prosecution must also establish that the article seized were Railway stores within its meaning. [192 G] (ii) The appellant was not called upon to prove that goods were railway property within the definition of section. [195 B C] (iii) The evidence in this case did not establish that articles seized from the appellant were railway properties within the purview of section 3. [196 F] (iv) The seizure of the goods was effected by the police and not by the appellant himself. [197 G] In the present case, the search which took place in the presence of the appellant and the manager of the transport company revealed that a large quantity of parts were contained in 23 bags of metal scrap booked the same day by the appel lant for consignment to Jullunder. The evidence did not prove that articles were railway assets within the description of section ' 2 of Act. [198 G] Moyalal Rostagir vs The State, ; , followed. (v) The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to establish that they were the property of a Railway Administration.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondent on the ground that they had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate court affirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the judgments of the courts below and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or compromise is established. [10E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not been able to prove that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of section 2(1)(iii) of the Act and also that they were entitled to be in possession since the statutory tenancy was amended by Section 3(ii). The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of tenants in respect of commercial tenancies on the death of the tenant after termination of the tenancy, as has been done in the case of heirs of the tenants of residential premises, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs should be the heirs. [11E F] 1:3. The mere circumstance that in a statute no provision had been made for the heirs to become entitled by virtue of the provisions of the statute would not make any difference so far as the present case is concerned. [12F G] 1 :4. In the absence of any specific provision, the legislature could not have intended that those heirs should continue in possession as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised property governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act. [13F G; 14A] 1 5. The High Court was, therefore, right in holding that the appellant is entitled to continue to remain as a statutory tenant even after the termi nation of the contract till a decree for ejectment against him is passed, continues to have an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises and tenancy rights in respect thereof are heritable. [14D E] 1 6. The question whether the appellants are tenants within section 13(1) (iii) or not has to be decided on the facts of each case.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Employees Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 to all its workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees ' Provident Fund Act applies. The employees also submitted their claims for bonus and gratuity. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees provident fund Act. The Tribunal held that the benefit of the Provident Fund was not extended to any additional categories of workmen. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the State Government is the financier of the Boards which charges interest on loans advanced to the Board and that the employees who are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not be covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Provident Fund is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion while the fact that the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer is to be taken into consideration. [47 D] (2) The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a Statutory obligation and it is a specific proportion while taking credit for any subvention from the State Govern ment. [48 E] (3) The Board has to pay interest on the amount of provident Fund and gratuity to the employees. [49 G] (4) The contributions to the development fund are statutory obligations and are a definite percentage whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the deprecia tion reserve. [50 F] (5) The scheme under section 59 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 provides that as far as practicable and after taking credit, the Board shall carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss.

The respondent husband filed a petition for maintenance under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate passed an order of maintenance to the wife and directed her to pay Rs. 500/ per month as maintenance from the date of application till the date she was actually paid. The respondent filed revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the woman to refuse her to live in the husband 's house and hence she is not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live at the husband merely because her husband was impotently placed under the influence of her husband, and that this salutary provision which was introduced with the clear object of arming the wife with a cause of action for refusing to live separately from her husband ', should be regarded as just ground or reasons for the husband to refuse the wife 's refusal to live together with her father.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for declaration of his title and for possession of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. The defendant contended that by virtue of these orders the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had been transferred to the State of Saurashtra, the Government of Saurashtra recognised the said Resolutions dated 19th January 1948 and 29th February 1948 as being binding on the plaintiff. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of any portion of the property. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that the title to the suit land was never recognised by the Union of India or the State Government and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show that as early as July 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of the erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the Union. The High Court also held since the plaintiff had not shown possession of these lands within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit for possession based on title to that property and the defendants had denied title. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the State had admitted the ownership of the lands in question and the structures vested in the Defence Department from the date of Financial merger and when the State took over the land, there was nothing on record to show as to how the Municipality was formally handed over the lands. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff has not shown that the Municipality is formally handedover the land in question, that its right over the suit premises and the buildings known as Rasala Lines are not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the written statement they did not claim the structures as belonging to the Municipality. [232G] 2. The State Government has corrected themselves in their communication dated 6th May, 1952 and stated that the claim of the plaintiff that the lands were vested in it was erroneous and that it had no jurisdiction to give a finding on title of the appellant even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. [231A] 3. The fact that the Government had corrected themselves did not mean that the land was vested in its full sense, but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the land. In the instant case, the Resolution No. 77 dated 29th Feb., 1948 by which the entire property was transferred to them by the orders of their Highness, Bhavnagar, State in 1948 and they are collecting the Revenue from the farmers. As seen earlier, possession of lands was also not taken by the Municipali ty at any time. In fact, it may be mentioned that the government of Saurashtra had corrected itself in their communications dated 6 5 1952 and 7th May 1952 and that they were collecting the revenue from the agriculturists. [234B C] 4.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947, and was convicted by the Judicial Commissioner. The Judicial Commissioner on appeal affirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of fine. On a reference made by the High Court of Bombay, the Judicial Commis sioner held that the appellant was not an officer within the definition of section 2(9), Indian Penal code and therefore he was not a public Servant within the mischief of section 3 Of Act II Of 1947. The appellant contended that the words "any person" in section 21 (9) were wide enough to include all railway servants from the definition, and that the provisions of section 137 of the Railways Act did not exclude all railway employees from the purview of the Act. Held, that an officer in the service or pay of Government performing as such a public duty entrusted to him by the Government and was therefore a public servants within the scope of section 6(1) Of the Indian Railway Act IIof 1947. Section 21 (10) of Indian Railways Act, 1890, which declared "every officer in any service or payment of Government" to be a public officer, was not ultra vires the Constitution. The words "other than a railway servant" in the definition were wide and comprehensive enough to cover all railway officers from the class or category of persons specified therein. The word "officer" in s. 21(10) meant only those who are employed to exercise the powers of Government and not those who perform any public duty. The expression "any officer" in that section was wide enough, to include a person performing a public function entrusted to an office for the performance of some public duty, and therefore, a public authority within the ambit of section 1(9).

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for recovery of a sum of Rs. 17,794/6/6 as arrears of land revenue due from him on account of the sale of his share in the property. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court and the first appellate court upheld the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of land was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court also held that a part of the said building was exempted from attachment, and sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Appellants that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from the attachment and sales under clause(ccc), but was in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery, of revenue due to the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect of the Respondent 's half share in a property was not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance thereof. [848C] 2. Section 60(1) provides that where an attachment and recovery of revenue is made under the provisions of the Act, the following particulars shall not be liable to such attachment or sale, namely: (a) name of the judgment debtor; (b) the amount due from the judgment debtors; (c) the date on which the decree was passed; (d) the name and address of the person who is ordered to pay the debt; (e) the names and addresses of the persons to whom the decree has been passed; and (f) any other particulars as may be prescribed. [884D E] 3. The words "such attachment or sales" in the proviso are wide enough to include the attachment, sale mentioned in sub section(1). The expression "such order" is not defined in the Code but is used in the sense of an order made under any other law for the time being in force. [881E] 4. Section 59 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1939 provides that the provisions contained in sections 60 and 61 shall apply to all suits and proceedings pending on the date of commencement of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1976. The opening words of sub section 2 of section 60 are "The following property is liable to attachment and sold in execution thereof". [847F] 5. Section 61(1)(c) provides for sale of immovable property by public auction or by private contract. The expression 'such sale ' in the said proviso refers to the attachment of and sale mentioned therein. The proviso to section 60(i) is not attracted to an attachment, but is in pursuance to the order passed by an Officer authorised to take action under the Act for realisation of revenue dues. [851C] 6. Section 62 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that any property which is liable for attachment and sell in execution shall be deemed to have been attached and sold as if it were a decree of civil court. The provisions of section 61(2) are not applicable to an application under section 60 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [861D] 7. Section 63(1), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g) and (h) of section 8 of the Haryana Urban Rent Control Act, 1973 deal with immovable property in any proceedings other than those mentioned in execution.

The respondent, a retired Government servant, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59. The appellant 's claim for compensation under section 23(1)(a) of the , was rejected by the Special Deputy Collector on the ground that the value of the lands in question had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as at the date of death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. The respondent 's appeal against the order of assessment was dismissed by the Assistant Collector, who held that the valuation of the land in question was not correct and that the appellant had no right to claim compensation for the lands acquired by the Government. The High Court upheld the view of the Assistant Collec tor. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands still formed part of the estate of the deceased and that having regard to the glaring enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the land, the said lands had escaped assessment to excise duty; (ii) the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent 'rejected the claim on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands still form part of his estate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the High Courts is correct and must be upheld. [334C] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent was entitled to receive compensation for lands acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 which were valued at the market value of Rs. 100 per acre. The valuation for those lands adopted on the basis of the valuation made by the special Deputy Collector did not represent their correct market value which was clear from the glaring increase in the compensation awarded by the civil Court and the High court. [330D E] 2:2 In the present case, since the assessments were made pursuant to the impugned notice issued under section 59(a) they had been rightly assessed to duty. The assessment for those years adopted on that basis was clearly erroneous. [328E F] 3.1 The respondent had merely accepted the value as determined by the Revenue Officer in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore, the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of estate by undertaking rectification proceedings. [332F G] 3:3.

The appellant was elected as a Director of the Bank from the Brewery, Chandrapur District Central Cooperative Bank. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the bank from the said Brewery. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank Act, 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of that bank as per the provisions of section 73FF of the Act and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The Deputy Registrar, however, did not pass any order under section 77(1). The appellant challenged the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having ceased to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan before the notice was issued would not be material for taking action under section 79(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Act, 1961. [680B] 1.2 The disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21.10.86 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. [681C D] 1:3. The disqualification under section 73F(1), as a result of default, is common both for election and for continuation as a director in the Committee. The special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, and the disqualification as a consequence of his having committed default is extinguished and consequently the appellant is not at any stage eligible to challenge the election as a defaulter. [682F G] 1 :4. The word 'debt ' in section 73(1 ) of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act, 1925 has been used with reference to the person who has incurred the disqualification.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on September 1, 1977. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the order reducing the pension by 50% of his pension before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Govt 's order dated December 4. 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has power to reduce the amount or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [33B] 1.2 In the instant case, the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. Therefore, the order of punishment was unauthorised and illegal. [34C D] 1:3. In the present case, there is no dispute that the respondent had retired from the service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 30, 1977 and charges were served on him on October 16, 1978 after about a year of his retirement. The proceeding culminated into an order of the Government reducing the respondent"s pension by fifty per cent. The question is whether the State Govern ment was competent to take action against the Respondent by reducing his pension. [35D E] 1 :4. In view of the facts and circumstances, the Government had power to impose any punishment. [36E F] 1 Whether the State has no authority to initiate any proceedings against an employee for misconduct as he may have committed while in service or after the completion of his service. The order was passed on December 3, 1982. The Collector of Kolhapur held that the Respondent 's action was helpful to him by selling sugar in black market and it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government Servant. He recommended that since the respondent has already retired he should be given an opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure prescribed under Note 1 to Rule 33 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. This order was not challenged either before the State Legislature or before this Court.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's premises. The appellant filed an application under section 3(3) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for permission to sue his tenant. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the permission granted by him was invalid in law. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to eject the respondent from the premises. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the words "any person who is not a District Magistrate" in section 3 (4) read with section 16 are clear and unambiguous, and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil court is completely excluded in relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the Act; (ii) the word "any" used in section 2(g) of Act II of 1947, means "any persons who are not District Magistrate". The High court held that it was clear from the language of section 3 that the Commissioner had no power to pass an order on the application made by the landlord for permission. In this appeal by special leave, it was urged on behalf Of the appellants (i). that the words of section 2 (g) read together with section 3 and 16 are wide enough to include persons who were not District Magistrates; (2) that the word 'any ' in section 16(4) has been used in a wider sense than the word in section 15(1); (3) that section 3 had no application because the words 'any person ' have been used only in the same sense as in section 18 of the , and (4). HELD : (i)(a) The words "other persons" in sub section (2), read together, are clear enough to indicate that they are intended to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner. [563 D] (b) The word 'person ' has been defined in section 4(1) of U. P. Act II Of 1947 as including a person who was not a district Magistrate. Section 3(4), therefore, clearly contemplates that the District Magistrate may deal with the application for permission under sub section 1(3). [563 E] (c) The expression 'any persons ' in sub s.(2) of section 16 is wide enough and it must be held that a person can move the Commissioner under section 33(3), if he is satisfied that the order was passed without notice to the party affected by such order. Therefore, there is no doubt that the relevant provision of the statute did not intend, even prior to the amendment of 1954, to limit the jurisdiction to cases where irregularity or illegality had been committed by the District Magis trate in granting or refusing permission. [564 E F] (d) The language of sub section 2 of section 15 clearly indicates that the intention is to confer wider jurisdiction on Commissioner. The word "person" has been given a wide connotation and it means "a person who has been granted permission to file an application for obtaining a decree against the tenant". Therefore, the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the application was not maintainable. [565 G] (e) The High Courts were right in holding that the provisions of section 23(4)(b) read along with section 18 are wide and must be construed as they are and not to be given a restricted meaning.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Assistant Secretary to the Government of Punjab in January, 1973. He was promoted as Deputy Secretary to that Government on August 1, 1974. In July, 1975 he was promoted to the post of Joint Secretary to Government of India. On September 30, 1975, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of his promotion and also praying for a direction to the State Government to promote him from the date of his appointment as Joint Secretary. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence was not properly recorded by the Chief Minister. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before making the reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of the alleged misbehaviour of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Chief Minister of Punjab and the Chief Secretary to Chief Minister are the final authorities in the matter of appointment of Joint Secretaries to the various States. [642C] 2.1 Article 317(1) of the Constitution provides that the President may by order direct that a member shall be disqualified for being chosen as, or for being, a Member of any State Public Service commission if he is of opinion that in the interests of justice it is necessary to do so. [643D] 2:2 The word "person" in Article 317 (1) has been used in contradistinction to "State Public Service". In the context of Article 317, it cannot be said that a person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court will be disqualified if he has not been allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. [641E] 2(a) The word 'person ' is used in the widest possible sense and includes all persons who are not members of a Public Service Commissions. It is not necessary that each person should have the same knowledge as that of the person concerned. [651B C] (b) In the instant case, the appellant was not able to show that he had been falsely implicated into the charge of assault because he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Justice of Punjab & Haryana and the hostility of thejj 's husband and that, therefore, the allegation against him is not proved. [631C] (c) The expression "person aggrieved" in article 317(2) has to be understood in a broad sense and it cannot mean only a person aggrieved by an order of dismissal or removal from service. It does not mean merely a person against whom an order for punishment has been made but also a person whose conduct is found to have been proved to have committed misconduct. [621D] (d) The appellant was rightly convicted under section 161(1). He had been given the opportunity of being heard before he could be called upon to answer questions put to him as to whether he was guilty of any misconduct and, if so, what punishment he would be entitled to. [611F] (e) The High Courts have not properly appreciated the evidence in a case where the appellant is alleged to have incurred the displeasure of the Chairman of the Public Service Commis sioner. It has been held by this Court that it will not be conducive to justice to decide the Reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [601F G] (f) The question whether the appellant should be promoted or not is essentially one of fact and no person who had not filed any affidavit in the High Courts can be examined or cross examined as a witness, except with the leave of this Court. [591G H] (g) It is true that the Chief Ministers of Punjab are the ultimate judges of the Supreme Court but they have to be independent Judges.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. 1 of 1939), for a declaration that the trust deed dated June 30, 1948 executed by the deity installed in the temple was not a private one and the deity was installed in a temple by the members of the public or their descendants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the endowment was of a public nature and the idol installed in it was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the temple being a family temple, the deity must be regarded as a private and not a public endowment and that the mere fact that members of a community were allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members or the public had a right to worship in the Temple. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the deity did not make any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members of public. [830C] 2.1 The mere fact of worship would not determine whether the user of the temple by members, of the community is as of right; that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the dedication was of such a nature. [ 832E F] 2:2 In order to decide whether an endowment is of a private or of a Public nature it must be established that the intention of the testator or the founder was merely to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members thereof. [883G] 3.1 A to come to its decision that the property dedicated is of public nature, it must also be shown that the family had a share in the endowment. The mere factum of worship will not determine the nature of the endowment; it would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case whether the use of the property by members was as of necessity or for a religious purpose. [873A B] 3:2. In order that a public trust may be inferred from the conduct of the parties, the existence of a particular religious institution must be proved. A to take advantage of the position under law, it is not necessary that the performance of the duty by members should be in the hands of the strangers or members of their family or in the hand of the members who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the deity. [877C D] 3 :3. In the instant case, the evidence shows that the founder of the institution did not give any specific direction for offering offerings or contribution to be paid by members. The fact that member of the family used to come from a particular community which also shows that even if the family was to become extinct, the private nature of endowment was not to be changed. [878E F; 833A] 4.1 In order for deciding whether an institution is of such nature, the mere factum or quality of worship may not determine its nature. It is a contingent provision and here also the founders did not confer the duty of performing all the work on the members.

The appellant Bank was a contractor of the military and other authorities. The contract provided that the contractor would pay to the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills, and if the amount due under the bill was not paid within the stipulated time, the bank would be entitled to recover it from the appellant. The appellant Bank then filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge against the respondent for recovery of certain amounts due under a contract entered into by it with the military. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decree holding that there was no equitable assignment of the moneys due under bills and that the appellant was not entitled to attach it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement between the appellant bank and the respondent was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant 's debts under the contracts. The power of attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 was a specific engagement by the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund coming to the debtor or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order directing such person to pay such funds to the creditor. [607 D E] (ii) The power conferred on attorney coupledwith the endorsement thereon on the bills dated July, 19,1948 was a general engagement by an agent to pay off the debts due under contracts and was irrevocable. The endorsement on bill dated 7th July 1948 was merely an express engagement by Malayalam in favour of the appellant and endorsed on it. [707 E F] (iii) The endorsement in the bill of 1948 was not a clear agreement between Malhotra and the Bank that the debts owing to it would be payable out of its funds in the hands of the Government authorities. [777 G] (iv) The High Court was in error in holding that the respondent had no equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. [779 C D] (v) The order dated July 13, 1948, created an interest in a specific Fund and was merely authorised to act as his agent. On a proper construction of the document the conclusion is irresistible that there is an agreement between a debtor and a creditor that the loan owing to him would be made out of an express fund coming into the debtor 's name or in the names in payment of such bills or other amounts and to pay interest thereon. [780 G H] (vi) The words "any other person" in section 2(g) of the Act are clear enough to include a person who is employed by a creditor to do any act for him. The expression "any person" has been used in contradistinction to the word "person". In the context of the definition of "trustee", it is necessary to bear in mind that there must be an agreement by a person to whom money is due and endorsed by a bank or other authority to his creditors upon a persons owing money. [781 E F; 782 A] (vii) The word "trust" has not been defined in the Act. It has been defined as including any trust, grant, mortgage, charge, lease, agreement or contract of sale. The definition of 'trustee ' is an inclusive one and includes a person by whom money becomes due to the bank. [783 B C] (viii) The expression 'trustees ' in section 3(1)(a) of Act means a person whose principal object is to pay money to the trustee.
