The word 'truster ' has been given a wide connotation so as to include any person who may be employed by him for the purpose of obtaining or receiving, any money on behalf of the bank or for carrying out any contract with the bank in any manner whatsoever. [784 E F]. (ix) The definition is not exhaustive and does not cover all kinds of persons.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co., Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. Under that scheme, the appellant was to be paid Rs. 27,948/ as salary and allowances to its employees in addition to their salary. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary, the same was his salary as defined in section 17(1)(iv) of the Income tax Act, 1961 and therefore the said income was his income. The Appellate Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipts in question were profits in the nature of salary and not income. On further appeal by certificate, the High Court held that though the receipt was an income as defined by section 2(24), it could be included in the total income under section 56. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the said receipts were profits within the meaning of section 17 (3) (ii). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The receipt of Rs.27,948 by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High court.

The petitioners, who were butchers of the State of Bombay and whose names had been included in the Schedule to the Constitution challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Act (Act No. XIII of 1956) on the ground that it infringed their fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g), (6) and (7) of the Constitution, as they were not able to prove that they were carrying on their occupation or business. The petitioners contended that the impugned Acts infringed their right to carry on their trade guaranteed by article 19 (1) (g) and were void as offending articles 14, 19(i)(g) of Constitution. Held, that the Act was constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cow or female buffaloes. The Act did not infringe any fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(6). The Act was not unconstitutional on the grounds (1 ) that it violated articles 14 and 19(2) of Part III of the constitution, (2) that it contravened article 19 of the Consti tution and was therefore void. The impugned Acts were valid in their entirety and did not contravene any fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III. The Bihar Act was a total ban on the slaughter Of cows of certain ages and the petitioners could not be allowed to complain of any total prohibition of the right of butchers to carry out their occupation, or business; (3) that a total prohibition on the exercise of the fundamental right of the petitioners under article 14 was void as it contravened articles 19(l)(g); (4) that the provisions of the Act were not violative of article 19 and were therefore void; (5) that in view of the decision of this Court in State of Madras vs R. V. R. M. S. K. A. T., ; , the impugned Act was unconstitutional as it infringed articles 14 or 19(I)(g). The provisions of section 3(1) and section 4 of the impugned sections were not discriminatory but were only regulatory measures to prevent the slaughter, of cows and cale animals of all age and calve cattle. The provisions relating to the imposition of a total restraint on the carrying of cows in certain specified areas were invalid as they contravened articles 14. The State of Bihar vs R V. D. R., ; and State of Madhya Pradesh vs RV. R, ; , referred to.

The respondent was a public limited company which had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh. The Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and its employees were governed by the provisions of the Act. Under Standing Order No. (e) of the Standing Orders, the Company was to employ such persons as it liked to carry on any business or trade or business in accordance with the conditions of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of the said Standing Order. The respondent was employed by the company at Nagpur and was paid a salary of Rs. 400 per month. On his retirement, he filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from him. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the Standing Order did not apply to the respondent and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Standing order did not provide for any punishment or dismissal, (ii) the respondent was an employee within the meaning of the Central Act and an 'employee ' as defined in the local Act; and (iii) the Labour Appellate Tribunal had wrongly held that Standing Order NO. (f) did not cover the respondent. HELD : (i)(a) The Standing Orders do not apply in the present case to the Company. Standing Order no doubt does not provide that the employee should be an employee of the company but it is only where a person is employed by him in connection with his business that he can be said to be an 'workman ' within the definition of the expression for the purpose of the standing Orders. [471 B C] (b) The word 'employee" in the Standing orders means such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen, and under Standing Order (e), a workman means such category of employees which may from times to time he declared to have been employed. [473 D E] (c) The definition of an employee is not exhaustive but only illustrative. It does not exclude the application of the definition to the employees in the absence of any indication that they are workmen within the purview of the Industrial Disputes Act. [474 G H] (d) The expression 'employee " as defined for the purposes of the , includes a person employed in connection therewith, whether at Nagpur or Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Orders No. 1 and 2. [475 B C]. (e)(i) The words 'employee who is employed ' in Standing Order Nos. 1 & 2 are not 'workmen ' for the meaning Of the Act, but they are only those employees who are 'employees ', but all ' employees ' are not workmen ' for purposes of section 30 of the local Acts. [476 C D] (ii)(a). The definition clause in Standing Orders is wide enough to include a person who is an employee and not a workman. [477 E F] (iii)(b) In the present cases, the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental muster rolls. He was employed only at Nagpur. The fact that he had no ticket shows that he was not an 'employer ' within section 30. [478 G H; 478 A] (iv) The High Court erred in holding that Standing Orders apply to a workman who is not an employee under the management of the Company either at Nagpur, or Wardha and that the respondent who had no tickets issued could be said not to have his name included in his departmental muster roll. [479 G H].

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 66 on the ground that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as a separate Establishment because under the Act a company is itself an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been even earning profits, so that exemption could not he granted to this Company in respect thereof. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Alloy steel Project was owned, managed controlled and run by the Hindustan Steel Ltd., and therefore, the point raised had to be decided on the basis whether under the proviso to section 3 the Alloys Project was to be treated a separate unit for purposes Of computation of bonus under the provisions of the Payment Of Bonus Act; (ii) that the proviso of section 3 would not apply in such a case. HELD: (i ) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because Alloy 'Steel Project is owned, control and managed, by Hindustan Steel Limited it has to be held that under the Proviso to section 16(2), the Allit steel Project is an establishment of so much as the appellant company is an established one. [638 C D] (ii ) The proviso to sub section (2) of section 15 only comes in the way it bonus is paid in any year to the employees of all the units on the same basis for each unit, there will be no deduction at all. [643 E F] (iii) The proviso does not stand in the manner of this claim because there is no evidence that in any particular year after Alloyel Project was set up bonus was paid to the workmen of all units on that basis.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of rayon grade pulp a base material for manu facturing of synthetics or man made fabrics. The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. The appellant company claimed that it was manufacturing rayons and rayun ghats, which were used for manufac ture purposes and therefore, it was not liable to pay cess under Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. The claim was rejected by the Assistant Collector on the ground that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The sugar manufacturing industry does not fall within Entry No. 15 of schedule I to Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. [526B] 1.2 The sugar factory does not come within the purview of Entry 15 and a fortio ries are grown in a kitchen garden or in a farm and are used for the table. It is only where the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it is said to be that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [525C D] 1:3. The sugar industry does fall within entry 15 as 'processing oil industry ' and hence, a forpo ration of cess under Item 15 of Sch I to Act 36 of 1977 is not attracted. [25F G] 1 Whether a particular industry falls within Entry 14 or not must be judged by the predominant purpose and process and not by any ancillary or incidental process carried on by a particular industries in running its business. [26H; 526A B] 2.1 In interpreting the word 'vegetable ' one has to keep in mind the object for which the cess is made. If the botanic meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule I like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry 25. The word 'process ' has been used in common parlance in Entry 15. [27H; 527A B C] 2:2 In interpreting a word in a statute the Court has to bear in mind not only the object of the statute but also its purpose and purpose. [28F G; 527B] State of West Bengal vs Hans Raj Narain, ; , referred to.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application and held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for the purpose of carrying on the profession as a professional lawyer. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the Rent Control Tribunal and restored the order passed by the Rent controller. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the practice of profession is not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'business ' has been used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of an Advocate. As mentioned by us earlier, the word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the background of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context. [14G] 2. The word 'business" has been defined in Section 10 (3) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease Rent and eviction) Control Acts, 1960, as meaning the business carried on by an Advocate but not the carrying on of a trade or business within or outside the meaning Of section 10(1). [14H; 15A] 3. The term 'business is used in the sense of being understood to include any profession. It is not right to ascribe to the word ' business ' occurring in the Andhra Act, the same meaning that the word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. [15B C] 4. The words 'business carried on ' are used in two different senses and they cannot be given a restricted meaning so as not to include an profession. [16D E] 5. The definition of business in Section 2(g) (iii) is used for the purposes of that expression in the Act. It does not say that it should be a profession or trade or calling which is carried on with profit motive. [17E F] 6. The meaning given to the term ' business in section 10 (1) (c) is not correct. The use of the word "business" is used to denote the practice and profession of the profession of a Doctor. [18F G] 7. The concept of business occurring in Section10(3)(a)(ii) is intended to include a practice of business within its meaning. [19G H; 20A] 8. The dictionary meaning of the term "business ' is used not in any technical sense but as a trade, calling or profession which is capable of being carried on in the market. It may be that the profession is carried out by an advocate but it does not mean that the professional must be engaged in a profession. In the instant case, the respondent was a practising Advocate and he had no business connection with the profession. The High Court erred in holding that the appellant could not seek the eviction of his tenant on grounds of his requirement unless it was for the benefit of the landlord. [20E F; 21A] 9. The practice of law is 'business of an advocate ' within the definition of section 10. It cannot be restricted to trade or profession. A profession may be carried on without profit motive, but not with profit. [21D E; 22B] 10. The appellant was a professional practising Advocate. He had no legal right to carry on his business as an Advocate and that he could not claim the protection of section 9(3). [22E F].

The respondent, a limited company, entered into an agreement with the appellant for the purchase of certain goods. The appellant paid Rs. 4,00,000 to the respondent as advance and also agreed to pay interest at 6/9 per cent per month on the amount of Rs.4,00.000 from October 1, 1943. The respondent accepted the said proposal and thereafter a letter dated 29th September, 1942 was written by the appellant to the appellant stating that it was not liable for return of the advance money. The letter further stated that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The company filed a suit against the appellant claiming the balance of Rs 4,000 as damages and interest at 12 per cent p.a. from October 30, 1943 till realisation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The respondent was not a party to the agreement for sale of the goods because the appellant had no separate firm and bankers. It was not necessary that there should be separate firms or bankers. [577 F] (ii) The letter dated September 29, 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not cover the advances which either party or their separate firms may have made to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course. [578 C] (iii) The agreement was that the appellant would pay interest on the advance amount from October, 1943 to October 30. 1943. There was no express term in the agreement between the parties that it should be paid on demand or whether it was a case of payment of any sum by the respondent with the appellants under an agreement that the same would be paid at the time of the agreement. [579 G] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return on the deposit. It is not a case where the respondent giving loan to the appel lant for the obvious reason that the history of the transactions between the appellant and the respondent showed that the amount was advanced by the respond ent to the appellants. The mere fact that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners would not make any difference. [580 G H] (v) The evidence in the letter is that the sum of Rs 5,00000 was debited to India Supplies as deposit. The terms were also agreed upon by the parties. The transaction was between the appell lant and the appellant. There were negotiations between the respondent and the appellants for the payment of the balance amount. The agreement provided that the entire amount would be payable on demand and that the balance would be deposited in their respective account. The contract was between appellant and respondent. The parties agreed to a certain sum of money as deposit by the appe lant. The document also showed that there were negotiations for the advance made by the appellants with the respondent.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him. He made an application to this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging that order of detention. This Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no summons and the detenu had been directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, and since the detenu was already in custody he was not likely to be released. In the appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for put ting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is already in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining author ity in making an order of punitive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining au thority was aware of the fact that he was already In custody and yet he was sub ject to be tried by the Court on the basis of the facts of each case. [845C D] 2. The question whether a person is in detention or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case. If the detaining autho rity was satisfied, that his detention was necessary, it would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention. [852E F] 3. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there were no summons, the detenu could not be said to have been orally directed to appear before the Court and produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th February, 1986. The Court then referred to the Constitution Bench decision in Rameshwar Shaw 's case (supra) and left it as a matter to be decided in every individual case on its own facts. [851C D; 846F] 4. In Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan, ; , this Court held that merely because the detenu has been directed by the authority to attend office by an authority concerned, he was bound to comply with the direction and it would be a matter of jurisdiction to decide whether his preventive detention was warranted. [853E F; 847A] 5. The detaining authority is not required to wait for the order passed by him for putting him back to jail. It is only when the detenu remains in custody that he is entitled to have the order vacated. [850F G] 6. In a case where a person accused of certain offences who are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub jection to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not militate against the order be passed for Preventive Detention. [821F G; 851A] 7.

The petitioners are working as casual labourers in the Telegraphs Department. The respondents, however, contend that even though many of them have been working for the last ten years as casual labour they were not being regularly employed and hence they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc., which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regular employees. They are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. [602C D] 2. The scheme on a rational basis for absorbing as far as possible the wage related to the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled (Rs.210 270) skilled ( Rs.260 350) and as the case may be, plus DA/DA admissible thereon. [613D E] 3. The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to casual semi skilled/skilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than six months. These enhanced rates of pay are applicable to the semi skilled or Skilled labour who strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 272 and Rs. 260 350 as the cases may be. [625E F] 4. The benefits of increased rate of daily wage will not, therefore, be admissible in respect of the casual semi unskilled/s skilled labour in their case. [600F G] 5. The Government is now pleased to decide that the rates of wages for the semi unskilled labour employed in the complex shall be as under: (i) Casual labour who have not completed 720/1200 days of service over a period Of three years or more, with the department; (ii) casual labourers who have put in 240 days of continuous service over one year or more; and (iii) casual skilled labour who has not completed 7 months of service. [599F G H] 6. The petitioner belong to category of Casual Labour and are being paid wages and other benefits as are being given to the regular and permanent employees of the Department in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union of India to regularise the service of the petitioners. [ 600H; 600A B] 7. The provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, 1948 are applicable only to those who had completed 240/1200 day of the year of recruitment as per the Recruitment Rules and not to those already employed in regular vacancies as and when they occur. [700B C] 8. The payment of increased wages will be without prejudice to absorption of casual semi labour/sick workmen against regular vacancies, if any, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourer for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraphs department. [ 700C D; F G] 9. The arrears of wages payable to the casual labourers shall be paid within four months from today. These petitioners are accordingly disposed of.

The appellant, who was a resident of Bombay, filed a return under section 22(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on January 5, 1950, and claimed that he had submitted a return for the assessment year or a notice under section 24(2) of that Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the return was not filed within the time fixed by the notice but was filed in response to a notice issued under section 34(1)(corresponding to section 34 (1) of Act, and that the appellant had failed to make a full disclosure of his income as required by section 24. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the Department ought to have issued a notice for filing a return within the assessment years or a fresh notice under s.23(2), but the High Court on reference, held that it was not open to the Income tax officer to issue a notice in respect of a return filed after the expiry of the time prescribed by section 34, and therefore the Department should have issued the notice for the first time in pursuance of the notice. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the department ought to be directed to issue notice under the first proviso to sub s.(3) Of section 34 of the Act and if no return was filed within that period, the Department could not have issued any notice under that proviso. The second proviso to section 23(2)(a) of Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950 which provided for a " voluntary return" showing a non taxable income is still a good return for all purposes under the Act. It would be open to an assessee to make his return disclosing his total income and the Income Tax Officer may serve a notice upon him requiring him to furnish within such period not being less than thirty days a return. The proviso to s. 23(3)(a), however, does not require that the assessee should have filed a fresh return before he can be assessed under section 23 (4). It is only when the return filed on January 4, 1950 was a return of income, there is no question of issuing a notice to the assessee under section 20(2). The proviso cannot be read as requiring that the Income. tax Officer should have made an assessment under section 21(3), and therefore, the assessee could not be treated as a return showing an income below the taxable limit.

The Central Government issued a Notification dated 23.8.1982 under Section 9 of the , declaring that the employees of the Directorate of Industries, the Director of Industries and the employees working in the Directorate were entitled to be appointed as representatives of the employees in the Board of Directors. The petitioners who were working as members of the Board, challenged the validity of the Notification dated 3.9.1982 on the ground that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of a Board of directors and the choice between them is left to the Central Government. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In the appeals by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that the impugned notification merely requires the election or nomination of the members of one body, furnished by the representative Union, to be elected or nominated in such manner as may be specified by the Central Govern ment; and that the choice of the mode of appointment is left open to the Government, but it is not an unrestrained or unrestricted discretion, but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the board of Directors; and, therefore, the Act contemplates only election or nominations. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of leaving the choice to the Parliament is to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to make the appropriate mode of choosing the representatives of employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. If the Central Govt. were to provide for election in the manner chosen by it so as not to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives, appointment of one such person out from the panel furnish ed by the representatives Union would not he a perfect repre sentation in keeping on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election.

The appellant assessee was imposed penalties in respect of certain transactions. The Appellate Tribunal held that the penalties were not justified and directed the recovery of the amounts involved in the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had no power under section 255(5) of the Income tax Act, 1961 to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. HELD: The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Tribunal are not given the power to stay any proceedings relating to the recovery or collection of penalty. [661 B] (i) Section 255(6) does empower the Appellate tribunal to regulate its own procedure but it is very doubtful if the power of stay can be spelt out from that provision. The power of staying the recovery is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [671 C] (ii) Section 256(6), which deals expressly with a situation when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner, does empower him to grant time for the payment of the tax. The Act is silent in that behalf when anappeal is pending. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the power Of doing all such acts or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial. He was charged with having committed offences under section 7 of the Police Act, 1861 and under section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that he had received bribes in the discharge of his duties as a Station Officer and that he was found to have made a false report against him. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police and the respondent was charged under section 409 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The Trial Court held that the respondent had committed cognizable offences and therefore, the Superintendent was not competent to proceed with the departmental inquiry without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (1) of para. 486 of the police Regulations. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the departmental enquiry was only a continuation of the investigation and not a mere formality. The order of dismissal was not a judicial order but was an administrative order and therefore it could only be made by a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent; and as no prejudice was caused to the respondent, the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect the validity of the order of dismissing him. Held, further, that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the disciplinary enquiry. The departmental inquiry was only an administrative direction and not judicial or quasi judicial. The High Court had rightly held that there were no magical directions in respect Of the matter in question.

The appellant was appointed as a Director of Health Services in November, 1963. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Medical Officer in February 1971. In March 1972 he was promoted as Assistant Surgeon in January, 1973 and was posted as Additional Medical Officer. On August 8, 1972 he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the promotion of Dr. P.K. Sen on the ground that his appointment to the said post was not in accordance with the rules framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had no right to be promoted as he was eligible for promotion to supertime grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' Grade I and his being the seniormost and otherwise qualified, he should have been promoted from that date. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the constitution before the Delhi High Court contending that the promotion to the supertime scale II on February 8, 1971 was not according to the rules and therefore he could not be promoted to super time grade II. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court holding that since the post in question was in Specialists ' grade and the strength of Specialists" grade posts was reduced by 28, when any post out of these 28 posts added to super Time grade II was required to be filled in, it could only be filled up by promotion from amongst those already working as Specialists. The appeal filed by the appellant before this Court was dismissed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has not been able to establish that he was in specialists" post and was not qualified for promotion. [53E] 1.2 In passing a contention of the appellant that all 28 posts which were deducted from the strength were added to the speciality in which the post was created, it is difficult to entertain the contention that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into a specified post, he was not competent for promotion and therefore the contention of his being considered eligible for promo tion to super hoc grade II cannot be accepted. [54F] 1:3. The fact that the post from which the appellant was promoted was converted to a specified cadre does not mean that the person to be appointed to such a post would be one who is eligible to be so appointed to that speciality and not some one who was on top of the general seniority list in Specialist 's grade or general duty officers ' grade. [55F] 2.1 In passing the impugned order, the High Courts have failed to take into account the fact that there was some substance in the contention which was raised by the appel lant that whenever unspecified specialists were converted from a specified specialists` post to a certain specified post in a speciality it is an addition to the strength and the filling in of such post shall be governed by rule 8 (3). [55G] 2:2. The contention that the appointment of the aforesaid four respondents should be set aside has no merit in view of the fact, that there is nothing on record to show that the said four respondents were qualified for being promoted to that post. It is not shown that any such qualification was ever possessed by them. [56A] 2 :3. In passing an order of promotion, the appellant is not competent to give a direction that the appellan tant should be considered eligible to the higher post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of the said respondents.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to provide for the acquisition and transfer of land in excess of the permissible limit. Section 19B provides that if after the commencement of this Act any person acquires any land by inheritance or bequest or gift from a tenant, he may acquire lands in excess thereof. The appellant 's father purchased some lands in the State of Punjab on July 1, 1957. In the year 1956, the respondent filed a suit for possession of these lands and obtained an order of eviction against him. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Act. On appeal, the District Judge held that the appellant was entitled to get possession of the lands in question on the ground that he had acquired the same under section 19 B of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1956. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government or any officer em powered by it in this behalf shall be competent to utilize any surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected, or to be ejected under clause (i) of sub section (1) or section 9. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language of section 19A is wide enough to cover all cases where land acquired by the State Govern ment has been declared as surplus land and the surplus area has not been determined in accordance with the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. [632C] 2. Section 9B provides for the compulsory acquisition of land and section 9B empowers the owner who acquires any right to acquire land in the excess of his permissible limit, to make a declaration of his lands within a prescribed time. The power to acquire is conferred on the State by section 19(1) of the act. [32F] 3. Section 10A provides that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest or transfer, it may be acquired in any other manner and the State has no right to utilise the surplus land for resettlement of the tenants ejected or to become ejected under section 9 A. The word 'vest ' has been used in the widest sense in the sense that the expression 'vest" means the right to dispose of the property by transfer, exchange, lease, agreement or settlement. [33G H] 4. Section 16(1)(a) provides for acquisition and disposal of surplus area. It is not necessary that the surplus amount should be paid to the land owner before he can acquire it. The section does not contemplate any compensation being paid to a person who has acquired any land under section 10 A. [34H] 5. Section 18(1), however, provides for payment of compensation in lieu of acquisition of surplus land. It provides that where the State Govt. or any other officer empowered by it is satisfied that the excess land is required for resettlement, he shall make a return indicating the permissible area he desires to retain. The provision is not mandatory but directory and the section doesnot contemplate any contingency. [35H] 6. Section 17(1A) provides that in case of acquisition under section 18, the State may acquire any land either by inheritance, or bequest, or gift or gift. The use of the word 'transfer ' indicates that even though the source is inheritance the surplus will be adversely affected if gifts and other transfers which will skim off surplus were to be allowed. [36H] 7. Section 23(1 A) provides a machinery for making an application for compensation in respect of land acquired under section 16. The scheme of the section is that the compensation shall be at the disposal of Government for utilization as surplus area, if among the heirs it is not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10(A). [37H] 8.

The appellants claimed the Zamindari of Amarshah on the basis that the lands in dispute were impartible and they were under the will executed by Amarshi. The respondent contended that the suit was barred by section 14 of the Act. The Compensation Officer held that the respondent was entitled to the Zamindari as he was found suitable to hold the Zamindari and decided the claim against the appellants. The appellants preferred an appeal to the District Judge who dismissed the same holding that the will was not binding on the respondent. On further appeal, the High Court held that section 14 did not invest the Compensation Officer with jurisdiction to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3 of the , and that the decision of the Compensation officer was binding upon the appellants because no suit challenging the decision was instituted within two months from the date thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order of the compensation Officer under sub section (1) of section 14 is not a final order and conclusive. [334 B] The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs. The decision of tho Compensation Officer did not operate as res judicata between the parties. The question regarding the pro priction of the suit for setting aside the decision must be decided against the claimor in a summary inquiry held by the Compensation Offi cer, and if no suit was filed by the plaintiffs for setting it aside, the order becomes final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. [340 C D] The question whether the respondent had acquired proprietary rights under the notification issued under section 3(1) or the order of Governor dated November 9, 1951 was a pure question of fact and it was not shown that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of his power conferred by the Chanda Patent. [341 E F] The decision in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the death of Amarzart was binding on both the parties and the decision did not bind them.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the respondent tenant had committed breach of section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the provisions contained in section 12 (3) of Act do not apply to the suit and that the suit was governed by the provisions of section 2(1)(b) of that Act. On appeal the High Court held that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the service of notice under section 12 of the Act and it was not enough to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The provisions contained therein are as follows: "The Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1948, is applicable to the premises let out to the tenant. Section 12(2)(a) provides that where there is a dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3). The provisions of sections 12(1) (b) and (c) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and Establishment Act, 1949 are as follow: "12(1). Where at any stage of a suit or proceeding for recovery or damages recoverable under the Act, whether with or without a claim for possession of premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the grounds that the rent is excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the court shall pass a decree for eviction in any such suit for the recovery of the possession. " The Bombay High Court in Ambalal 's case (supra) held that in order to attract the applicability of section 11(4)(a), it must be non existence of the dispute at the date of the notice and such non existence must continue right up to the expiration of one year from the date on which the service is effected.

The Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors of the respondent company to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd., in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of shareholders of the company. The appellant, who was a director of the Respondent company, appointed one of the five directors of a company to act as directors of another company. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the Articles of Association of the Company, the Aluminium Company and its directors of respondent company held the shares as trustees and were entitled to vote in breach of trust, nevertheless, as between them as shareholders and the company they were the shareholders, and as such, have "a controlling interest" in the company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of the votes which under the articles of association of the appellant, carry the right to vote. The question for determination was whether the directors of an Indian Company were holding the majority or not. Held, that the shares of the respondents were held by them as trustees, and the appellant could not apply either of the tests mentioned in section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, to the present case. The words "a controlled interest" occurring in section 21 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, are wide enough to include all shares held jointly by the company and its shareholders. The word "control" is not defined in the Indian Companies Act, 1913, but it has been used in the sense in which it is used in English law. The term "control ' is not confined to a controlled interest but extends to a controlling interest only to a limited interest. The shares held as trustees are not controlled by the Indian Company Law and therefore they cannot be said to have "an controlling interest". The word control" has been defined in section 3(21), of the Income tax, Act, and it is not necessary that in order to have a controlling interests the person or persons who hold the majority shares must have a beneficial interest.

The respondent was promoted as Accounts Superintendent on 30th December, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent in the year 1967 and he was promoted later on to the same post on 1st October, 1968. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the promotion order dated 30th Decem ber, 1969. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the departmental examination before qualifying for promotion. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board had no power to modify or supersede the Regulations and the resolution of the Board was not applicable to the allottees. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Resolution dated 19th May 1969 is not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the Resolution it cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the resolution itself. [512E] 2. The resolution dated 19. May 1969 was not intended for the benefit of the allottees and therefore, it is contended that the allottees are by impli cation exempted from complying with the requirement of passing the examination and therefore allowed the Writ Petition. [511B C] 3. The Board by a subsequent Resolution had resolved on insisting on the passing of the examination. Examination for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be in sisted" the court found that it would mean that where the passing was insisted prior to that Resolution in the same shall continue to be insisted in future also, and if passing of such S.A.S.

The petitioner, a retired High Court Judge of the High Court, was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, District:agarh. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation in respect of contravention of fundamental right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to compensation for violation of fundamental rights under Article 14 of the Constitu tion, and directed payment of compensation to the petitioner. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) award of compensation is a remedy available in public law, based on strict liability for contravention of the guaranteed basic and indefeasible rights of the citizen; (ii) award is not to be understood as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental rights of citizen; and (iii) award in such cases is not the mode of redress available. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages awarded against the wrong doer for the tort committed by him. [608C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner has not only the power and jurisdiction but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of the Consti tution. The compensation was in the shape of compensa tion in respect whereof the petitioner had failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental right of life under Article 19(1)(g) of the Indian Constitution. [613D E] 1:3. In the light of the above principles, it is clear that the Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32 are unfettered and unguided.

The petitioner, a prisoner under the Prisons Act, 1894, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of the sentence were rejected by the President. The petitioner then moved this Court for relief by way of special leave against the order of the President dated May 2, 1981. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right but only a right to express any particular view or opinion. [1187G] 1.2. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to expressed any particular views or opinion but the right of the press, which includes freedom of the Press, is not a right which can be claimed by a press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. [1103A B] 1:3. The fundamental right to free speech and expressions guaranteed by article 14 of the constitution are not an unfettered right but a right conferred on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. It is not absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the press. [111D E] 1 :4. The Supreme Court has no power or jurisdiction to issue directions for the exercise of such freedom of expression by publishing a matter which does not invade the rights of other citizens and which does neither infringe the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. [112E F] 1 5. The Constitution has made a distinction between freedom of press and freedom of Press. It makes no difference whether the right is absolute or not. [113G H] 6. The petitioners have been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President has rejected the petitions. The authorities are bound to allow the petitioners to interview them. [114A B, D] 7.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the High Court in appeal reversed that decree and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered from the appellant. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) The bond was executed both by the Receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge of Agartala" his successors in office and assigns. By virtue of section 150(c) the Subordinate Judge was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District judge himself. [360 F] (ii) The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Court and on transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the court of the Subordinate judge. Thus, by virtue of Section 150(C) the Sub Judge was enti tled to exercise his same powers as the High Courts in the case of a decree holder. [361 F G] (iii) The appellant 's surety bond had been executed both before and after January 22, 1950, but the transfer of suit the whole proceedings including that of the Receiver were pending before District Judge and on the transfer, the entire proceeding including the surety bond stood automatically transferred to Court of the Sub judge.

The appellant was a dealer in foodgrains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, Uttar Pradesh. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Essential Commodities Act, 1955 on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and assessed it under the provisions of the Act. The appellants challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the transactions were not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable because there was nothing in the Control Order to prevent the State from imposing tax on the transactions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because the goods were supplied pursuant to directions issued under cl. 5 of the Control order; (ii) the transaction of supply was not a sale within section 2(h) of the , and therefore the assesses were liable to pay sales tax on its sales made to the State Government under the Act; and (iii) the tax payer was under the control Order compelled to carry out the directions of the Controller. HELD: (i)(a) The transactions of supplies did not involve any sale within tho meaning of section 2 (h) Of the U P. Sales tax Act, but were on the same account as sales effected by the dealer in the course of inter state trade or commerce. [517 B] (b) The words "sale" and "purchase" used in cl. (a) of section 3(1) of U. P. Act are wide enough to include a transaction which is not a mere sale but which is made for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the statute. [525 C D] Ram Bilas Ram Gopal vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. (c) The sales effected in the present case were not on account of any contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods had been sold within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2 of the Uttar Pradesh Act. [500 E] (d) The tax payer could not be said to have purchased the goods for a consideration, because, the transaction was not one of sale within s.2(h). [525 G] Ramesha Gopal vs The State of U P., ; , referred to. (ii)(a). The sales were on account inter state transactions and were in the nature of sales. The taxer could not therefore be said that there was any contract with the State prior to which goods were sold within that meaning. [511 B] Ram Dhani Ram Gopal 's case, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted by the Trial Court on May 26, 1986. The State Government confirmed his conviction and sentence under section 302 IPC. On appeal, the High Court confirmed his acquittal. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended that the report of the Advisory Board was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of detention though it was within three months from the date of the second order of conviction and that the mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The report of such an Advisory Board is more than 3 weeks after its subjective satisfaction. [206G] 1.2 In a habeas corpus proceeding it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date when the order was passed, but it does not affect the validity of the detention. The report must be obtained within three weeks from the day of the first order of the detain ment. [207B] 1:3. In a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitu tion, the question is whether the report submitted by the Advisory Boards is correct or not. If it does, the Court will not interfere with the detention unless it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause. [208C D] 1 :4. The Court has to see whether there was a sufficient cause and if so, what should be the nature of the action taken. If the report is not made within three month of the date on which the order is passed, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three years from the first date of detention. [209D] 1 5. The question to which the Advisory Committee has to apply its mind is whether on the date the report or beyond the period prescribed by article 22 (4) was made before the hearing of the case. If a reference to an Advisory board is to be made within 3 months, it is no answer to saying that the reference, though not made in three months, was made after the hearing.

The petitioner filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell dated 18th January, 1977. The respondent filed written statement and denied the execution of the agreement. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award. The petitioner preferred a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that (1) the notice under section 17 of the Act was not served upon the respondent and (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute in writing to the arbitrator. [538C] 2. The notice under Section 17 of is a letter addressed to the respondent. It is clear from the narration of facts that the petitioner had agreed not to refer his dispute to arbitration of the named arbitrator. In that view of the matter, it was not open to the petitioner to challenge the award in terms of the arbitration agreement. [540D] 3. The petition for special leave to appeal against the judgment and order passed by the High court is dismissed. [541E] 4. The Judicial Committee held that the validity of a decree could be challenged in execution proceedings only on the grounds that the Court which passed the decree was lacking in inherent jurisdiction in the sense that it could not have seizing of the case because the subject matter was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the defendant was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matters of the suit or over the parties to it. [542F] 5. The judicial Committee held in the case of Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, ; , that they had perfect jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (namely, whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it. In this connection, it may be useful to refer to the observations made by this Court in Seth Hira lal Patni 's case. [543F] 6. The practice of the High Courts in dealing with applications under section 151 C.P.C., is that the High courts should not take cognizance of an application for setting aside an award under sections 14 and 17 of a. The jurisdiction to take cognizance is conferred on the High, Court by section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But in the present context, it is clear that the conduct of parties that the there was no arbitration agreement or by signing of the Award it could he said that they have agreed to referred the dispute to the arbitration of named arbitrator and that he made an award. This, in our opinion, is not a proper arbitration agreement in terms. [544G H] Seth Hiralal Patni v Shri Kali Chand, ; ; , followed.

The appellants were the original mortgagee of a mortgage debt in respect of which a suit was filed by them in the Court of Subordi nate Judge, Asansole. The respondents contended that the sub mortgage was not an assignment of debts but only an assignment and that the court was called upon to exercise all or any of the powers conferred on it by the section. Held, that the words and that he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 28 make it clear that an assignee of a mortgagee debt is within the sub section, since section 28(1)(c) is concerned only with assignment of debt" and not with any right which the mortgagor would have otherwise become entitled to recover from the original mortgagor. The words and the words "all the rights of the mortgagee" in cl. (a), of sub s.(5) of s.36 make it plain that an assignment made under section 28 is a transfer of the mortgage debt and not a sale of the mortgaged property. The word "transfer" in section 2(22) of the Act means "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January, 1939, or pending on that date and includes a proceeding in execution for (among other things) the recovery of a loan advanced before or after that date. The expression "all such rights" is not defined in section 28 (1)(a). It is not disputed that the order of January 30, 1937, was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the Calcutta High Court.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided into two equal shares by metes and bounds, one for himself and the other for himself. In 1954 he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1955 he transferred some properties to the respondents. On the death of the appellant 's widow, the respondents filed a suit against his widow and sons for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree in appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appel lant in view of past illicit cohabitation, and that the transactions were not supported by any consideration by way of cash or delivery of jewels. HELD: (i) The transfer under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras School of Mitakshara law by which Venkatachallulu was governed, he had no power to make a gift of the joint property to his concubine. [475 B] (ii) The transfers were without consideration and were by way or gift. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h). The properties gifted under exhibit 186 were coparcenary property. Under section 2(d) of the , a Hindu female is entitled to make any gift of her undivided interest in the coparcenary property to her husband but she does not make any such gift. [498 C] (iii) The gifts are not hit either by section 3 or 4 of the . [497 E] (iv) The properties transferred under exhibit186 were coparcenary assets and were therefore liable to be partitioned. [500 G] (v) The fact that the transfer was made in consideration of past cohabitation does not affect the validity of the transfers.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the erstwhile State of Bombay, was carrying on business as an agent of its employees. The company had been paying interest to the respondent company at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of the expiry of the period of the policy. The appellant company made an application under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for refund of the amount paid by it on account of insurance policies and also for payment of interest thereon. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer on the ground that the policy had been issued in contravention of section 244 of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Incometax Officer. In further appeal, the Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 245(3)(vi) of Income Tax 1961 and directed the IncomeTax Officer to make payment of the interest on the amount of insurance policy in case of delay in payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The question whether a particular sum is due to a company or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [114D] 1.2. In the instant case, the award of interest was made in the year 1975 and the award was made on 5th December, 1975. The award of the Tribunal was made within three years from the end of the financial year. The operation of the notice under section226(3), 1961, by the I.T.O. to the L.I.C., in the present case, was after a lapse of three years, award of compensation for delay in making the requisite statement on oath under section 240(3). [114E F] 1:3. The contention that such a statement was not made since it involved the likelihood of exposing the L to personal liability has no substance. It is obvious that the question of revoca tion of the cheque within the time given by the LC. does not arise in the instant cases. [115G H] 1 :4. The delay in filing the return under section 245 (3) cannot be said to have caused prejudice to the appellant because it was not a case of any loss to the company.

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in Madhya Pradesh. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession of those lands on the ground that he had been dispossessed by the appellant without due process of law and that the appellant had not paid the amount within the time prescribed under section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal reversed the decree holding that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the first limb of section 29(2)(a) applies only to proceedings under special or local law for which a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule; and (ii) that sub section (2) will apply even to suits where the First schedule to the Limitation Act has not prescribed any period of time. HELD: (i ) The first limb is concerned only with proceedings under the special or Local law for a suit, appeal or application a period which is different from those prescribed therefor in the First and Second Schedules. [143 B] (ii)(a). The first part of section 5(2), as amended by Act No. 23 of 1963, provides that where any special or other law prescribes for any suit, Appeal or application, a period Of limitation different than the period provided therein by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor, in that Schedule and for the purpose of determining any period Of Limitation prescribed for any suits, appeal, or application by any special and local law. [144 C D] (b) The second part of sub section(2). is concerned with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under a special orlocal law for the same type of suit, which are different from that prescribed therefor. [145 E F] (c) The first clause of section 4(1) of Act No, 23 of 1962 provides that a special and other law prescribing for any such suit, appeals or application shall apply as if it were prescribed thereof in that schedule.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring the old bus stand of the appellant as a bus stand. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the State Government to fix the places for the bus stand and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the power to fix any area as a Bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate, and that since the route run by the appellant was only an halting place, the order passed under section 77 of the was unassailable and could not be interfered with. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power to fixing any area is conferred on the Regional Authority having jurisdic tion over the areas and not by the district magistrate. [710E] 2. Section 76 of Act confers wide powers upon the State Transport Authority to fix places for carrying passengers in a notified area. It also empowers the District Magis trate to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the said Chapter. The Regional Transport Author ity has been empowered under section 68(2)(r) to issue a notification fixing the places where the bus stands are directed to stand for the purposes specified in the Schedule. [700H; 700A] 3. Section 68(1) of the provides that no area shall be notified by the State Govern ment unless it is satisfied that such area is not a notified one or in the vicinity thereof. The word 'notified ' has been defined in section 2(g) to mean "a notified area" and includes any area notified under section 3. [610B C] 4. Section 77 of Act provides for the establishment of Regional Transport Authorities having jurisdiction. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by Regional Transport authori ty, Mathura to determine the area in question as a ' bus stand ' and the power of issuing a notification under section 75 of the , was confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified. [750D E] 5. The District Magistrate had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946. The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961, the appellant and his companions were found carrying paddy in a truck which was loaded with 75 bags of paddy. The appellant was tried for offences under sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but acquitted them on appeal. On further appeal the High Court set aside the conviction of the appellant on the ground that there was an attempt to commit the offence of export and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the goods were exported. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there had been no attempt on the part of the prosecution to commit any offence of exporting paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case, and that there could be no attempt to committing the offence by the appellant for export. HELD : (i) The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt. [667 B] (ii) There was no attempt at committing the offences of export within the meaning of Para 2(a) of Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. It was only a preparation on the parts of the goods which would constitute its actual commission if it were not interrupted. The sufficiency or the extent of the actsus reous is not a question Of law which had led to difficulties because of necessity of distinguished between acts and omissions which are essentially connected with the commission thereof. [668 E F] (iii) There has been no effort on the side of the appel lant to commit an offence of exported. It must be shown first to have had an intention to commit it. Secondly, there was no attempts at committing it. The fact that the appellant was driving the truck which he was carrying with him did not make any attempt to cause the accident. [669 G H] (iv) There is nothing in Para 2 of the Punjab Padel (Exports Control) order, 1959 to indicate that there has been an attempt on a part of appellants to commit offence of exports. The mere fact that some of the accused were carrying the goods with him would not make them liable for export under the Act.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as commission agents of the respondent companies. The Managing Agency Agreement provided that the remuneration for the entire year 's work accrued to the respondent company and was to be paid by the company to the transferees. The appellant claimed that in view of the provisions of section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, it was entitled to deduct from its gross profits the amount of commission received by it on the managing agency agreement. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The remuneration for each year is not by itself sufficient to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee, either as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof. [532 B] (ii) The definition of "income" in section 2(14) of Income tax is wide enough to include all income received from the business carried on by the assessee. It does not mean that the income received by the assesee must be deemed to have accrued to him during the chargeable accounting period. [540 C] (iii) The expression "profits and gains" in the definition of the word "income", is wide and includes all profits and gains which arise from the carrying on of a business, profession or vocation. [541 D E] (iv) The term "profits" has been defined in section 10 of the Income tax. Act to mean "the total income of an assessee computed under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession". The expression is wide in its amplitude and includes not only profits but also losses which arise out of a transaction entered into by the assesses with the other parties, for example, where the assessee has no interest in the business. [542 E] Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s. Doypack Systems Ltd., ; , referred to. (v) The word "profits " in section 12(1)(a) of Act means profits and loss which are earned by an assessee from his business or vocation under a contract with the company, but does not include any profits and losses incurred by him during that period. The expression 'profits and losses ' is wide to include profits and gain arising out of the business or activity carried on in the course of the carrying out of that business. It may be mentioned that the word 'profits ' has been used in section 13(1), but it does not necessarily mean profits and profit which arise in the carrying of a particular business. The definition is wide, and includes both profits and income. [543 E F] (vi) The words "profits or gains" occurring in section 5(2)(a)(iii) of that Act are wide enough and include all profits or gains arising out Of the business, carried on or carried on with it a right to carry on any business or trade or business. In the present case, the assessee was carrying out the managing Agency agreement with the respondent Companies under the terms of the Managing Agency Agreements which were not by themselves sufficient to vesting in the respondent Company a beneficial interest in them as they could not be said to have vested in the assignor a beneficial rights to the company.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. open to the prosecution to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. HELD : (i) The evidence in the case is circumstantial. It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the Accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. [803C D] (ii) The High Courts have held that the accused must have committed the murder. There is no reason why the statement implied in the confession should be given only by witnesses who heard the admission or confession, as the case may be. It cannot be used as a corroborative piece of evidence. [904E F] (iii) The circumstances found by the High Court are found to be not consistent onlywith the hypothesis but the conclusion drawn from the facts found on a consideration of the relevant provisions of the Evidence Act. [596F G] (iv) The statement of the appellant can certainly be proved as a confession made by him. But, there is no rule that the evidence given in the course of an investigation should be corroborated by other evidence. It may be used only as corroborative piece or evidence. But it cannot be accepted in evidence merely because it is not corroborated.

The appellant was appointed as an officer of the respondent. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer in the year 1976. The Board of Directors of the appellant 's Corporation Service Regulation, 1976 came into force on May 1, 1976. By notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central Government also framed the scheme called the General Insurance (Rationalisation of Pay scales and other Conditions of Service of Development Step) Scheme, 1976 which came into effect from May 1.1976. The appellant was terminated by tendering one month 's salary in lieu of notice and also a direction to pay all allowances upto that date including the period of suspension. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order terminating his services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to hold the post, and that the termination was illegal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An employee whether permanent or temporary has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days ' notice in writing of his intention to do so.
