The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the . The prosecution alleged that the goods were smuggled into India without an import licence and in contravention of the provisions of the Import & Export (Control) Act, 1947. The appellant denied having been in possession of the offending goods but stated that he had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles in question were smuggled goods and that the appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. On appeal, the High Court held that the evidence of the appellant did not establish that he knew that the portion in which the boxes were kept was in appellant 's exclusive possession with all that was contained in it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The onus of proving that the article in question was smuggled goods lies on the person from whose possession the goods are seized. [541 C] (2) The burden of proof is not always upon the person who asserts that he has been in conscious possession of any contraband goods but it is also upon him to prove affirmatively that the contents of the goods have been smuggled or imported into India. In the present case, the appellant had not produced evidence to prove his possession at all. [542 E] (3) The fact that the boxes contained the keys from which the goods had been recovered was not mentioned in the Act. It is immaterial whether the goods actually were smuggled or brought into India after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [543 G H] (4) The appellant had failed in proving that he was dealing in them knowing they to be smuggling goods. He had not led any evidence that his possession was known to him to be prohibited or imported in contravention thereof.

The appellants were the President of a Association which was registered under the Madhya Pradesh Societies Registration Act, 1935. The members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of yarn and yarn. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for accounts of the profits and yarn on the ground that the Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Act. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1934, are mandatory in character and do not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. The object of the Act is to provide for the acquisition by the company of gain and to make provision for the distribution of profits among its members at a fair price. The Act does not contemplate that the company should be registered as an unregistered firm. It is only when it is registered that the registration can be granted that the provisions of the section apply. The scheme of the , shows that the object of a registered firm is to carry on business which has for its objects the acquisition or sale of gain, and not to enter into any contract with regard to the profits of the business. The fact that the members of a Registered Association are not registered would not make them liable to be registered under section 4 of the Indian Companies Act.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 5(2)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0.1986 they along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1 of the compartment No 1 of a train. On 8. 6. 1986 at about 2.00 P.M., they alongwith two others were travelling in a car driven by one of the respondents. The car was stopped by the driver and the driver. The respondents were arrested on 8th June, 1986 and taken into custody. The police filed charge sheet against the three respondents under section 120B read with Section 420 I.P.C. and section 5 (2)(a) readwith section 5 of the Act. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the respondents on the ground that an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police. On appeal, the Judicial Magistrate held that the charge sheet was not maintainable because the two offences were substantially "the same offence" as Section 120B I. P.C., and quashed the proceedings against the respondents and ordered issuance of process against them. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the respondents holding that the two charges framed against the two respondents were not maintainable, and directed issue of a fresh notice to the three accused under section 251 Cr. P C. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The test is whether taking the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Court will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 Cr.P C. [463E] 1.2. In the instant case, the ingredients of an offence under section 499 I.p.C are not part of the offences under sections 500 and 501 I.PC. The ingredients of the said offence are not parts of the same transaction between the respondents, but they are merely a part of that transaction. [464F] 1:3. In view of the fact that the ingredients in the present case concern the specific act of killing of an elephants, ald that such an offence at all events, falls within the overlapping areas between of section 42 I.A.C and Section 9(2) (a) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act, the High court was justified in setting aside the proceedings of the Magistrate taking cognizance of an offense under section 498 I.I.P., 1973. [465G H] 1 :4. The question whether the two accused are liable to be prosecuted for offences under Section 9 (1) or Section 5(3) read alongwith 50(l) of Act, is a matter which falls within its ambit and scope. [467B] 1 Whether the two persons who have been charged with an offence punishable under section 500 I.C . 1973 and section 506 I. PC. are liable for prosecution under any other law. The answer to this question depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The petitioner was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) the law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges, and (2) the courts have no power to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law in this case is that the accused should ordinarily be released on bail by the court to further the ends of justice and nothing in Sec. 389(1) which reads: 389 (1): Pending any appeal by a convicted person the Appellate Court may for reasons to be recorded by it in writing, order that the execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and also if he is in confinement, that he be released from custody on bail or on his own bond. [343G H] 2. The vice of the system is brought out in the Report: "the evil of bail is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. " [344H; 344A B] 3. A liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own bond, with or without sureties. [344C D] 4. The practice which is now being followed in the United States is that bail covers both release on a single bond, but not a heavy punishment and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [345D E] 5. An accused in judicial custody, actual or potential, may be released by the Court to further, the ends Of justice and anything in Sec tion 389( 1) which read with sec. 389 (2), Cr. P.C., reads: 390 (1). The best guarantee of presence in court is the reach of the law, not the money tag. [346E F] 6. An under trial is worse of than a convict or that the power of the court is better than the power to release increases when the guilt is established. [347G H; 347A B C] 7. The courts have to be satisfied on the basis of the material placed before them that the detenu has his roots in the community and is not likely to abscond, he can safely release the accused on his personal bond without sureties, and this would be a case where the court may for reason to be recording an order of release on bail impose a heavy penalty. [349B C] 8. An offence under section 307 I. P .C. may appear to be serious but not serious. The discretion is left to the Court in the matter of granting bail and it is only when the Court decides to grant bail that the question of granting the bail arises. [350F G] 9. In the instant case, an accused in a judicial custody has been released on his self bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. The Magistrate has not only to keep in mind the gravity of the offence but also the circumstances which are likely to lead to the conclusion that the petitioner is not entitled to bail. [351B C; E] 10. An order of bail covers all release on his person and is released on the same condition as a convict, or that he has been in confinement for a long time. The best guaranteed interest of the community is the reaching of the judicial discretion. [352F G]. 11. An arrest is an exception to the rule of law and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against the accused, it is not the only deterrent and there is no other relevant considerations which are enough for the Court.

The assessee, a registered firm, had at different places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity 'Eldee '. The business carried on by Eldees ' Castle Mills was that of a registered partnership firm. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of six years from the income of Eastle 's business as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle `. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not been included in the assessment of the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assess ment in question of the income from 'Cantle '. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the findings of the Appellate Tribunal were one of facts and not conclusive. [434 C] The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is based on a conclusion of fact. It must be shown that the Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at its conclusion. If the finding is based upon some evidence ignoring other relevant matters, it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the Income of 'Cultle ' in the income by the Incometax Officer may have been a relevant circumstance but its effect has to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had relied.

The Minister concerned in the writ petition filed by V.P. Duggal respondent challenged the order fixing seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The respondent filed an appeal against that order before the High Court which directed that the Minister concerned may give a personal hearing to the parties. The High Court dismissed the appeal in limine. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant State that since the Minister had been called upon to file his personal affidavit, he should be impleaded as a party in the petition, as in the view of the Judge allegation had been made against him and therefore the High court was in error in directing that the respondent be impleaded. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent is set aside. [972C] The direction regarding impleading of a person as a necessary party is given by the High Courts with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petitions and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. [963D] In the instant case, the direction for impleaded was given by a High Court with a direction to the Minister to file an affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister dealing with the allegations contained in the application as to whether he should or should not file an affidavits. The other part of the order whereby the Minister was directed to file the personal affidavit is set at naught.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of rent and other payments under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in revision reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the view taken by the High court that arrears of rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section259 of the Act is incorrect. Held: (i) Section 259 of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1913, does not confer any power on the Board to recover rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the section. The provisions of section 259 are intended to protect the interests of the public and it is only when the rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Act or the rules made thereunder that the Board may require any occupier of such property or of any part thereof to pay to it, instead of to the owner. The words "any tax" in section 259 do not mean that the provisions of the section will apply to rent on land and buildings provided such rent is claimable by a board under the management of the Cantonment Authority. (ii)The words "claimable by the Board" in the proviso to section 259(1) are intended only to cover rent directly claimable under the provisions Of the Act and not to confer any right on the respondent under the general law. The word "recoverable" is used in the sense of a debt or demand for payment of money. (iii)The expression "any other sum recoverable by the board" in s.259 of Punjab Municipalities Act, 1916, doesnot mean that arrears are claimable only when they are due to a Board under the Administration of the Cantonments Act, 1924. The definition of "rent" is not exhaustive and it cannot be extended to rent directly claimed under the personal law of the parties. (iv)The word "income" in cl. (i)(b) of section 260 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, does mean that a debt is payable by a committee or a military Estates Officer. The expression "recoversable by him" in cls. (a), (b) and (c) of s.260 of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi Act, 1956, means that the rent on which it is payable must be realisable by a local authority under the , or the Rules made thereunder.

The appellant was in the service of the respondent company as a Section Salesman. The respondent company terminated his services on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The appellant challenged the termination order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent Company had been appointed as a section salesman for certain number of districts and in the area of each section salesmen and local travelling salesmen were appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services of the appel lant by the respondent was illegal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of this enactment and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Disputes Act. [474G] 1.2. In order to come within section 2(s) of the Industrial Dispute Act, as it stood in 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated, the employee has to be 'under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature. The finding of the Labour Court on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. [473A B] 1:3. In the instant case, the appellant was employed to do canvassing and promote sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study Of the market condition. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. [476B C] 1 :4. In view of the finding that the is not applicable to him and in view of his fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage.

The respondent Company was a company registered under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007. The Company was in possession of land in question at any time prior to the coming into force of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950. The company had been paying rent agreed upon between the Government and the Company prior to its grant of the lease. The State Government issued a Notification under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue & Tenancy Act 1950 declaring that the land in dispute was held by the Company as a tenant under the State Government. The respondent Company filed an application before the Additional Collector for eviction of the Company on the ground that the Company had been holding the land for a period of more than three years prior to 1.10.1977 and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The Additional Collector held that the company was not a 'pakka ' tenant within the meaning of section 181 of the Code and that the respondent Company had failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the tenancy. The appeal filed by the company before the Collector was dismissed. The High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Collec tor. In the Special Leave Petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State was not an 'pagka ' within the definition of section 185 of the code and that, therefore the Company could not be evicted by summary proceedings provided for under that section. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "pakki" in section 181 means a person who holds land from the State Govern ment or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by the State. [179F] 2.1 In terms of Act 66 of 1950, the Company was not 'pakhka ' but was at all a Government lessee in respect of the land. The word "paga" has been defined in section 2(i) to mean any person who held land from a State Government or to which a right is granted under the Land Revenue Act. [180G] 2:2 In terms, the Additional collector made his order for eviction. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for compulsory acquisition of land in an estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The Act was amended by the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment) Act 15 of 1965 which provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part, on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. Section 1(3) of the principal Act provides that where any law does not provide for the transfer of the ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the state, it "shall not be deemed to provide, for the compulsory acquisition or requisitioning of property, notwithstanding that it deprives any person of his property. The appellant who was a member of the Orissa Legislative Assembly and whose land was acquired under the Act, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 47 of the Land Reforms (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1965 which provides for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 47 was inconsistent with article 31 A of the Constitution and was void as it contravened article 14 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 1 (3) is not a law in force when the United State was formed. It was never made operative by a notification. The power to bring into operation the provisions of Ch. IV could not be exercised by the successor State. [357 B] (2) The Act did not provide that the compensation payable under the principal act should be paid at fifteen per cent of the market price of the property, which was within the limit prescribed by the principal statute. The right to compensation which is not less than the market Value under any other law providing for the acquisition by the Government of any land in a estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within tho ceiling limit. [328 C D] (3)(a) The power conferred on the successor state to issue an appropriate notification under section 1(1) of Act 16 of 1960 is not an absolute power but must be exercised in accordance with the principles laid down in article 31A of the Consti tution. [330 E F] (b) Section 47 of Act 15 Of 1965 is undoubtedly a law relating to compulsory acquisition, and where no notification was issued before Ch. II of the Principal Act was repealed, there was no ceiling limit available to the landholders under any statute for the lime being in operation. [332 B C] (c) The provisions of section 1 (1)(3) were not intended to be exhaustive but only illustrative. The legislature could not have intended that the provisions should be extended to all cases where the law did not provided for the payment of compensation at fifteen percent of the value of land, which is within its ceiling limit under any laws providing for acquisition by State of any estate in an Estate in the Personal cultivation of such person.

The widow of her husband 's estate had, in fact, no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversionary heir. The widow died leaving behind two sons, namely, the appellant and the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that the widow had no interest in the property and that the appellant had no right to claim any share therein. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The widow 's right to challenge the right of a prior alienee from the widow is not a limited interest of her own at all and, therefore, could not be surrendered to the reversioner. [355 D] (ii) The rule that a surrender by a Hindu widow of his property without any legal necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse possession against her is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. [356 F] (iii) The position of a person who has acquired by adverse Possession the limited interest in his property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as the widow remains alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of the widow which no doubt benefits the reversioner in the sense that he gets the inheritance even during the widow ' s lifetime. [358 F] In the present case, the widow was under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. The reversionary right to question it is no part of her estate at all. [359 B C] (iv) The reversional right to challenged in a suit is no separate property and cannot be surrendered by a stranger who has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on his expectation of enjoyment by the reversioner, which no question of fraud or collusion that might arise, is not available to the reversioners. [360 F G] (v) The fact that the reversioner does not derive his title from her will is immaterial because she does not possess any title in the estate.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Uttar Pradesh. The Cotton Mills Company was formed on March 1, 1956 and it had been running a textile mill for the manufacture of cotton yarn. In the year 1957 the Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., which was a public limited company, was declared an insolvent by the High Court of Allahabad. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of Rs. 10 lakhs from the respondent on the ground that the shares in question had been pledged with the Government of Uttar pradesh and that the sale proceeds thereof were not sufficient to discharge the debts due to the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to join as a requisitionist of a meeting under section 169 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 and that he had failed to comply with the provisions of the Act. The High Court also held that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member under section 170 of the Income Tax Act readwith section 190 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the special notice under section 284(2) and (5) of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertaking (Dies Recovery) Rules, 1958 issued by the Collector of Kanpur in exercise of his powers under section 149 of the Indian Income Tax Acts were invalid as they contravened the provisions contained in sections 172 to 178 A of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment of the shares of the Polytex Company held by the Cotton Mill Company had not deprived the holder of the share whose name is entered in the Register of Members of the company the right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under Section 169 of Act. [878C] 2.1 The attachment was made with a view to protect the interests of the shareholders and to prevent the holding of the meeting of the Company or to give effect to the provisions thereof. It is not necessary that the order should be passed in the nature of a charge under section 168 of the I.T. Act read along with section 190(1)(a) of that Act. In view of the fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour of the Government, the Cotton Company continued to be the member of the polytex Company in respect of the aforesaid shares and could exercise its rights under section 171 of the , [875E G] 2:2 The order passed by the Commissioner was an order in the character of a charging order. It was not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a Receiver under the Land revenue Act. It did not affect the contract of pledge.

The petitioners, who were owners of a house in the State of Punjab, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners in possession of the land along with some others. The Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The Gram Panchayat in its written statement inter alia pleaded that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 and therefore the suit was not maintainable. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the question involved in the suit being merely one of title to the suit land and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit property was shamlat deh or not, the suit could not be maintained by virtue Of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court which held that since in the case involved in a suit was merely one such of title, it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Panchayat that the court before which a suit had instituted had not framed any issue as required under section 13A of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation). Act 1961 and consequently the suit filed against the Panchayat was not competent. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the trial court had jurisdiction in the matter. [833C] 2. The plaintiff in the instant case had not claimed a declaration that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat or that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. It was therefore, not possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamilat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under Act or in respect of any matter which the Commission or the Gram panchayat is empowered by or under the provisions of the . [834E F] 3. The suit had not be filed against Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the suit lands belonged to them as shamillat deh. It will not be possible in this case for the Civil Court to make any declaration in respect thereof without deciding whether the land was shamat deh or otherwise. [884G] 4. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration of that property. They have, however, claimed that they had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Land Revenue Act and not by the Civil court. [894A] 5. The civil court has jurisdiction to decide such claims in such manner as may be prescribed. [90G] 6. In the instant cases, the Panchayat which had been impleaded was raising the plea that the plaintiffs were owners along with others of the suit house. It would not be difficult in the circumstance for the revenue authorities to make the declaration in their favour without deciding them whether the properties in question were shamlat lands or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat or not. The plaint had been filed against a Panchayat and Panchayat had specifically claimed that it was a part of shamlat ties. It is no doubt true that the Gram Panchayats in question have not been joined as defendant.

The appellant Board, a public limited company, had been supplying electricity to the respondent consumers. The respondent consumers were required to pay interest on the security deposit for one month 's estimated consumption charges and bank guarantee equal to two months estimated charges as contemplated by the terms of supply. The appellant issued notice to the respondents demanding payment of interest on delayed payment of the amount. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the demand. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that there was no order of this Court adjudicating the rights of the Board on the consumer in respect of the validity of consumption security deposit being condition precedent for the supply of electricity by the Board as it had direct hearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is no order or decision of this court adjudicating the right of the respondent on the consumers in respect the validity or otherwise of consumption of energy and in particular, the demand of interest by the consumer for violation of any conditions of supply, in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tampering with meters and such other methods adopted by the consumers. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect to this money since the money is deposited by the complainant with the Board to secure the Board against default in payment of its interest. [278D] 1.2 In the instant case, there was an order of the High court directing the respondents to pay the interest on security deposit and in that event the claim of interest would be payable at the rate of 12% per annum. The direction of this High Court is set aside and the writ petition filed by the appellant is dismissed. [279E] 1:3. In view of the fact that the respondent had been directed to allow interest at the rates of 12%, it cannot be said that there were no orders of this nature on the basis of which the demand was made. The order of payment of Rs. 45,000/ which was disposed of by consent and the other in W.P.No.576 of 1990 where the writ petitioner was directed to pay Rs.45,000 to the Board is set at naught. [280F G] 1 :4. In the circumstances, there is nothing wrong in the order of adjudication made by this Court directing the respondent to pay Interest on the amount due to the appellant.

The petitioners are the members of the Indian Telecommuni cation Research Centre and are working in the Telecommunication Research Centre. The recruitment to the different cadres in the Telegraph Engineering Service is now being made under the Sect ion of the Recruitment Rules. The petitioners have challenged the validity of the said rules on the ground that they were violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution by not grant ing them the same special pay which was granted to the trans ferred officers who are working In the Telecommunications Research Centre in the same posts and discharging similar duties. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly held that the denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners is attempted to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed by Shri C.L. It is not the case of the Government that the petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharge their duties. All the direct recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Telephone Research Centre, and it is paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the telephone Research Centre by the Union Public Service Commission. [1010C D] 2. The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred official had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same. [1001D] 3. The discrimination between the direct recruit ment officers and the transfer officers regarding the payment of special pay is attempted tO be justified on the basis of the Ministry 's consensus on the question of granting of Special pay to the direct recruitment as in the case o f transferred officers as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on the petitioners (Annexure XIX) and that of the Association (Annexure XX). The Government has virtually admitted the fact that all rele vant things such like qualif ications, function, duties or responsibilities are tO the same which is similar to between direct recruit ents and transferred officials. [1002C D; 1013E] 4.

The appellant, an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, was governed by section 2(1) of the Act. The respondent employer filed a complaint against the appellant under section 7 8 (1) D.P.C. alleging that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of that Act read with the proviso to sub section (2) of section 39 of the said Act and that the appellant had failed in complying with the provi sions of section 40 of the Bombay Act. It was alleged that the respondent employer had failed and neglected to comply the provisions Of section 42 (4) and (5) of Act No. 1 of 1947 read with proviso to section 39(1). The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Court for relief under section7 8 ( 1 ) D. P.C., and directed the appellant to pay him wages for the period beginning can the date of such order of dismissal, discharge, removal, retrenchment, termination of service or suspension as the case may be. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending that the third respondent had failed not comply with section 42 and that therefore the Labour court should have directed the reinstatement of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that it did not comply the mandatory provisions of Section 42(1), and in particular, the attractability of section 78(1D) D; F] The appellant 's contention was that the second respondent had not complied with the requirements of section 7 (2). The High court held that the first respondent had committed breach of section 41(4)(b) of Bombay Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 and therefore the order of the Labour Commissioner should be set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions in section 78 (1D), D.p.C.; and proviso to Section 39(2) were mandatory and not directory and that since the first respond ent had failed, no relief could be granted under section 42.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were occupying the property under a registered lease for 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The respondents contended that the appellants had no right to continue in possession after 31.1.1971 as tenants from month to month. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable before the Munsif, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The High Court held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not tenable before the Munsiff, and directed the appellants to restore possession. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents had no locus standi to file an applica tion under section 13 of the Act before the Civil Court for evicting the appellants if they did not vacate within the time allowed by court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the Court by an application under section12(3) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 is a mixed question of law and fact. [975C] 2.1 In the instant case, it is the Civil court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or making an application Under Section 12(3), if the tenant fails to vacate the building on the termination of the lease or as the case may be, on the expiry thereof, the Court shall, on an application by the land lord, pass an order for ejectment which shall be executed as a decree and may further order that the tenant shall pay to the landlord such amount as may be determined by it as daily compensation. [936D E] 2:2 In the present case, the Civil Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the applica tions under section 11 of the . The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application for eviction under section 10 of the , before the civil court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. [981F] 2 :3 In view of the fact that the Civil Judge, Ranchi had passed a decree against the appellants on 31st July, 1971, it would be open to them to choose which course to follow. The order passed by the Munsif as a result of which the suit filed by them was dismissed and the second appeal filed by him was also dismissed.

The appellant Society filed a suit for declaration that the respondent society was not duly elected Secretary of the Society. The trial court after holding that the appellant 's application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable, proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected secretary of the society and had, therefore, full authority to withdraw the suit. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiff respondent had been duly elected as the Secretary of a Society. On appeal, the High Court held that the trial court had committed several errors in deciding the question whether the appellant was the validly elected Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw it. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Trial Court had committed many errors in determining the question of who was a duly elected representative of the appellant Society and had also failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it by law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that since the appellant had been validly elected as Secretary of respondent No. 2 society, entitled to prosecute or withdraw the Suit under its inherent powers, if it is ultimately satisfied that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary and was, therefore not authorised to withdraw his suit, the prayer for withdrawal was not made on behalf of the appel lant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. [237B C] 2. The question whether a person is duly elected or not has to be determined by the Court having regard to the provisions of section 15 of the Act. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on the grounds that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the judgment if it was satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [238C D] 3. The jurisdiction of the Court is not to be exercised in an arbitrary manner or on mere suspicion, but only when there are strong reasons for doing so. It is not necessary that the Court should always act in a judicial manner. If it does not act in good faith and does not exercise its power properly, it has no jurisdiction to set at naught the order of the trial Court permitting withdrawal of the suit under its extraordinary powers. [239D E] 4. The courts below were right in holding that there was no error in deciding question as regards who was actually a party to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent had been procured by fraud, the Court cannot investigate the matters in exercise of its inherent power and the only remedy to the party is to institute a suit. [240E F] 5. The Courts below were wrong in dismissing the appellant"s application as not maintainable.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years under section 3 of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. The period of emergency referred to in section 72 of the Act was to be determined after April 1, 1946, when the emergency was declared to have ended on April 1. 1946. The appellant contended that as soon as the declaration that the emergency had ended on May 4, 1946 was made on April I, 1946 and the Ordinance in question which had been promulgated on April 2, 1946 ceased to operate on April l, 1946. Held, that the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 3 Of the India & Burma (Expenditure) Act 1940, were omitted from section 72 during the period specified in section 1(3) of the Indian and Burma Act, 1935, and the ordinance having continued in operation even after April I. 1946, the Ordinance having ceased to be in force on April II, 1946 could not be repealed by reason of the non obstante clause in section 2 Of the Indian , as it originally stood. The words "for the space" in the section were omitted and the position in law was that the period of the duration of the Ordinance had to be computed after April l. 1946 when the Emergency was declared, to have expired on April 11, 1946; and the period during which the Ordinance was promulgated would not be deemed to have been extended until it was repealed. The effect of such omission was not to continue the duration for a period of six months beyond April 1., 1946.

The appellants were convicted by the High Court under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that they had committed murder of a woman, and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the death sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts were not justified in confirming the death penalty under section 307 I. P.C.; (ii) the sentence imposed by the trial court was excessive; and (iii) the death sentences should be awarded only for life imprisonment, while the High court had confirmed the sentence of death on appeal to it. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The death sentence should be upheld as a rule of universal application. [1065B] 2.1 In the instant case, the High courts were justified in affirming the death punishment and the judicial discretion vested in them regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid. [ 1066C] 3.2 The High Courts have been justified in upholding the death imposed under section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, being satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354 (3) Cr. P C., 1973 so as to bind all courts in the country. [1006C] 4.1 The High court was justified in confirmation of death sentence under section 366(1) Cr P C. [1017D] 3:2. The question whether the death of a person is life imprisonment or not must be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. If the general observations on sentencing jurisprudence made in Rajendra Prasad 's case (supra) are to be regarded as "law declared by this Court" within Article 141 so as not to bind any court in the Country, then the observation or the so called guideline as to the effect "special reason" necessary for imposing death penalty must relate not to the crime as such but to the criminal" occurring in the majority judgment. [1000D E] 4:3. The sentence of imprisonment to life imprisonment is a rule and not a rule. It is not a matter of law that has to be judged on the facts of each case. [1001F G] 5.1 There are no rationes decidendi, much less any ratio decidendi. The judgment in Rajendra Kumar 's Case (supra), relied upon by the appellants, does not lay down any principle or principle which is binding on all courts. It merely lays down certain principles and rules for determining when a sentence of life imprisonment should be imposed. [992A B] 5:3 A court has to judge the circumstances in which the sentence is imposed and the manner in which it is to be executed. The court has only to see whether there are special reasons for imposing the death. If, on the other hand, the general principles of law laid down by Rajendra Prasad vs State of U.P., [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869 and Rajendra Prasad Singh 's cases (supra). it is not correct to say that the award of death penalty to any of the two appellants was neither 'erroneous in principle ' nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ', or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department. He was promoted as an Income Tax Officer in 1942. In 1953, he was placed under suspension on 30th September, 1953, by the Commissioner of Income tax, Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry on allegations involving corruption and violation of service rules. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the order passed by the commissioner of Income Tax, Lucknow on 2nd April 1956, reducing the appellant in rank from the post of an Income tax Officer to that of an income tax Officer was void and inoperative. He also prayed for a declaration that he had been exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. In appeal, the High Court held that the preliminary enquiry was not properly conducted and that the appellant had been wrongly exonerated. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is essentially a question of fact; (2) that in any case, this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully inquired into by officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether an officer was given reasonable opportunity of leading evidence or not was essentially a questions of fact. [586G] 2. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial can be material. In the case before us, it has not even been shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could help the appellant 's case on specific charges. The questions raised by the appellant were obviously not argued before the Division Bench. [588H; 589A] 3. It was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he has suffered some injustice which to be set right. And, it was probably because the appellant is absolved of charges involving corruption in the discharge of his duties that he was given the lesser punishment of demotion and neither dismissed nor removed from service. [589C D] 4. The High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made by the appel lant which could have had that effect upon the departmental proceedings. He urged that the result was that the High court did not dealt with a large number of issues which should be, initially raised before it and finally heard arguments. [591D] 5. The fact that the witnesses who were alleged to have denied having been allowed to produce them could not lead to any inference that they had suffered some prejudice on account of their non production. [592F] 6. It would not by itself merit a revocation of special leave at this stage after hearing arguments. The point sought to be raised was not argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High. [593C D].

The appellants are the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The sales tax authorities levied and collected tax on the sale of manganese ores in the State. The appellants challenged the levy of tax by filing writ petitions before the High Court. The High Court held that the contract between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. was integrally connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with their foreign buyers and that the contracts between the appellant and the foreign buyers were not integrated activities in the course of export, because the export sale is an independent one between the Corporation and its foreign buyers. The writ petitions filed by the respondents were allowed by a Single Judge of the High court holding that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into between the parties with their Indian buyer and the sales tax was not payable on the sales effected by the M/s. T.C., but the Mm.T.,C. The Division Bench held that there was no privity of contract between them and the appellant, and therefore, the Mn.T had no right to claim the tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Mimmament Agreement was integrically connected with a contract entered by the appellant with their other foreign buyers; that the agreement between the M and the S.T.; and Serajuddin 's case (supra) did not render these contracts F.O.B. contracts with the foreign buyer as parts of the same transaction, and that therefore, there was a concluded contract between both the parties to be treated as integrated activities; that in the special leave petition before this Court the appellants contended that M/S. T.,C., and Serrajuddin ' s case were not identical; that Mmmament agreement was integrating the contracts entered into with their American buyers on F.0.B, basis; that there were no privitys of contract in the present case to be considered as export sales; that even if the MM. T had been a party to the contract, it could not be said that the appellant had any right to the goods; and that M.mmaments were integrated activities within the meaning of section 2(f) of the . Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The agreement between M and S. T.; and the appellants was integrually connected with each other. [445C] 2.1 The contract between M.T and S., a foreign buyer, is not a contract in which the goods under a separate contract with the Indian buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte rised or the contract would be different. If they are different contracts, as they are in the instant case, the last purchaser within the state is the M., and therefore the purchase by the merchant from the mine owner was the last purchase in the state. [444D E] 2:2 The agreement entered into on the one hand and the contract of sale between the seller and the buyer on the other are different transactions and it is the S,T.P.C which entered into independent contracts with their Foreign buyers on the same terms and conditions. In the special circumstances of this case, there could be no doubt that the transaction between the two parties was integration of the contract in question. [441F G] 2 :3 The normal presump tion attaching to F.o.B., contracts is that property in the goods passes only when they are put on board the ship. In such a case, it is not necessary for the foreign seller to have any right or interest in the property of the goods passed from the appellants to the M, and the transaction was integrated with the appellant 's foreign buyer.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was served with an order terminating his services with effect from 19th October, 1974. The appellant challenged the said order by means of writ petition before the High Court which held that the termination of service of the appellant was invalid and inoperative and directed reinstatement of the respondent with full back wages. The High Court also held that since the termination was illegal it was not a retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of services of the appel lant was ab initio void and inoperative. [532C] 1.2 The termination was not termination simpliciter but a discharge of a temporary servant. It is enough if he has worked for 240 days in a period of 12 months, it is not necessary that he should have been in the service of employer for one whole year. Therefore, both on principle and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in continuous service within the definition of section 25(1). [533E F] 1:3 The termination is ab initio valid unless it is shown to be in contravention of any provision of law or rules made under the Act or the Rules. [525F G] 1 :4 In the instant case, the termination order was not passed by way of punishment but a punishment and therefore, the appellant could not have been dismissed from service on the ground that he was a temporary employee. [500G H] 1 5. The termination order is not a punitive one but only an order of termination simpliciter. It does not contain any stigma or stigma nor does it contain any particulars as to how many employees were employed in the respondent 's establishment. It merely mentions some of them as work and conduct. It also mentions some other work done by the appellant. The fact that the appellant had rendered service for a period exceeding 240 days within a period Of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore, his case falls within section 25 B(2)(a) and he shall be deemed to be In continuous service for one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. [511B C] 1 6. The question whether the termination is illegal or inoperative does not arise in this case because the termination has been made with a view to avoid retrenchment. It may be that the workman was in service for more than 240 days but he had rendered services for a long period of more than 12 months. Therefore his case fell within section 2 (oo) and the appellant should be deemed as in continuous employment for a further period. [506F G; 507A] 7. The respondent company is not liable to pay any retrenchment compensation under section 25C(2).

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet on the appellant alleging that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and had demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from him. The enquiry officer found him guilty of the charges and dismissed him from service. On appeal to the High Court the appellant contended that the order of dismissal was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order was at all given to him. Held, that the appellant was a temporary employee and had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant had been dismissed from service without giving him any reasonable opportunity. The order of termination was in the nature of punishment and an order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed, is not of that nature. The third proposition in Ram Narayan Das 's case referred to above was not applicable to the present case. The appellant was given no such opportunity and article 311 of the Constitu tion did not apply. The second proposition in the latter case was not applied to the facts of the present cases. The State of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , followed. Ram Narayan Dass 's Case referred to. The High Court was right in holding that the enquiry was made by the Settlement Officer for the purpose of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanour.

The Jammu and Kashmir State Judicial Service Rules, 1969 were framed by the Jammu and Kahnde State Government under section 133 of the Jammu & Kashmir State Act, 1966. The rules were made by the Commission in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 133 read with section 135 of the Act. Rule 3(b) of the Rules provided that the Commission shall be consulted before making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. Rule 4 provided for consultation with the Commission, and Rule 5 provided for appointment of members of the Commission by promotion from one Service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 under section 132(2) of Jammu & Kahrde Act, 1967, appointing the Commission as Professor of Law in the Medical Colleges. The appellant who was working as Professor in the College filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the selection made by it for the appointment to the posts of Professors. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the rules were not properly interpreted and that the Public Service Commission had been consulted in accordance with its requirement. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The State has not been able to refer to any averment in the writ petition that the Commis sioner was not consulted either in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments or on the competence of the Committee. [875 B] (2) The High Courts erred in holding that Rule 3 had been correctly interpreted and whether the Public Services Commission for the State of Jammu andKahndie was consulted in regard tO the principles laid down in section 133(2)(b). [876 D] (3) The rules are not properly construed. They are intended to be applied only to the making of appointments to posts of Professor, and they do not apply to the selection of candidates to fill up the same post. [887 E] (4) The Commission was consulted on the question whether the rules in question were properly interpreted or not. It is not provided by section133(2).

The petitioner was elected to the Lok Sabha from the constituency of the Bihar Assembly. He challenged the election on various grounds, including that the House of Commons had no privilege to prevent the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings. The question for determination was whether the privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State were protected by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Held, (per Sinha, C. J., Gajendragadkar, Wanchoo and Ayyangar, jj.), that the privileges conferred on the House by article 194(3) of our Constitution are not those of the House or Houses of the legislature of a state and they are not protected by articles 19(2), 19(5) and 31 of the Constitu tion. The privileges and immunity of a member of the Legislative Assembly of a Union Territory and of members and committees thereof, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law, and until so defined, shall continue to be those of that House of Parliament of the United Kingdom and of its members and Committees. The provisions of article 194 (3) are not intended to apply to a member who is not a member but who has been elected to a House or a Committee thereof. The expression "the House of Legislature" in article 194 means the House which has been constituted under the Constitution, and the expression "all the Houses of Parliament" means the Houses which have been constituted by the people themselves. The words "all such Houses" in Article 194(1) are wide enough to include all the Houses and the committees thereof and they cannot be equated with those of a Legislative Assembly or a House. The word "the Legislature" is not defined in the Constitution but has been used in the sense of the expression 'the House or the Committee of such Legislature '. The term "the Legislative Assembly" is used in two ways: (1) that the Legislative Council of a Part B State and the members and the Committees thereof must be, like the powers, privileges and dignities of a Government of the State, and (2) that even if the House is not duly constituted by or under the provisions of the Act, it has no privilege or immunity from any action taken in respect thereof.

The respondent was appointed as Reader in different faculties in the State of Orissa. He was promoted to the post of Reader on 4 9 1969 and was drawing a salary of Rs.600/ . The appellant, who was working as Reader, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of his promotion. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the teaching experience of the Readers in the private college was completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible for appointment as Readers. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in directing the Gov ernment to take into account, as experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the public sector. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The condition of draw ing of Rs,600/ or more on the date of taking over is arbitrary and discriminatory. [778C] 2.1 The condition for draw ing Rs. 600/ or less on the dates of take over is a seriously grim issue. It is thus clear that all the Respond ents are eligible to be referred to. the Public Service Commission for consid eration of suitability for appointment to the posts of Reader. [777G] 2(a) The condition regarding draw ing up of Rs.,600/ by the appellant was arbitrary and irrational. [774B C] 3.1 In the instant case, the condition of drawing Rs.630/ was not a matter entirely for the respondent in any way. It was not relied upon by the State in connection with the appointment of the respondents as Readers after the College had been taken over by the Government on March 9, 1971. [779C D] 3(b) The conditions of drawing of Rs,.600/ were laid down in the said circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment. [780E F] 3.(c) The requirement of experience of one year in a college is completely efface to the full extent that it will not even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment of Reader is a serious grim order in the High Courts.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted temporary permit to the appellants on certain conditions. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of the Act, and the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, the Regional Transport Authority or the Regional transport authority as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred specifically upon it by section 68F(1 A) can grant temporary permits to persons other than the Corporation to operate vehicles on the route for which the scheme has already been published. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme has not been prepared in respect to the route in question and the appellant has no right to obtain temporary permit. [985C] 2. Section 68 F (1 A), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that if no application for a temporary permit is made under section 69F(I A) by the Corpora tion, the State Transport authority or the State Road Transport Authority as the ease may be shall grant such permit to any person in respect thereof. The Regional Transport Officer has power under sub section (1 C ) to grant temporary permit only to persons who are not the Corporation. [89 E F] 3. Section 69F of the is a self contained provision and confers power on the State Government or the Corporation, as the cases may be. It is open to the State transport authority or Regional Transport authority as its case may, in exercising its powers conferred specifically on it by s 68F (1A) to grant such temporary permits if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But section 68 G(1 B) clearly envisaged a situation where application for temporary stage carriage is not made under s 68 F. [90 E] 4.

The appellant was the son of a grandson of his maternal grandfather. He died in 1947 leaving behind his widow, his wife and children. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the property on the ground that the appellant had no right to alienate the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the property inherited by the respondent was not ancestral property as it belonged to him and that the respondent had no title to the property and so it allowed the appeal preferred by the appellant. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decision of the first Full Bench is wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of law which has been consistently followed by the community since 1895. [140 D] (ii) The High Court was in error in not following the earlier Full Bench decisions on the question of the appellant 's title to property. [142 E] (iii) The view taken by the first full bench that the suit in question attracted the provisions of article 2 of Act I of 1920, is correct. [143 F G] (iv) The contention that the High Courts were wrong in not applying the earlier decision of this Court in Narotam Chand 's case to the facts of the present case was wholly untenable as a finding on the issue of the relevant custom was clearly unsustainable. [144 C D] The question whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral or not, has to be decided by the court having regard to the provisions contained in section 3 of the Act. [145 B] (v) The question as to whether property acquired from a paternal grandfather is not ancestral or whether such property is capable of being treated as ancestral property or not must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. [146 C D]. (vi) The decisions of the High court are wholly unsustainable because they have been rendered in ignorance of the provisions relating to custom.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, he had come to the house of one of the appellants armed with dagger and Ebris. He was attacked by the appellants with dagger on the neck with a dagger. The appellants were convicted under section 448 read with section 34 of the I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307 read with Section 34 of I. P. C. The High Court acquitted the appellants but convicted them under section 302/34, I.p.C., and sentenced each of them to rigorous imprison ment for four years under s. 449 and to rigorous 'imprisonment for one year under section 323/34. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the offence committed by the appellant Matiullah was not sustainable in law; (2) the charge under section 34 read with s.34 of I P.C.; and (3) the conviction of the appellant under section 324 read with sections 34, 449 and 457 of the Penal Code were illegal. HELD : (i) The offence committed was not only punishable under section 450 but in the two succeeding sections, namely, section 449 read withs. 34 of Indian Penal code. [882 D] (ii) Section 449 of the Code does not provide for a charge under s, 449 or section 457 of I .P. C., and it is quite clear that the punishments prescribed have been graded according to the nature of the offence "in order to" the commission of which house trespass was committed.

The appellant was the son of one Harnam Singh who died in 1947. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the properties in dispute were ancestral and not self acquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the parties were governed by Hindu Law and not by custom, and that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial within four degrees, but only a member of the Punjab Civil Service. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to succeed to the properties as the appellant had failed to prove her case. The appellant appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High court. Held: (i) The custom in favour of the daughter 's succession to the self acquired properties of her husband has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter from inheritance to the father 's ancestral property of the father. It is well settled that a Hindu widow who is a member and whose father was the last male holder excluded the daughter of her deceased father from succession to her father 'Sarswat Brahmin, cannot succeed unless she has proved that she had been born in the village before her death. (ii) The appellant was a collateral and the respondent did not now dispute the custom of the district of Gurdaspur which was compiled by him in 1913 and which was followed by a memorandum dated July 10, 1914. (iii) The High Court was right in holding that there was no custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collateral could claim to succeed in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degree.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was acting as Managing Agent of several companies. The Managing Agent executed two deeds in favour of the company and one deed in favour Of the company. The respondent filed a suit against the Managing Agent for the recovery of certain sums of money on the ground that the two deeds were not properly stamped and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. The trial court held that the deed was not properly registered and that it was chargeable only with the difference between the two duties payable if different instruments were passed and that therefore the instrument could not be split up into separate instruments. On appeal, the High Court held that though the instrument is executed by one person, if he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct matters for the purposes of section 5 and that section 6 provided a different procedure and that in construing the section in the light of that scheme, the expression "distinct matter" must be construed as distinct from the other. Held, that the words "distinguished matters" in section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act were intended to convey two distinct matters and the difference was one between the difference in the description of the instrument and the amount of the duty payable on separate instruments which were executed by each person. The words "continct matter " in section 6 meant a single matter and not merely a single transaction. Held further, that when a person executes a power of attorney in respect to all matters in which he could act, it should be held as a matter of law and without regard to the contents of the document, to comprise a single item of instrument in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in the State of Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50. The Income Tax Officer included depreciation which would have been allowed if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was in force in the past. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the depreciation was not allowable under the Indian Incometax Act, but the High Court on reference answered it against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "or which would" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order mean "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income Tax and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of business". [230 D] (ii) The expression "or who would have otherwise been allowed" in para 2 of section 13(5)(b) of the Ordinance was not used in the sense in which it was in existence. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that where two interpretations are possible, one which will advance the object and give effect to the intention of the legislature, the Court should adopt the construction which would advance the purpose of the legislation. [230 E] (iii) The word "or" occurring in para. 2 of Section 13(1)(b), as equivalent to "any law relating thereto" in the proviso to paragraph 2, means "any such law relating" and not "any other law relating", so that it could have been intended by the legislature to include a provision in the written down value.

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded contract by the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (K.P.C.) for carrying out certain works in the State of Karnataka. The contract was to be executed within three months from the date of execution of the contract. The petitioner submitted his tender on 30.11.1988 and the same was accepted by the K.P C.C., which was later cancelled on 16.12.1989. Thereafter, the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the cancellation of the agreement and also the cancellation order dated 16.1.1990. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contract was not for supply of tender forms but only for information and hence the rejection of the tender of the petitioner was justified. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The K. P.C. cannot be said to have satisfied the preliminary conditions Tendering it eligible to tender for the contract, no injustice can be said lo have been done to the appellant by reason of its non supply of all the documents called for in para V. [240E] 1.2 In the instant case, the KP C was not a party to the contract and the K P C. had no experience in this line of work and that the appellant was much better qualified for the Contract. The very purpose of the Notification inviting Tenders was to go by the minimum qualifying requirements of para I.1 of the notification. It is clear from the language used in the Notification that at least some of the conditions set out therein were intended to verify the fulfilment of the three prequalifying requirements of Para I.2 and that he fulfilled the three conditions called for vide para 5(c) of the N.I.T. and other details called for. [241F G] 1:3 The very object of the said Notification is to go in by the qualifying minimum requirement as stated in para I of the Schedule to the Notification. It was for the K .P. C. to assess the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if the Kpc C.c. considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form to the applicant, it would not be possible to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. [242G H] 1 :4 The question whether there is any difference between the requirements in para II and V or VI of the Notifications are intended to verifying the fulfilment and as such the question of rejection of tender does not arise. [243H, 244A] 1 5.
