It may be said that the interpretation placed by the learned single Judge on the Notification is correct but it is clear that the Division Bench was right in holding that it was only para I3 that stipulates the pre conditions and that all the three requirements set out in Para I of N.l.T., were only for the information and are such they could be met before consideration of the tenders. [244B C] 1 6. The question is whether there was any difference in furnishing the information about the fulfilment, as stated by the Notification, and whether it was necessary to furnish the same. If the answer is in negative, then the question would arise for consideration. [245C D] 7. It cannot be disputed that the KPCC had no expertise in this behalf before opening of the price documents, the Chief Engineer had come to the conclusion that the firm had fulfilled all the prequalification requirements and as a result thereof the tender was found to be in order. The appellant had no doubt also urged that the M.C C.

The appellant was a displaced person from Pakistan. He was served with an order of the Custodian under section 27 of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947, on the ground that he had been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. The order was confirmed by the Additional Custodian but the High Court in revision set aside the order of confirmation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the order was not appealable under section 25 of the Act as the appellant had not filed any appeal against the order, (ii) the orders were passed without jurisdiction and (iii) the proceedings before the Custodian General were quasi judicial in nature and therefore the setting aside of the order against which no appeal was filed by any one could not be sustained. HELD : (i)(a) The order under appeal is one passed by the Custodian or Additional Custodian and it is specifically declared to be final and conclusive. [1127 B] (b) The orders passed by an Additional Custodian are quasi judicial orders, and they cannot be equated with orders of a quasi judicial tribunal. The orders of the Additional custodian are quasi administrative in character and therefore they could not have been passed without any authority of law. [1105 C D] (c) The jurisdiction to revise an order under section 26 of the , is not affected by the provisions of section 27, but only by reason of the fact that the order has been passed by a competent officer. [1027 G H] (d) The Custodian General himself in his order under Appeal had held that the orders of confirmation passed by him were quasi administrative and therefore he could not exercise revisional powers. [ 1028 B C] (e) The power to revise is not subject to appeal or revision but is subject to the revisional power of the custodian General under section 6 of the Central Act XIV Of 1947.

The appellant company was a private limited company. Its main object was to provide for the payment of puja bonus and other benefits to its employees. The claim for puja bonus was based on custom or condition of service, and in that light, it claimed that the festival bonus should be paid to its workmen. The Tribunal held that the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 was not such a matter as had to be adjudicated and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the claim for Puja Bonus could not be sustained on the ground that it was based solely on custom and condition of services, and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject, and the question about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Act and the Court took the view that it would be subversive of the scheme of the Act to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. [603 D E] (2) The question whether a particular festival is a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees or not, has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [508 G H] (3) The object and reasons of the Bonus (Amendment) Act, 1965 are clear and unambiguous. It does not require any further clarification as to what is the nature of the festival. [595 A B] (4) The Tribunal was right in holding that the bonus scheme was the question of payment of bonus based on profit to employees employed in establishments '. [596 C D] (5) The Bonus Act, as it stood in 1965, does not bar claims to customary bonus or those based on conditions of service. It is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are left untouched. The fact that the Bonus Acts were made applicable to all establishments before 1966 and so, in later years such a ground was barred by the general principles of res judicata. [597 E F] (6) The scheme of bonus Act indicates that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of bonus ' based on profits to employees who are either excluded or exempted from the Act. It may be payable as a customary bonus, but it is quite possible that the code of employment in which the employer makes profit part of which is due to the contribution of labour, a claim for bonus may be legitimately made by the workmen. [599 F G] (7) The definition of "industrial dispute" in section 2(g) of the Industrial Disputes Act includes disputes relating to bonus and the expression "any other matter" does not include disputes relating thereto. [600 A B; 600 C D].

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana by promotion on August 25, 1976. The High Court of Punjab & Haryana struck down Rule 12 of the Rules as violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the rules governing seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed to a Superior Judicial service of Punjab were governed by a rule of quota only and not by the rule of rotation; that the High Court had no power to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees; that in any event, the High Courts were not justified in applying the rule as rotation at the time of confirmation of the members of the Superior judicial Service who were appointed on or after December 31, 1976 and that the seniority of all officers appointed to that service by promotion and by direct recruitment was governed by the rules of quota; that since the rules had been amended by the Haryana First Amendment Rules 1972 providing that the inter se seniority of the member of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the Service irrespective of the date of their confirmation, there was no direct decision on the question whether the Governor, in the exercise of power conferred by the proviso to Article 309, has the power to frame rules regulating the seniority. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rule of reservation is not violative of any constitutional provision but is only a rule framed under Article 309 and it cannot be said that the rule is arbitrary or unreasonable. [1039C] 2.1 Rule 12 in so far as it confers power on the Governor to frame Rules regulating the recruitment and service conditions of judicial officers of the State, is expressly, by the terms of that Article itself made subject to the law which the State Legislature may pass for regulating the appointment and service condition of judicial officer of the state. [ 1039D] 2:2 The High Courts in Punjab and Delhi were not right in applying rule 12 to the rules relating to seniority of members of service, since the rule was amended by Haryana First amendment Rules 1972 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976 for the mere reason that on August25, 1976 the High court had issued a notification fixing seniority of promotees and direct recruits appointed to those posts on or before December 31. 1976.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, were appointed as Junior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh State Public Works Department on temporary basis for a period of one year by an order dated 15.12.1974. The respondents Nos 4 &5 were promoted as Junior Assistant in the year 1975. In the year 1976, the Government issued orders promoting them to the post of Junior Assistant with effect from 1.1.1977. On the expiry of twelve months from the date of promotion, the respondents Nos 5 and 6 were appointed on temporary posts in the cadre of Junior Assistants. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated 30.6.1976 made by the Government appointing them as Junior Assis tions for a limited period of two years. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior assistants and Senior Assistants for different parts of the State is illegal, contrary to order issued in G.O.Ms. No. 1 dated 15th December, 1974. [573F] 2.1 The power to organise class or classes of posts of civil serv ices of, and class or class of civil posts under the State into different local cadres for different part of the state is not a matter of right but one of discretion. It is open to the Government to create class or categories of posts in respect of any category of posts.

The plaintiff was the auction purchaser of a plot of land in the village of Bamnapur. The defendants, who were the auction purchasers, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage and obtained an order of sale of the mortgaged property. The plaintiff contended that he was the highest bidder at the auction and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage, it could not be said that the lease in question had been granted by him. Held, that the plaintiff was entitled to redeem the mortgage on payment of the price fixed by the Court. The suit was therefore maintainable. The mere fact that the defendants were the highest bidders did not affect the rights of the plaintiff. The question whether a mortgagor in possession has power to grant a lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land for purposes different from the mode in which he himself used it before he granted the mortgage, could not arise out of the provisions of section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act. The fact that a mortgagor is not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing takes place to impair the value or impede the operation of the mortgagee the mortgagor does not exceed his powers in making a lease for a term, does not affect his rights under section 66. Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumari, I.L.R. , referred to. The case of Banee Pershxd vs Beet Bhunjan Singh, I., L. R. , distinguished. The present case was one where the mortgagor had no power to sell the mortgaged land and that he could not in the usual course of management create a lease. The mortgagor could not therefore in the ordinary course of administration create a tenancy from year to year in the case of agricultural land or from month to month in the cases of agricultural lands or from months to month.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, was awarded work of construction by the respondent for a period of 9 months. The petitioner sent a bill on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. The respondent filed a suit against the petitioner for damages and damages for breach of contract alleging that the petitioner had committed breach of the contract. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the claim was barred by limitation under section 8 of the Limitation Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the period of limitation would apply to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Courts and making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration. Hence this Special Leave Petition. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Indian Limitation Act would apply only to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in an arbitration agreement to the contrary, cause of action shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect of such matters at the time when it should have accrued but for the contract, if the claim is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from the date on which the cause of arbitration accrued. [366B C] 2. The Court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. The court should exercise the discretion sparingly, cautiously and with circumspection to permit a party to rescind the arbitration contract and declared that the arbitration clause shall cease to have effect in respect the dispute or difference. [367C D] 3. In the instant case, by consent the parties have substituted the arbitrator for a Court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences. The period of Limitation for commencing an arbitration runs from the dates on which cause of Arbitration accrued, that is to say, from the time the claim accrues, that was to say from the relevant date when the claimant first acquired either a right of action or a right to require that an arbitration takes place upon the dispute concerned. It is, therefore, open to the parties to plead in the proceedings before him of limitation as a defence. [368D E] 4. The proceedings before the arbitrator are like civil proceedings before a court within the meaning of section 14 of the , By consent the party has substituted the Arbitrator for a court of law for arbiter his disputes or difference and to order that the arbitrator shall not take any action in respect thereof at the date when it would have accrued, but for such contract. [369E F] 5. The procedure under sections 5 and 12(2) (b) to permit the respondent to rescind an arbitration clause is a matter of discretion vested in the Court by section 3 of the Act. It would be open to him to approach a Civil Court for reference to arbitration, but not to approach the Court for relief under section 12(1)(a). [369F G] 6. The Courts below have rightly exercised their discretionary power and jurisdiction under sections 15 and 16 of the . [370G H] 7. The High Court has rightly exercised its discretion under sections 10 and 12 (2) of the Arbitration Act, by not exercising its discretionary power, and jurisdiction thereunder. [370A B] 8. The jurisdiction of the Court is not barred by section 14 to permit an contracting party, to rescind a contract or a part thereof, at the same time to say that if an arbitration is not so commenced the claim concerned shall be barred. [371F G; 371G H; 371A] 9. The law of Arbitration by Justice Bachawat in Chapter XXXVII at p.549 is stated in the case of actions under the Indian Law.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in Bihar. The State of Bihar, on the basis of a notification issued under section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, framed a mortgage decree against the appellants for possession of the lands. The appellants objected to the same on the ground that the execution was barred by the principles of res judicata and further contended that the bar of section 4(d) pleaded was not tenable. The executing court held that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred under section 4 (d). On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree holding that the objections raised by them were barred by res judicata. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the question whether a mortgage debt is barred by principles of Res judicata and (2) that in construing section 4 of the Act, it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the statute do not fall within the protection of the provisions. HELD : (i) The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to scaling down of debts due by proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s 3. Therefore, in construing s 4(a), it would be necessary to bear in mind the object of the enactment which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of the interests and so it would make no difference whether the interest of the debtor affected by provisions of a statute does not fall under the protections of the legislation. [916 D E] (ii) The words "any other object" in section 4 are wide enough to include all matters which are connected with or incidental to the main purpose of the law and, therefore, they must be construed as including within its scope the object which is sought to be achieved by the Act. [940 G H] (iii) The language of s.4(d), in regard only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debt sought to proceed, does not exclude the application of section 5(d).

The respondents, who were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal and were within the permissible age limit and have succeeded are now before this Court. The respondents, however, have been allocated to any of the Central Services, Group 'B ' or I. P.S., and who have appeared in the next Civil Services (Main) Examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central Service Group 'C ' and have been permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to so appear, shall be eligible to do so subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S.(Prelimi nary) Examination Rules, 1988. The Respondents have filed their counter affidavits stating that they have been allotted to the Indian Police Service Group `A ' or Central services Group 'D ' and they have appeared for Civil Services Examination, 1989 or 1989 in pursuance of interim orders passed by the Tribunal. They have also stated that all those candidates who have been selected to any one of the two Services, including the I P. S. or C.P., Group 'E ' and above, shall not be eligible for appearing at the next CSE (Main). The Respondents further state that they are within the permitted age limit, and have failed to resign from service to which they were allocated, nor would they lose their original seniority in the service to whom they have already been allocated. They also state that all these candidates who had been allocated for IAS and IFS Group ' A ' shall be deemed to have been appointed to any post under the Central Service, Group `B ' and not under the orders of this Tribunal and are within permissible age limits and have thereby failed to exercise their right to appear in the subsequent Civil Services examination. The Respondent No. 1 has also filed a counter affidavit stating that all the candidates who were allotted to IAS and C.A. or the Central services, Group A 'and who had joined the I .P. S., Group `C ' have been allowed to sit at the first Civil Services, and they are not within the eligibility limit. The Tribunal has used their expression "may be allowed to appear at the second Civil Services Examinations for the services indicated in Rule 17. The respondent No. 2 has also stated in his counter affidavit that he expressed his intention to appear for IAS in the first C. S.(Prev.) Examination, 1987 or 1989 and have participated in the second C.B.S./89/1989 under the order of this Court dated 15.10.1990. The Union of India has filed a statement stating that the respondent No 2 is not entitled to sit for the main examination since the Tribunal has upheld the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the said Rules. The petitioners have also filed their rejoinder affidavit stating therein that they were not eligible to sit in the main Civil Services examinations for the service indicated in rule 17 of C.C.S (Prev.), Examination Rules 1988 or the order dated 15th October, 1990 passed by this Court in C.W.P No. 1052/1990 and C .A. No. 905/90. The learned counsel for the respondents has also submitted that the Tribunal had allowed the candidates to appear on the first occasion and had accepted their contention that they would be eligible only for those appointments. The counsel for respondent No 1 has stated that he has been allocated from the I C.I.S or Central service Group 'F ' to a State Service Group A and in view of the fact that the respondents have been allo cated to any other Civil Services Group `D ', they are entitled to be considered for the post under Rule 17 and that the said candidate when allocated to IAS or Central Civil Services would have one more attempt in the subse quent Civil Services.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short). The grounds of detention stated that he was not a friend of the detenu and that he had no legal assistance to represent the case of the appellant. The Advisory Board after considering the representation of the appel lant, rejected the detenu 's request for assistance of a friend. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant on the ground that the grounds were not in dispute. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of detention is quashed and set aside. [792B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Government merely informed the detenu that he has no statutory right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board. Since it was for the Advisory board and not for the Government to afford legal assistance, the latter, when he was produced before the Board could have, if he was so minded, made a request to the Advisory Committee for permission to be representa tion by a counsel. [789D] 1:3. The detenu had no right to appear through a lawyer at the hearing and the Advisory Boards did not consider it proper to allow him to represent his case. [788E] 2.1 In the facts of the instant cases, the detaining authority merely informed that he would be represented through a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, was denied the assistance of the retired Assistant Collector of Central Excises. The position, therefore, is that on 25th November, 1986 while the detaining authori ty was assisted by a Deputy Collec tor and a superintendent of Central excise, the detenu was denied his assistance.

The appellants were the owners of certain premises in Calcutta. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the premises on the ground that they had been requisition and acquired by the Government of India under 0. XXIX, r. 75 A (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it holding that the notice of acquisition was not properly served and that the appellants were entitled to possession of certain properties on the grounds that they were requisitioned and acquired for a pucca delivery orders and in view of the usage that pucca delivery order was only issued against payment, were passed from hand to hand by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they related. The High Court held that the notices of acquisition were not properly addressed and that it was not necessary for the holders of the pucca delivery Orders to make a proper service of notice on them. Held, that the respondents were entitled under 0., XXIX to possession on the basis of the service of the notices in this case. The appellants had been served with the notice as required by r. 2 of 0. XXI A (3) of 0., XXI A, and as there was no service of any notice on the owners as required under r. 25 A(2), the property in the goods passed to the Government. The delivery orders were not valid and binding on the appellants. Held further, that it is well settled that a person who has been served by an order of requisition must be given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The service of notices of requisition and notices of acquisi tion in this Case was effective service on the mills as owners for the purpose of r. 74 A (1) of Order XXIX of the Civil Procedure Code. Held also, that a notice of requisition is not properly sent by post under r, 75 A(3). The service must be effected by delivering it to the owner or consignee and the delivery must be made in accordance with the provisions of r, 2 of O. XXI, r., 75 A.

The assessee company was a private limited company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. In the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1963 64, the assessee claimed that it may become liable to pay additional tax under section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. In appeal by Revenue, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of "provision" in section 2(14) of the Act is very wide and includes a provision for reserve. [113E] 2. The expression "reserve" has been defined in the Income ' Tax Act to mean "the reserve". It does not include any reserve. The word " reserve" has not been defined. The term "provision", as used in section 23(1) of Income Tax, is wide enough to include a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of issuance of a notice was a provision and not a reserve. In other words, the broad distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision "and a reserve" is stated. "A reserve is in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business". Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheet by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they are made. [114F G] 3. The question whether a provision is a reserve or not has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is only when there is no specific provision that the provision can be said to have been made. In this case, the finding of the Tribunal relating to assessment year 1964 65 was subsequently rectified by an order dated February 15, 1972 and the said item was held to be a provision. [115G H] 4. The High Court was right in holding it to be so. [116H] 5. The assessee itself called it a provision, and it did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve, as a Reserve. It did not calls it a Reserve nor was the set apart as a reserves. [117A B] 6. The description given or the book entries made by the assessee are conclusive.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Assistant Engineers on the basis of competitive examinations held by the Railway Board. The appointments were made on the recommendation of the Union Public Service Commission, which was constituted under the provisions of the Indian Railways Act, 1890. The petitioners challenged the validity of the classification of personnel into those that were recruited on the ground that they had been appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the principle of continuous service in working posts in Railway prior to their permanent absorption into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the classification was not discriminatory or violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the impugned classification. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the State is prohibited from creating separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably, falls to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by direct Recruit 's case (supra). Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The classification of persons recruited on a particular date is neither discriminatory nor violative of Article 14 or 16 of Constitution. [1022C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners were appointed to permanent posts on temporary basis and that they were not entitled to any promotional avenues. They had been given weightage in seniority cum seniority as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. The classification was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's Case (supra) and the important question of equality was once for all settled. [ 1022D E] 1:3. In Katyni Dayal ' case this Court held that the seniority of the absorbed Assistant Officers would ordinarily reckon from the date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to the maximum of 5 years, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at this point of time to dig up old issues. [1002F G] 1 :4. The distinction between the two services was well settled in Katyanani Dayal vs Union of India and Ors., ; , and the crucial question of equal opportunity for equality before law was considered by this court with weightage to be given to temporary Assistant officers on the strength of their continuous service, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on a regular basis were not available. [1012G H] 1 5.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to a period of two years ' rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance in so far as it authorises the State Government to direct any class of cases or classes of cases to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act is ultra vires and void. The notification issued by the State of West Bengal under section 4(1), of the Act directed certain individuals to be prosecuted for offences under the Indian Penal Code, and it was not necessary that the notification should have been issued in respect of those cases or class of offences. The Notification issued by a State Government under section 6 of the Ordinance authorised the State Govern ment to direct an individual case to be committed by Special Courts constituted under that Act. The object of the notification was to provide for trial of certain offences and classes of offences, and the notification issued thereunder offended against article 14 of the Constitution. The notifications were different from those issued by section 11 Of the Saurashtra ordinance and could not therefore be held to be invalid. The State Government had no power under section 11 to direct a particular case to he tried by Special courts constituted under it. The fact that the State Legislature did not have the power to make a class of persons or classes for trial by Special Tribunals was immaterial because the notification did not specify any particular offence or classes or classes thereof, and could be held invalid only if it was shown that the classification was based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from other offences and that differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of legislation. The Government had power to direct the Special Courts to try such offences or classes as were specified in the notification.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 2, 7 and 8 could not be relied upon because they were interested witnesses; (2) the prosecution had failed to prove the presence of the accused persons at the scene of occurrence; (3) the conviction of the appellant under section 302 I. P.C.; and (4) the High Court erred in holding that the evidence was corroborated by the evidence given by P.W. 1. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The evidence of the eye witnesses is not convincing. [955B] (b) The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High Courts for rejecting the evidence are not convincing and they are not reliable. [940F G] (c) The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants beyond reasonable doubt and that the conviction was not justified on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. [943C] (2)(a). The evidence regarding the presence or non presence of any of the assailants at the time of occurrence could have been relied upon since it is admitted by P,W. 2 that he had gone to the house of his brother Mauji Lal where the occurrence was taking place. It is not improbable that all the appellants were in the eastern kotha where the main part of the occurrence has taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify the witnesses with the help of the lantern which was burning the appellants. [942D E] (3)(a)(b) In the instant case, the evidence regarding presence of P,Ws.1, 7 & 8 at the place of occurrence cannot be relied on because they are interested witnesses. The prosecution had proved the presence and non presence at the spot of occurrence. [948F G; 955A] (4)(a), (b), (c), (d) and (e). [948G H] (5)(a): The evidence relating to the presence, of P 's brother in law, at the relevant time and the fact that they were injured by the assailants is not satisfactory. [947F G]. (6) The High court erred in rejecting the testimony of P W. 1 altogether. [946G] (7) The reason given by both the courts below for rejecting their evidence was not convincing because they had intentionally made improvements in their version about the occurrence. There was sufficient opportunity for them to explain the same. [945A B] (8) The fact that P. Ws. 1 and 7 were injured witnesses to the extent that their evidence is corroborated by medical evidence, does not mean that they are chance witnesses.

The appellant Corporation terminated the services of its employees on the ground of unsuitability and it was not a case of retrenchment. The respondent employer filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33C(2) of the for reinstatement with full back wages. The Labour Court held that termination of the services was bad, but the High Court set aside the order of termination and directed reinstatement with continuity of service. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the termination of services was in violation of section 25F of the , as the termination was by way of punishment inflicted by way off disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman, retirement of surplus labour force and termination of his service on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment '. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the services have been terminated on the grounds of unsubservation and it is not a fit case for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. [789D] 1:3. The termination order passed by the Labour court was in accordance with law and was valid. [788C D] 1 :4. In the circumstances, the High Courts have rightly come to the conclusion that in the instant cases the order terminating the services is bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour 'Court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. [783E F] 1 5. The effect of the definition of retrenchment under section 2(oo) and as used in section 25FFF has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word, it means the discharge of surplus workmen or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted on the workman on reaching its age of superannuation if the termination is by way or otherwise howsoever severe. [784G H] 1 6.

The assessee, a dealer in goods carrying on business of selling scrap and unserviceable material, filed returns for the four quarters ending March 31, 1959. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the appellant to sales tax under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The respondent assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Act. The Sales Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on any business as a "dealer" within the meaning of the Act and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sale effected by the assessee was sales under the provisions of the Bengal Taxation (Sales tax) Act 1941 and therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the said Act. In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the appellant and that therefore the respondent fell within section 2(c) of the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the good came into possession of the assessee. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of goods. It seems to South Eastern Railway that the activity of such disposal was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It appears to South eastern Railway that it was a " dealer" for the purposes of the Calcutta Sales Tax Act, 1940. [781C D] 2. The sale effected in the instant case did not indicated that the railway concerned was carried on any other business as carriers liable to assess under the West Benabari Tea Estate Act enabling it tO sell the goods. The Railway was a carrier of the same goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activities of so disposed of the Goods were adjunated to the Principal activity of carriage of thegoods by the railway. It was an activity incidental or subsidiary to its own business as it was regarded as incidental or auxiliary to its commercial activity as carrier and if that activity was regarded not as necessarily ancillary or ancillary, it would be a "business" within section 10(1)(c) read with section 2 (c). [781E F] 3. The decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423 is not applicable to the instant cases.

The appellant was a Director of the Indian Bank, Bombay. He had been appointed as an officer of the Bank in respect of certain transactions between the two parties. The account books of the bank showed that he had received Rs. 1,00,000 on behalf of the Union Agencies and Rs. 2,00.000 on account of the loss incurred by the Union agencies. The appellant was charged with having committed an offence under section 409 I.P.C., for having caused wrongful gain to the Bank. He was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 10,000 in default to undergo simple imprisonment for six months. On appeal the High Court acquitted him but on further appeal by special leave it was contended that the appellant had not been authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf Of the Insurance Company unless he was authorised by the Chairman. Held, that the transaction was a mere ruse to show that the amount which his company viz., Bhagwati Trading Company, received from the Insurance company must have purported to be on account Of securities sold to the Insurance Companies and not through transfers which transactions had to be adjusted. The fact that the money was received in cash and not by transfer did not make any difference as the appellant was not authorised to buy or sell shares at all. The transaction was for the purpose of securing the payment of money to the Union Agency and it was for him to decide whether he was entitled to purchase securities on his own behalf or through transfer of the funds from the Bank to the Reserve Bank. The transactions were not for the purposes of section 409, I. P. C., but only for the benefit of the Insurance Co. and were not covered by section 409.

The appellants were appointed to the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The State Government by a notification dated November 1, 1956, transferred all the ministerial officers of the department of the Government of Gujarat and transferred them to the Secretariat in the District of Kutch. By an order dated August 19, 1966, the State Government directed that the appellants be absorbed in the Secretariat with effect from April 1, 1966. The appellants were not absorbed in any other department of Government. On November 1. 1956, the appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the orders of the Central Government and the State Govern ment. The High Court held that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to Gujarat was not open to objection. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the transfers were made in accordance with the rules framed under article 309 of the constitution; (2) that there was no violation of any statutory right of transfer; and (3) that since the appellants were posted between 1956 to 1960 in the Districts they will not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. HELD: (i) The High court was wrong in holding that the State 's order transferring the former State and Kutch to the administrative department of Gujarat was invalid. [517 B] (ii) The transfer of a person from one State to another is not open, because, it is made by an authority competent to transfer and does transfer the appellants to perform service in connection with the affairs of the other State. [511 C D] (iii) The power conferred on the Central Govern ment under section 116(7), read with article 309, is subject to the provisions of article 309. [525 E F] (iv) The expression "transfer" in section 115 (7) of the Act means transfer of an officer from one state to another. In the absence of any provision to that effect, it cannot be said that when the State "regularised" the service of a member of the executive cadre is not transferred to the service in the new State which was equivalent and on terms which were not, unless the previous approval of the appropriate Government was obtained, disadvantageous. [500 G H] (v) The word "transfer " in section 116 (7), means transfer from one person to another or from one authority to another, and it is not necessary that there should be a transfer from another State to the same authority.

The petitioners were dealers in cotton and other goods. They were registered as dealers under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The petitioners challenged the validity of the tax on the ground that they had been wrongly assessed to sales tax by the State Government under section 5(2)(a) (vi) of the Act. The High Court held that the tax was not at all leviable on the goods manufactured or produced in the State and that the levy of tax was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the provisions of section 5 (1) were ultra vires as they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they infringed articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: The levy of sales tax is not at the same time a tax at more than one stage in the case of goods manufactured by the last dealer liable to pay tax under section 3 (2) (a) of Central Sales tax Act, 1957. [553 B] The expression "goods" in section 5 of the Central Act includes goods which are sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce. It is not necessary that the goods should be sold in a State or in the territory of India. The expression 'goods ' has been defined in section 2(g) to mean all kinds of movable property and includes all materials used in the manufacture of goods for sale or purchase. [554 C D] In the present case, the petitioners were not liable to tax under the Act because they had purchased cotton and sold it after the period provided for in section 3(2) of that Act. They could not therefore be taxed at more then one stage. [555 E F] The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , followed.

The respondent mortgaged the mortgaged property to the appellant for a sum of Rs. 3,215 and odd. The mortgage was scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 to 7 only and the amended decree directed that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of RS. 1,05,000 and odd and it is on payment of this amount that redemption would be allowed of the mortgaged properties. The appellant contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment Of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2 and 7. Held, that the High Courts had erred in holding that the view taken by the District Judge was correct. The fact that the decree holder did not pay the amount ordered to be deposited by defendants 1 to 7 would not make any difference because the decreeholder did not deposit the amount within the time allowed by the court and the decreeholders were bound to comply with the terms thereof. The High Court had rightly held that the suit was barred by limitation. The decree holders could get the benefit of the scaling down of the debt in favour them only on payment or adjustment of the amount due under the decree as scaled up by the trial court in favour Of defendants 2, 4 and 7 and not on payment by defendants 8 to 7. The judgment debtor did not become entitled to any benefit of a decree which had been scaled off in favour by the executing court.

The appellants were the tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant. The first respondent instituted a suit against the appellants for eviction on the ground that they had been lawfully subtenants of the first plaintiff and were entitled to protection under the Act and that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful subtenants. The appellants contended that the first respondent was not a tenant of the appellants as he was not in possession of the suit premises as sub tenants thereof, and that therefore, the suit was barred by section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the grounds that there had been no lawful subletting by the first appellant of the said premises to the second respondent. On appeal, the High Court held against the first and third defendants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The City civil court could not decree the suit of the plaintiffs unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the provisions of the Act or any of its provisions. [374 B] (ii) The Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1946, is a law relating to landlord and tenant and it does not affect the jurisdiction of courts to try such a suit. It does not deal with the rights of the landlord and those to whom he had sublet the premises. [375 C] (iii) The provisions of section 28 clearly indicate that all claims or questions arising out of the statute or any provision thereof, even though they may be in the nature of title to the premises, were to be determined by the courts specified in section 28 and no other. The provisions in the Act, on the other hand, clearly indicate the filing of any suit relating to possession. [373 E] (iv) The High Court correctly decided that the suit filed by the plaintiffs was not one between a landlord and a tenant because the defendants of this suit did not admit that the plaintiffs were the licensees of the defendants.

The respondent company was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., a company which had been incorporated under its name and styled as Oriental Metal pressing Works. The appellant, who was the managing director of the company, was appointed as the managing directors of the Company by the will of Dadoba. On July 7, 1955, the respondent wrote to the appellant that he had not been appointed as managing director but only as the Managing Director. The company then applied for appointment of a new director and the appellant contended that the appointment of the appellant as the director was void under section 86B of the Act. The High Court held that the word "assignment" in section 312 of the new Act meant a transfer of office, and so the appointment by the company was not an assignment of his office by him for the old Act contained in section 83B. Held, that the appellant had no right to appoint the managing Director as he was not the chosen representative of the shareholders and the respondent could not claim any right to have a say in the appointment. The proviso to section 86 B does not indicate that it was intended that the words "assign" would include appointment. It is only when the word 'assignment ' is used in the main part of section 86A that an appointment of an alternate director by a director can be deemed to be an assignment and would not therefore be rendered void by the section. The respondent could, therefore, claim to have the say in his appointment as the Director.

The appellants are the partners of a partnership firm. The respondent filed eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart, on the ground that they were unlawful sub tenants. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart without joining any of the partners as respondents or serving them as partners and hence the eviction petition was not maintainable. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the ground established by the evidence on record was sufficient to warrant a finding that the sub tenants had sublet the premises to the appellants. In an appeal under section 23 of the Rent Act, the respondent contended that the partnership firm was carrying on business in the name and style of M/S Adeshwar Industries and that the firm was carried on business at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Road, Madras. The appellate Authority dismissed this contention holding that it is only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction proceedings were filed against the appellant firm and one another partnership firm and that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellant had sublet shop to M/ S Adeshwar Chettiar. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The partners of the firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. [420C] 2. The partner of the partnership is before the court although in a proper case, it would have been open to the respondent to amend the eviction proceeding and join the partners. In such a case, the High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of eviction passed by the trial court. [426D E] 3. The question whether the appellants sublet the business to M was a matter which could be decided only at the stage of the proceedings under the Rent Control Act either and hence, the ratio laid down in Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case is directly applicable to the case before this Court. [416E F] 4. In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage when Special Leave and it is surely not open to this court to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1961 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land in excess of the ceiling area. Section 2(n)(A)(ii) defines 'family unit ' to mean a family unit which is owned by or under the control of the Government and includes any other unit which may be notified as an urban agglomeration under section 2(1). The Andhra Pradesh Act was amended by the Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings (Amendment) Act 1974. Section 3(j)(A) provides that where any land held by a person in excess thereof is not a member of a family units, the whole of such land shall be deemed to be an urban land and the provisions of section 4 shall apply accordingly. The Andhra Act was repealed by the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1974 which came into force on 1st January 1975. Section 7(1) provides for the levy of ceiling area on land held in excess. Section 8(2)(A), (B) and (C) provide that where a person is not holding any agricultural land in the urban agglomerations referred to in section 2 (n) (A) (ii) of the Act, he shall be liable to pay a sum equal to one half of the amount of the tax payable on such land. Section 9(1)(b) provides, inter alia, that where an area is notified as urban agglogenation under section 3(2), the Central Government would have power to make rules for the purpose of determining the ceiling on holding of land in such area. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the validity of the Andhra Act and the Andhra Area (Ceiling) Rules was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the definition of 'family Unit ' in section 3 (j)(a)(ii), as amended by Act 1 of 1975, was an inclusive one and therefore the entire land held under the urban land Ceiling Act would be liable for levy of the Ceiling on land situate within such area, and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 4(1 ) of the Central Act was an isolated one, it was not permissible to enact that definition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of family unit in section (j) of Central Act is an inclusive definition and any land which comes to the share of a divided minor son would be included in the family unit and by reason of section 3 of that Act the entire property held by him whatever acquired is liable to be clubbed with the land held as such. [1158H 1159A] 2. The expression 'family units ' in Section 3 (f) of that act includes a family Unit which may also include a family, but every family unit shall be treated as an industrial unit and the entire family unit will be treated separately for the purposes of assessment to land revenue. [1102C D] 3. The word 'family" is defined in the Act to mean any person who has been allotted any land or other property by the Government or a local authority, but does not include a member or a family after the operation of the definition. [1058D] 4. The term 'family ' is defined to mean the wife and children of a member, whether an individual or a Hindu undivided family. [ 1059E] 5. In respect of land situate in any area other than that comprised in the Urban agglomeration referred to under section 4 (1) of Act 1/75, the Andhra area would be treated on par with that comprised therein and by virtue of section 2 of that section the entire house property would be deemed as an agricultural land and would not be liable as part of joint family property. [1002F] 6. The land obtained by the divided minor sons on partition would be assessed to land tax under the Andhra Land Reforms Act, 1964. [1013B] 7.

The appellant company was a public limited company and its workmen were dismissed from service. The Company terminated the services of the workmen on October 2, 1953, but did not pay them wages for the period. The company filed an application before the Labour Appellate Tribunal under section 33 Of the , for permission to dismiss the workmen. The Industrial Tribunal held that the workmen had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence and dismissed the application. On appeal by the Company, the High Court held that all the workmen were entitled to be taken back as of right without any condition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Industrial Tribunal that the respondent workmen failed to prove their absence was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. [617 D] (ii) The Industrial Tribu nal found that the appellant had failed in proving his absence and that the evidence showed that he was not taking complete rest as required by the notice dated September 17, 1953. The Tribunal also held that there was no proof of any misconduct on the part of the respondent workman. [674 E] (iii) The fact that the workers were suspended for a long time did not mean that they had been discharged without any reason or justification. It is only when the workmen are found guilty of misconduct, that it would be open to the employer to dismiss them with effect from August 24, 1953 and the notice terminating their services was given on October 1, 1953 but failed to do so. [676 G] (iv) The Tribunal had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and held that it was not justified in refusing leave. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as in this case, the work of the Company will be paralysed if the company is forced to give leave to all of them for a " more or less indefinite period" and that would not justify the dismissal of the appellant. [677 G H] (v) The evidence showed the appellant 's absence from October 2. 1953, when the strike was over and the workmen did not take any part in it. The fact of the workman having been suspended for some reason or other did not show that he had taken any part of his activities in the course of his employment. [678 C] (vi) The appellant 'rejected to the plea that the work was not satisfactory and that there were no sufficient reasons for the absence. The evidence shows that the workman was not taken back by the company but was engaged in doing some "public work". The fact, however, that the men were suspended during the period of strike did not lead to any inference that they were not taking part in the discharge of their duties. [679 G H; 678 A B] (vii) The question whether a workman had been dismissed or removed from service without holding an enquiry is one of fact depending on the circumstances of each case and no hard and fast rule can be laid down as to what really is a finding of fact. In the present case, however the Tribunal found that there had been absence without any leave and in view of the circumstance that the man was suspended for certain reasons, it could not be said that the discharge was mala fides. [680 E F] (viii) The contention that the company having held a regular and proper enquiry in which Samar Sen had an opportunity of meeting the charges against him, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribun al should not have interfered with the decision of the company unless it found that it had taken into account the relevant circumstances.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the University Act, 1974 recommended the name of Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list. The appellant Dr. (1) was a teacher in the department of Bothis. He was appointed as Professor in the Department of Botswright. He joined the post on the ground that he had joined the said post without any objection. The appointment of Dr, UreaK was challenged by him before the High Court which allowed his writ petition and quashed the selection made by the Selection Committee. The High Court held that the Committee constituted for the selection of a professor in BotsWright was not properly constituted and that once a selected person joined that post then selection made under section 6 would not be less than five, out of which at least two shall be the experts, if the Selection Commit tee were to be considered for appointment. The Committee while making its recommendations to the Syndicate under sub section (2) shall prepare a list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and shall further prepare a reserve list in the same order and to the extent of 50% of the vacancies for the posts of teachers or officers for which the Selection committee was constituted. The Syndicate, therefore, made its recommendations on the basis of the reserve List. The Chancellor of the High School and Intermediate Education Department, however, did not agree with the recommendation of the Selection Board. The University filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the selection and appointment of the appellant Dr Urea Kshatra as Professor. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the committee constituted for selection of the respondent was proper and in accord ance with the provisions of section 5(1) of the Act. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the University against the judgment of the Single Judge was dismissed by a Division Bench. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve List would be defeated if the view taken by the High Courts is accepted that once the person selected by the selection committee has joined that office then selection is exhausted and the reserve select list is of no avail and becomes extinct. There was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve lists alive for a long period of one year, as no person selected for the said posts can at all be expected not to join for such a long time of one ye ary year. If the view adopted by the high Court is accepted, it would lead to chaos and confusion if the views taken by High Courts are accepted. [419G H; 418A B] 1.2 The very object of preparing the reserve s list would be frustrated if the opinion given by the Chancellor is accepted. In the instant case, according to the university such a procedure was in vogue in all the universities of Rajasthan that a reserve sistent for the appointment on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserved list, and many appointments had been made in the last decade from the reserve panel.

The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of sections 4 and 11(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the ground that they were violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that their lands were earmarked in the development plan originally published under section 17 of the Act for a public purpose, namely, for development of land for a housing scheme, and that the reservation and re inclusion of these lands for recreation centre and green belt by the first respondent was in contravention of section 9 of the . The petitioners also contended that the provisions of sections 14, 15 and 16 were violative Of article 14. Held: (i) The combined operation of sections 3 to 17 of Act No. 1 of 1964 is not a mere executive action but an administrative act which is quasi judicial or quasi judicial. It is not necessary for the purpose of any particular statute to be considered in each case whether it is a mere administrative act or quasi administrative act. The provisions of the two Acts are intended to serve as a social welfare measure and they have to be construed in their widest amplitude, so that the object of the legislation may be achieved by giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the equitable distribution of land among the people. (ii)The provisions of section 17(3), which were enacted for the benefit of the owner of the land for housing scheme and for the development of the area within its jurisdiction, are not in any way inconsistent with the object sought to be achieved thereby by the Act. The purpose of the statute is to provide a speedy remedy for the acquisition of land designated for public purposes under section 7 of the , and if it does not vest in the local authority, the State Government may, and if so required by the State Govern ment after the date on which a development plan for any area or, as the case may be, the part of such plan has come into force, make a declaration of its intention to prepare such a plan and send it to the State Govt. for public purpose. The scheme is intended to provide for the improvement of the areas in the area so that there may be no conflict between the two. (iii)The Act does not contemplate any acquisition of any land designated as an alternative for a purpose under section 4 or section 11(1). The provisions are not inconsistent with any other provision of the law. The preparation of the tentative plan or the final development plan is not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authori ty. If the provisions are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the act.

The appellant, a displaced person from Pakistan, was granted a lease of certain land in the State of Kutch for a period of five years. The lease was renewed by the Government of India on the basis of the report of the Collector of Kutch that the land had been acquired by the State and that the compensation payable to it was adequate. The appellant challenged the validity of the grant of the lease by the Bombay High Court in a writ petition filed by him under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Government had no power to make laws for the acquisition of land for the purposes of the Act, and that there was no question of any conflict between the two States. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the alignment of the boundary under the award was indefinite and by the award of the Tribunal the true boundary of India was not disturbed; (ii) the compensation awarded by the Tribunal was inadequate, because the dispute was to be decided by arbitration, (iii) the award did not purport to, nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. HELD: (i)(a) The High Courts were right in holding that the award made by the tribunal was not a valid award and that it was not open to challenge under article 226 of the Consti tution. [329 B] (b) The award did no more than define on the surface of the earth a boundary which had at all material times remained indefinite, because of the nature of the terrain, the shifting nature of border between the States and the distance from the two states was not indefinite. [313 C D] (c) The reference to the High Court was not in any way inconsistent with the award. It was not evidence of the fact that it had been territory over which the Maharao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territory became Indian territory, and therefore, the rule earlier laid down by this Court applied.

The appellant mortgagor had leased out his lands to certain lessees for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments, the first in the month of June 1946 and the second in the third in the monthly instalments. The mortgagee was entitled to recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bahaldih from the appellant. The mortgagor 's right, title and interest in the mortgaged properties were transferred to the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage money on August 27, 1922, and obtained an assignment of the rights of the mortgagees under the two deeds dated June 14, 1922 and August 27. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 1, 1937, by the auction purchasers. The High Court held that the claim was within time both on account of part payment and on the cause of action furnished by the dispossession and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the covenant in the mortgage deed dated June 18, 1946, which was a usufructuary mortgage was not given in mortgage to the mortgagees as evidenced by the endorsement on the first mortgage deed, and (2) that by the covenants in the deed dated July 12, 1922 the mortgagor had lost all his interest therein. HELD: (i) The suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell was barred under article 120 of the Limitation Act from the date of destruction or deprivation of the property. [695 D] (ii)The words "the person liable to pay" in the two mortgage deeds dated July 13, 1922 were not given as a condition precedent to the payment of the principal and interest. The words "any person liable" in either of them were intended to convey the right to recover from the mortgagor 'in respect of any sum due by him on account by sale or otherwise. [641 D] In the present case, the mortgagee had lost his interest as a result of the sale of the mortgaged property and the suit filed within twelve years from the dates of dispossession was within limitation. [651 F] (iii)The appellant 's claim to enforce the mortgage dated August 27 , 1922, was at the date when the mortgagor died and he could not therefore maintain the appeal.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. The company was prepared to grant free transport facilities to the supervisory staff and the appellants also undertook not to charge any charges for the transport facilities granted to the employees. The appellants contended that the services rendered by them were not liable to be taxed as and when they paid the tax, and that the amounts collected by the appellants from their employees were not in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the company was preparing a scheme for grant free Transport facilities to its supervisory staff there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and that even if a nominal charge is realised from the employees, they would be provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax could be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public service vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [361 E F] 2. The word 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules. It is true that the term 'public services vehicle ' had not been used either by Act or the Rules but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the Act it is of a nature of public service vehicles. [362 F G] 3. The definition of 'stage carriage ' in section 2(7) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public Service vehicle. [363 A B] 4. The transport service in the present case falls squarely within the ambit of the definition of the expression 'stages carriage ' as contained in section 3(7). [362 C D] 5. The words "public service vehicles" have not been mentioned either by statute or by any other statutory provision. It has not even been shown that the transport vehicle provided to the employee by the appellant could be a public serv ice vehicle in any sense of the term. [364 E F; 362 A] 6. The expression 'public serv ice vehicles ' has neither been defined nor is it defined either in the Act, or by Rules. The meaning of the word 'private service vehicle" has not created any difficulty. It may be that the word `public service ' has been used in a statute or statutory provision but that does not confer any right on the owner to claim compensation for the services provided by him. [365 E F]. 7. The appellant had not charged any amount from the respondent for providing transport facilities, and no charges were levied on the employees for providing the transport facility. The High Court was therefore in error in holding that the Transport Authority imposed tax on the appellants. [366 G H] 8. The services provided to employees by the company were reserved for them only and no other member of the Public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that the transportation vehicle provided in the instant case was not a public servant within the meaning of section 2 (7) or section 3 of the . [366 A B].

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a "no objection certificate" under Rule 101 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972, filed an application before the State Government for a writ of mandamus directing the State to consider their objections and to grant a licence in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants had not been afforded any opportunity to show cause against the grant or refusal of a licence. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the detailed provisions for the grant and renewal of a license at three distinct stages by the licensing authority in the process of licensing a cinema house, viz., (ii) no objection certificate for the site on which the cinema house is to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence had been granted under Rule 102 of the Rules; and (iii) the appellants who had not applied for a licence were not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act does not confer any right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authori ty. [897G] 2.1 The Act did not confer an absolute right of appeals on a party who might not have raised such objections but whose objection had been overruled by the State Govern ment. [798H; 899A] 2:2. The provisions of the Act do not confer a right of second appeal on any person who may have raised the objections before it against the order granting a licence, and they cannot now be permitted to reagitate the claim of the applicant for a cinema licence. [800B C] 3.1 A combined reading of sections 3 to 6 of the shows that the licensing authorities are not bound by the provisions of any statute or rules made thereunder. The only thing which is required to be done in exercise of such powers is to see that there is no conflict between the two. [901C D] 3:2 The Act, does not give any right to appeal on the person who had raised objections against the granting of a cinema license. It merely provides for an appeal against the decision of the licensing au thority refusing to grant or renew a licence under rules 101 and 102. The appellants not being entitled to challenge the grant o f a "No objection" certificate, and their objection having been overruled, could not now be allowed to plead a right to oppose the grant. [900D E] 3 :3. In the instant case, the appellants objected to renewal of the cinema licence on the ground that they had not filed any objections. The State Government did not give them any opportunity of being heard and decided the appeal at their back. The order granting the no objection Certificate was therefore violative of the principles of natural justice.

The respondent, a partnership firm, entered into an agreement with the appellant for assigning to the plaintiffs ' leasehold rights under a mining lease in respect of certain lands. The appellants filed a suit against the respondent claiming a declaration that they were entitled to remain in possession of the mining area. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaint was not an acceptance of the offer by the appellant 's plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957. [584 F] (ii) The respondent did not agree to purchase the mining lease. The contract was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that in breach of the contract the defendant failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the central government to the assignment of the lease. [585 G] (iii) The High Court rightly held that the plaintiffs accepted the offer of September 2. 1957 by their plaint in the suit. The plaintiffs had not agreed to purchase a mining lessee under a contract dated August 3, 1957. The respondent was at liberty to revoke the offer at any time before its acceptance by the appellants. [585 H] (iv) The plea that the contract was not concluded on October 31, 1957, was not accepted by the High court. [583 F G] Bloxam 's case, referred to. (v) The plaintiffs were entitled under the contract to remain In possession of mining area and the respondent was bound to deliver possession within a stipulated time. [582 B C] (vi) The suit was not one for specific performance of the contracts. The plaint in that suit was an offer to assign the mining leases. No acceptance was made or communicated to the defendant before November 6, 1957; nor was it communicated to him before November 5, 1957 when the suit was instituted. [587 C D] (vii) The appellants had not given notice of allotment to the respondent before November, 1, 1957 in which case they could not get a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mine lease. In fact, no such notice was given to the appellant before November 7, 1957 nor was any intimation sent to him by the respondent that he would perform the contract and that he reserved his right to file a suit for specific enforcement.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 for contravention of the provisions of the Act. The prosecution alleged that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The appellants contended that the price was not a fixed price and therefore the complaint was not maintainable. Held: (i) The Central Government could not take up the investigation into the same.
