The power under section 33 of the , is a part of an administrative power and it can be exercised only in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law. The Act does not provide for any delegation of legislative power to the Central Government. The Central Govern ment was also well within its powers in issuing the Sugarcane Control Order, 1955 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III. (ii) The regulation of the price and control of the prices is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 and therefore there could not have been any delegation. The State Government was well within the powers in legislating in regard to sugarcane and the Central Govern ments were well within their powers in passing the impugned order. (iii) The power conferred on the Government under section 2(b) of that Act cannot be challenged as invalid. The complaint made before the police did not disclose a preservable offence and as such the police could not had taken up the Investigation of that complaint. The offence complained of is punishable with three years ' imprisonment and as there was no agreement in writing to the contrary between the parties the police can not have taken up investigation of that offence.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of iron and steel products. The Government of Karnataka issued an order dated 30th June, 1969 which recited that the Government had decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation and that in pursuance thereof the Government has on 30th November, 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. On 12th January, 1977 the Government of India issued another order which stated that the reasons for making the said order of 12th February, 1977 were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limit or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The appellant company filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th April, 1969 when the order dated 12th June 1969 came into effect and before 949 the order was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concession constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order of 30th July, 1969. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the State Government that the concessions granted under the said orders were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same; (2) the concession granted by the earlier order dated 13th January 1977 was a policy decision to encourage urban industrialisation, and that the concession was given to those industries which had been granted prior to 30th May, 1969; (3) the concessions in question were of no legal effect as there was no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order granting the concession constituted an estoppel against Government on this basis. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the present cases because it is found by this Court that the State had no authority to provide for the grant of refund. [950C] 2.1 In order to test the validity of the order passed by 30th of June 1969, one has to see the substance of the concession and not merely certain words used out of context. The second submission of the learned counsel is that since the benefit given was called a refund, it cannot be said that the doctrine was good law now. [951F] 2:2 In order that the grant may be justified, the State should have made an express provision in the order itself for granting refund. It could not therefore be said to be an exemption or reduction as permitted by section 8A. [953B C] 3. The fact that the order is passed by the authority which has issued the order does not establish that the benefits were, in fact, misused. In effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of sales Tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the Order. [952C D] 4. The mere fact that a decision has been taken by the authorities that the benefit was not extended would not establish the plea that the promise was made or undue advantage taken of.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegation that they caused the death of one Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused but convicted them under Sections 148 and 307 read with section 149 I P.C., and sentenced each of them to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302 readwith Section 34 I.p.C.; and acquit ted them on the ground that they formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I. P. C. The High Court also held that the appellants were guilty under section 148 and sentenced to imprisonment for seven years. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1 to A7, the named persons, formed the Unlawful assembly. A 4 to A 7 having been acquitted, the remaining three appellants cannot be convicted under Section 148 and on applying 149 I .P. C., they are guilty of offence punishable under Sections 302 read wo 34 I P C. [8D] 1.2 The High court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction of the appellant under Sections 149 and 307 I.PC. if the evidence disclosed commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. [9E F] 1:3. In the instant case, there is no doubt that A 4, being three in number, could not have formed an assembly within his definition. The non applicability of Section i49 I.A.C was, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants for offences punishable under sections 148 and 149 I PC. [10F G] 1 :4. In view of the fact that A 2 gave blows to the deceased with their respective weapons, it is in evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between the parties. The deceased and the appellants belong to a different family. There was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn and manufac turing cloth, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1964 65. The assessee claimed that the value of the goods sold by it should be taken as the full value of consideration declared by the assessee by an amount of not less than 15% of the value so declared, which was accepted by the assessing authority and confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that since the actual consideration received by the asses see is not declared or disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income tax officer to determine precisely what is actually paid by the assesses and permitted the assessee to take the fair market value of its capital asset as on the date of transfer exceeded the full amount of consideration declaring the true value of that consideration declared. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The real consideration received in respect of the transfer and sub section (2) applies only where the consideration for the transfer is under stated or in other words, shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by assessee. If therefore the Revenue seeks to bring a case within sub section(2), it must show not only that the fair price of the capital asset transferred by the assessees as on that date exceeded the value declared by them, but also that the consideration has been under stated and the assessee has actually received more than what is declared by him. [643E F] 1.2 The real test of determining whether a transaction is one which is not in fact an adventure in the nature of trade or business is to find out whether it is for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. If it is shown that the transfer was made with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability, then it would be a case where the real consideration has actually been received by it and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gains or any other type of income. [642C D] 1:3 The true test of ascertaining whether a particular transaction is a genuine one or not is to see whether the consideration paid represents the price at which the property is sold, the price actually received and the market value. If the consideration is not disclosed and the consideration declared in respect thereof is shown at more than a lesser amount than that actual received by him then it will be a transaction of sale. [ 643D E] 1 :4 The real question to be determined in each case is whether the fair and reasonable price of a capital asset has been paid or not. If, therefore, the Revenue wants to bring into existence an adventure which is more beneficial than that in respect whereof the assessee seeks to take a larger consideration for transfer than what was declared by it, then the difference between the market price and the full consideration for such transfer would amount to a gift liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act. [ 644E F; G H] 1 5. The real criterion of ascertaining the true nature of the transaction is whether it has been effected with the intention of avoidance of liability or not, and whether the assessee had actually received the excess amount. If that was so, then there would be no question of attracting the applicability of sub section 2 of section 52. [466G H] 6. The true criterion for determining whether the transaction was one which was not in reality an adventure of trade is to look into the nature and character of the consideration received or deemed to have been received. If a capital assets are transferred for a consideration below its market value, the difference would be liable to be added as part of capital gains taxable under the provisions of the Gift tax Act, 1958 but if the construction of sub sections (2), (3) and (4) is accepted, such difference would also be liable for deduction. [641A B] 7.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that the Food Inspector, who stated in his examination in chief that he had seen the appellant and the Food inspector on the day of occurrence at about 8 a.m. on 3 12 1968 at night, when he was alleged to have been taken by the Food Inspectors to the shop of the appellant, that he took the signatures of Tambe from the cash memo, but not on the packets, although he had deposed in his cross examination that he did not know the contents of the cash memos. The trial court acquitted the appellant holding that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was more credible and that it was corroborated by what the Inspector stated in the examination in Chief that Tambe had signed the sealed packet also. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the presence of the FoodInspector at the shop on 3 2 1968 at 8 a .m. and that the appellant could have been kept for the purpose of being sold without giving such information to the Food Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of food meant for human consumption, and that in any event, the purpose for which the articles were kept in the accused 's shop was more probable because it was supported by what he had written on the cash memorandum when he sold these Til seeds. HELD: (1) The evidence of a prosecution witness is not to be discarded merely because he has deposed in favour of the accused. [330 D] (2) It is true that the signature of Tamis are absent on all those documents on which they would have been present if section 10(7) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, was strictly complied with. But it is not correct to say that this case had been repelled by mere statement of the Inspector that they could be used as food also. [334 E] (3) The fact that the signatures were absent on the Cash memo when he purchased these Til seed from the appellant did not mean that it should reach the consumer to be used for the use as food whenever reasonable doubts arise. It is more likely, for the reasons already given by us, that Tamis were not there at all to witness the occurrence. [328 E] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , followed. (4) The appellant was rightly convicted under section 10 of the . [330 G] (5) The prosecution has failed to establish that the article which is the subject matter of an offence is ordinarily used for human food when reasonable doubts arose. It cannot be said that this is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as 'food '.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th of January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was also dismissed on 31st August, 1966. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to claim any salary from 13th January 1966 till his retirement. The first appellate court confirmed the decree but the High Court dismissed the second appeal on 31.8.1966. In the second case, the question for consideration was whether the order in the proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High court was an order prior to the Constitution and, therefore, the High Courts had no jurisdiction to issue a writ to the appellate authority. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed in appeal therefrom and an order dismissing the appeal therefrom by an appeal court and the order dismissing it, if no such order is made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the said date. [54H; 55A] 2. The order of the High COurt was communicated to the appellant on 19th September 1960. He filed an appeal before the Divisional Commis sioner and that was dismissed on 30th August 1966. In his appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that the orders of dismissal were bad and that the suit was within time. The High Court held that the impugned order in proceedings under article 226 of t he Constitution before it was an ex parte order could not be equated with any propriety or irregularity in the procedure adopted by the subordinate courts. [55E F] 3. In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of a action shall first accrue and where such order was not made, on the expiry of six months from the dates of preferring of the appeal, or making of the representation shall be take to be the date on which cause of the action shall he taken to have first arisen. The expression "any other sufficient reason" in section 5(2) of the Act means a reason sufficiently cogent and convincing. [56A B] 4. In each case only where the appeal is disposed off, cause is first accrue.

The respondent filed a suit for partition of his share in the property which was decreed by the trial court. The appellant contended that the decree was not a decree of affirmance but variation and this was not binding on him as he had not been given notice of the appeal under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the decision of the trial Court was final and the appellate decree did not bind the respondent. The decision of a court which passed a variation in the decision is final and its effect is not affected by any change made in the judgment or decree. In the present case the appellant had not filed an appeal against the decree but only applied for leave to appeal to the Privy Council. The question whether the appellate court was bound to give notice of appeal under s 35 of that Act was a matter which could be decided by the Privy council and not by reference to the part of the decree under appeal. The words "decree" in section 110 of the Civil Procedure Code mean the decision or the decree appealed from. In view of the fact that the appellant did not file an appeal, the respondent applied for permission to appeal and urged that the appellate Court was bound by the judgment of the lower court. Held further, that if the appellate judgment does not expressly say so, it is a decree in rem and the High Court has no power under section 115 C.P.C. to interfere with such an order. The word "decision" in the Code means the decision on any matter in controversy in the proposed appeal.

The respondents were the owners of certain properties in Uttar Pradesh. The appellants filed a revision petition under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court against the order of the District Judge under section 25 Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, disposing of a revision application. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that the High court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 5(e) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 to make a clear cut division of jurisdiction between the High Courts and the District Court resulting in exclusive revisional jurisdiction to the High 'Court in cases arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above. The respondents filed revision petitions before the Allahabad High Court under section 116 Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 against the orders of the Additional District Judge, Lucknow, and the Magistrate, Lucknow. The U. P. President 's Act was amended by U.p. Act No. 1 of 1978 with retrospective effect from 1st February, 1977. The amendment made in 1972 added a proviso to section 25, U.Ps. (Amendment) Act No 1 of 1979, which declared that in relation to any case decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising under the original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by the District court, the High Commissioner alone shall be competent to make an order under this section. The appellant filed a writ petition in the Allahabad high Court challenging the constitutional validity of the amendment made by U P. Act 1 of 1980. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the provisions of section 115 Code of civil Procedure, read with section 115 CPC were not applicable to the State of Uttar Pradesh and (ii) that a revision under section 114 Code of ' Civil Procedure was maintainable against an order of District Court under Section 25 Provincial small Cause Courts. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 An order passed under section 20, Provincial Small Causes Courts Act by a District Court is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Curt under section115, Code. [38C] 1.2 The High Courts have exclusive jurisdiction in a revision Petition filed before them under section 120 Code of the Civil Procedure, and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional power of the State under section 105, Code, of Civil procedure. No. 9752 of 1979 is therefore, amenable to revisional jurisdiction. [39D] 1:3. The provisions of Section 115 Code read with Section 115 CPC are not applicable in case this Court is of the opinion that a Revision Petition under section I21, Provincial small Causes Courts act by a district court is not appealable. [40E F] 1 :4.

The respondents, a private limited company, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959. The High Court held that the service of notice under sub section (2) of section 52 was not an integral part of the cause of action and was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the notification dated February 8 , 1984 issued by State Government of Rajasthan under section 51(1). The respondents filed a special leave petition against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The writ petition filed by the respondents was not maintainable in view of the decision of this Court in State of Orissa vs M/s. Orissa Cement Ltd., ; , which held that section 52 of the Act did not apply to the case. [605C] 2. The notification issued under section 49(1 ) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 by the Government of India under section 5 (21) of Act for acquisition of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz., the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, the Civil Line Extension Scheme and the Land Acquisi tioned Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur. The entire cause of actions culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 53(1), of the , arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the Rajaswa High Court at Jaipur. [613H; 602A B] 3. The respondents did not raise any objection as to the power and authority of the State Govern ment of Rajasthan to acquire the land in question at Jaipur and wanted to challenge the validity or propriety of the notice issued by it under section 50(2) or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section 54 (3). [606C D] 4. The State Government had no power to acquire any land for the purpose of executing a development Scheme at public expenses viz., for implementation and execution of a scheme at Public expense. The only thing which was required to be done by the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 55(1)(a) of that Act was to issue notice to the respondents in compliance with the provisions of section 54(3). The entire purpose of the acquisition was for the implementation of development scheme and not for the purposes of executing any scheme at a public expense. [ 602D E] 5. The Government of the Jaipur Development Authority, Jaipur issued a notification under section 48(1 )(a), Or the Act and the notified land vested in the State Govt free from all encumbrances. The whole purpose of acquisition was to provide for the development scheme for the benefit of the public at large. [ 603E] 6. The provisions of sections 52(2), 53(3) or section 54 of the are not applicable to the instant case because the respondents had not raised any objection in the proceedings before the Special officer, Town planning Department, Rajasthan under Section 52(l)(a). [613F G] 7. The scheme was duly published and published in the official Gazette and the land vested with the State government free from encumbrances. It is not necessary for the respondents to plead the service or opportunity of hearing on them by the special officer, town planning Department , Jaipur under Section 55(2).

The appellant was the tenant of a building in 1968. The landlord filed an application for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the building in question had been constructed in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court rejected the application holding that the construction of the building was completed in 1968, and that the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Judge that the buildings were not ten years old on the date of the suit and, as such, the new rent Act had no application to the building. The High Court, however, allowed the revision petition holding that since the building had been completed in 1969, it would be deemed to have been completed on 1st October 1971, the date when the revision came into force and, consequently, the newly constructed building was not ten year old on 1.10.1971. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) The High court had rightly held that the payment through the cheque may have been made by the appellant towards rent for some period prior to April 7, 1976 and held it to be manifestly erroneous and without any basis. [334C] (2) Section 20 of the new Act provides a bar to a suit for eviction on the specified grounds. The provision is intended to protect tenants from eviction on certain specified grounds and not to create new tenancies or to impose new obligations on them. [340D] (3) The expression "premises" in section 2(2) means any building which has been constructed principally of the one or more of the buildings mentioned in the definition clause. The expression 'premises ' is defined in section 3(1) to mean any building or part thereof which has not been constructed on any date before the commencement of this Act and includes a house, shop, stable, shed or other structure which has become vacant after the date on which the completion thereof is reported to or otherwise recorded by the local authority having jurisdiction. [341E F] (4) The word "premises " in section 20 means any land or building which is let out for residential purposes and includes any building used as a place of business or for any other purpose. The word 'premises" has been defined in the Act to mean all buildings, whether existing or not on the appointed day. [343G H] (5) Section 2(1)(a) defines "building" to mean a building which was constructed principally with the consent of the landlord and includes also any building let out by him to another person for residential purpose. [344H; 344A] (6) The words "premises used as such in the section" are not defined in that Act. Section 2 (1)(b) defines 'building ' to mean land or buildings which have been constructed before the date specified in the notice issued under sub section (2). [346B] (7) The building was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed that the new building would be assessed on the basis of the date from which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and not on any other date.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Director, was appointed as the sole arbitrator. The respondents filed their written statements denying the execution of the works contract. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed that decision. Held, that the award passed by the arbitrator was not a nullity and no decree could be passed in terms thereof. The award was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 12 of the Schedule to the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated if it does not fall within item 2, and in consequence no decree can be passed thereon. The question whether the award was a original or a copy thereof could not be decided by the trial court on the basis of a notification issued under section 35 of the Stamp Act. The High Court was right in holding that the agreement to refer to arbitration was not an original instrument but a copy of it. The document actually before the court was, what it purports to be, "a certified copy" and that under section 36 of the Indian Evidence Act there can be validation only if it is unstamped or insufficiently stamped. The fact that the Executive Engineer had been authorised to execute the agreement did not affect the validity of the award.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. He was charge sheeted under section 120B IPC and Section 5(2) read with Section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under Section 161 I.P.C. The Trial Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been given a reasonable opportunity to defend himself against the charges framed against him. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the acquittal order and convicted the appellant under section 5(1)(a) readwith section 5 (2) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court also convicted the accused under Section 5 of the Act for having caused damage to the property of the appellant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the State that since Kailash Nath and the prosecution as against Kailash Nath were acquitted, the order of acquittal could not be sustained. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly quashed the First Information Report as against the appellant in criminal appeal No. 422/88. [914C] 1.2 In view of what has been said above and keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2.2, there is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said rule. [936D] 1:3. The object of the rule making power under Article 309 and the purpose for which it can be exercised are not to be found in the main rule 2.1 but in the third proviso to clause (b) of Rule2.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The shares were allotted to the appellant company. In September 1936 the respondent company sold its preference shareholders 's share capital in the name of " Amrutanjan" and the appellant was the managing director of the company. On October 3, 1936 the appellant issued a notice under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon it to show cause why the said shares should not be compulsorily acquired and carried on by it for the purpose of carrying on the said business. The respondent submitted its explanation and the Income Tax Officer held that the respondent was one in which the public were substantially interested and there fore the income tax officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 22A of Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Incometax Officer but the Tribunal held that since the respondent had not been able to show that the shares were acquired by the appellant for the purposes of carrying it on the trade of manufacture or sale of 'Amrutn ' and that the appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. The High Court, in reference, held that section 23 A was applicable only where shares of the respondent were not entitled to a fixed rate of dividend but were acquired unconditionally by the parent company and that there was no question of any transfer of shares being made by the respondent to the parent Company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Explanation to sub section (1), of section 23, as it stood at the material time, did not apply for the three relevant years and on that footing the income Tax Officer had no jurisdic tion to pass an order under s.23A of Income tax; (2) the respondent could not be said to have acquired any share in the public company 's business by reason of the fact that the public are substantially interested, because, the shares of Amrutn were held by the parents of the first respondent and the latter were not substantially interested; and (3) the proviso to section 23(1) was not applicable for the assessment year 1955 56. HELD: (i) The Explanation to section23A is in substance a clause which defines what a company, in which public are generally interested, is. [417 B] (ii) The expression "public" in section 23 is wide enough to include all persons who are substantially concerned with the carrying on of any business in which they are substantially interest. It does not mean that the word "public " must be construed in a narrow sense and its meaning varies from person to person. [517 C] (iii) The definition of "public company" in s.3(1)(a) of the Act is wide and includes all persons engaged in the business, profession or vocation. It is not correct to say that the expression " public" must be given a wider meaning so as to include even those who are interested in such accumulation. [525 C D] (iv) The word "Public" in the Explanation means "any person who is substantially interested". The expression 'public ' in section 3(1), as it stands at the relevant time, does not include any company which is substantially concerned or a group of individuals acting in concert with others.

The appellants were the purchasers of certain bales from a firm called M/s. Shree Kishan & Company and were carrying on business as dealers in jute. The goods were delivered to the firm for delivery at Dharsi Moolji. The firm was not registered under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948, but was assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the Bombay General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1951, which came into force on April 1, 1951. The appellants contended that the goods were not delivered to M/S. Shree Kirloskar & Company as they had been authorised to take delivery of the said goods and therefore the sale was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. Held, that the transactions in question were not sales within the definition of "sale" under section 2 (g) Of the Bombay Act and the High Court erred in holding that the transaction was not one of sale. The words "any other person" used in section 2 of the Sale Tax Act are wide enough to include a firm or a company which is carrying on any business, but they must be construed as including a firm. The word "person" occurring in section 3(g), of the Sales Tax Acts, includes a firm and a limited company. The expression "any person" in section 4(1) of Bombay Act means a firm, a company or a firm which is carried on by or for the benefit of the principal. The definition of the word "Person" in the Bombay Sale Tax (Second Amendment) Act 1951, includes any firm or association which is engaged in the business of buying and selling goods. The sale of goods was not an inter State sale within section 2 Of the Act and therefore no sales tax could be levied on the transactions of sale of the goods.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 Indian Penal Code. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that he had been entrusted with the work of conducting an investigation into certain allegations against him and that he was acting as a public officer in the service or pay of the Government or was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty. The trial court convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal, the High Court set aside his conviction and sentence on the ground that he did not commit any offence under the Ninth clause of section 2(a) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the ninth clause as it stood at the material time was an independent clause which could be used for the purpose of securing the public service and therefore, the expression "public servant" in the Ninth Clause did not include a public servants within the definition of the Ninth cl; (ii) the words "in any case" occurring in the proviso to section 21 of the Act were wide enough to cover all cases where public servants were entrusted with public duty or remuneration for the service of the government or were remunerated, by fee, or commission, for the purposes of any public duty by the Government; and (iii) the expression 'public servant ' in the Tenth clause meant a person who was in the employment or pay or commission of the Govern ment or was otherwise abusing his position as public servant. HELD: (i)(a) The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his positions as a Public servant. [724 D E] (b) The abuse of position as apublic servant is clearly implied. It would be reasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. The abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise, it could not be said that there had been any abuse by him of his position in the discharge of his duty as a teacher. [624 D] (c) The use of the word "admitted" in clause (a) to mean a person in the employ or pay ment or pay etc., for the benefit of the public servant without there being any question of his misconducting himself in the discharging of his own duty, he has not committed an act under section 3(1) of Act. [524 D F] (d)(i) The expression "obtained" on whom the word is used in the first clause of s.2(a), means a person employed or paid by way of remuneration for any work done by him, and includes a person engaged in any work which is done by a teacher or other person under his control. [525 F G] (ii)(a). The use to which the word 'obtains ' has been used does not exclude the idea that the public servants should do some thing in the performance or discharge of their duty as teachers and therefore the abuse being one of the employees, the abuse is clearly implicit. It is not necessary that there must be a public element of efforts on the side of the prosecution to commit an offence of criminal misconduct.

The petitioners, who were working as casual labourers for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the construction Department of Signal Unit in Northern Railway, challenged the constitutional validity of the Railway Establishment (Amendment) Act, 1984 by filing writ petitions before this Court. The petitioners contended that since they had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and have applied discriminatory rates of wages. They also prayed for absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that the petitioners were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to the same pay as is applicable to regular employees. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgment of the High Court, this Court, HELD: 1. The Railway Administration has not taken any action to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. [144G] 2.1 The petitioners should be entitled to similar pay as was granted to regular railway servants in the Construction Department of the Signal unit in Northern Railways, and steps have been taken to screen those of the petitioner who have failed to get a favourable order from the Court. [145B C] 2(a) The Railway Board 's order of 1st of June, 1984 has not been given effect to. It is only on eventual absorption in temporary employment half the service rendered with temporary status is counted as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. [146F G] 3.1 In the Signals and Telegraphs Department under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway Board further privileges of being regularised in permanent service is affirded by giving them access to their regularisation against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line. For such purpose, casual labour in open Line as well as willing project casual labour are combined for the purposes of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. This Court directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this Court in paragraph 2511 of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual, though such status were acquired on completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. [147G H; 148A] 3(b) The petitioners shall be entitled for the same scale as is 1, admissible to others either in the project or in the open line, and not with those who have already been tested by the Court, obviously the Administration will have to be blamed. Such an unfortunate situation will not arise again and in the event any such allegation coming to the Court obviously the administration will haveto be blame.

The Forward Markets Commission, Bombay, constituted under the Forward Markets Act, 1952, was constituted by the Central Government in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 12(1) of the Act. The Forward Markets Com mission was to consist of a number of members who were elected by the members of the Forward Market Committee from amongst themselves. The President of the Association was appointed as the President and the President was appointed by the President as the Secretary of the Exchange. The appellant, who was one of the members, filed an application before the Central Govern ment under section 12 (1) Of the Act for a direction that the Forward markets Commission be constituted in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the bye laws framed by the Forward market Commission were ultra vires and void as they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they infringed articles 19(1)(f) and (g) of Part III of the constitution. Held, that the power conferred on the Central government under section 2(2) Of Act No. 1 of 1956 was not a judicial power but a legislative power and therefore the bye law made by the Commission could not be challenged as invalid. The provisions of section 12 of the , which were in conflict with article 19(6) of that Constitution, were void because they contravened articles 14 and 19(i)(f). The Act did not provide for any machinery to deal with the disputes between the parties and it was not open to the Commission to make a bye law with retrospective effect. The power conferred by section 2 (2) of Act No 1 of 1957 was not an administrative power but was a legislative function. The Act was therefore ultra vires the Constitution as it contravened articles 19 (1)(g), 31(1), 32 and 33 of the Constitu tion.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B.S., Rs. 20,469/ for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax as dividend for each year in question. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948 was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from other sources. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the entire sum for each assessment year was income in the hands of the asses see and taxable as the income of assessee from others. The High Court on reference answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) part of it being dividend, but not income assessable under section 12 of the Indian Income tax act, 1922, was liable to be grosned up and (2) interest which is statutorily payable on compensation is income and is not capital gain. HELD: (i) The High court had rightly held that distribution to the assessee of the sum attributable to the salami earned by the Company for grant of short term leases was taxable. [737 B] (ii) The expression "income" in section 2(6A) of Income tax, 1922 is not defined in the Act and it has been used in a wide sense. It has been understood in the context of the Act as meaning income from business or profession. [ 738 C D] (iii) The word "income " in section 12 means income derived from property and includes income from other source. [ 739 E] Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs M/s. K.M. Senairam Chettiar, ; , followed. (iv) The words "income from other assets" in the definition of dividend are not defined by the Act but by the Indian Companies Act, 1913. [769 G H] (v) The definition of "income", as given in section 3(6), is inclusive and includes all income derived by way of dividends or gains arising out of property.

The Kerala Forest Act, 1963 was enacted to provide for the regulation of forest produce and for matters connected therewith. Section 2(f) (1) of the Act defines 'wood oil ' as including a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest area. The definition of 'wood Oil ' is not defined under section 2(g) of that Act. The expression 'timber ' defined in section 2 (f)(1) must receive its colour from its context and connotation. The word 'wood ' has been used in the Act to denote a species of wood oil which includes wood oil, and also to enable the word as used in section 3(g). The definition is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary, popular and natural sense whenever that word that would be properly applicable, but to enable it to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values. [164G H; 165A B] In the instant case, the Kerala Forest (Amendment) Act, 1992 was passed by the legislature and the definition of the word 'cotton oil ' was not meant for the purpose of the definition in section2(f)(i). The expression "wood oil" is a term which includes both wood oil as well as wood oil. [165C D] In view of the fact that the word "wood Oil" has been defined in Section 2 (g) to mean 'a species of trees which include, that is to say, the 'enumerated items in clauses 1 and 11 "wood oils". The expression used in clause (1), must receive a wider meaning than the word wood. [166D E] In order to attract the applicability of the amended definition, it must be shown that the timber oil is not a forest produce within the meaning of Section 2.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons" for setting aside the judgment of acquittal. The Supreme Court has power to interfere with findings of fact arrived at by the trial court only where such conclusions are manifestly perverse or based on no evidence or are based upon no evidence at all, or where the conclusions of the trial judge are manifestly unjust or based upon an erroneous view of law or on no material or where there is a gross and compelling error which has resulted in manifest injustice. In the present case, the High court was not justified in interfering with the findings of the Sessions Court. The evidence in the case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The judgment of the High. Court did not disclose any such reasons justifying interference with the conclusions arrived at on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the appellant. The conviction of the appellants was therefore set aside. The State of Rajasthan vs Ram Pratap, ; , followed. The appeal must accordingly be allowed and the order of acquittal set aside and the accused were acquitted. The Sessions Judge was of the opinion that the evidence in this case was not sufficient to warrant a conviction and that there were no compelling reasons for setting it aside.

The appellant company was incorporated in Bihar. In the year 1963 it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1947. The workmen of the factory were paid wages at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided by the Bihar Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1950. The appellant company had two mills in different parts of the country. In Bihar there were two factories, one at Ranchi and the others at Ranchi, and the third at Ranchi at Ranchi where the factory was situated. The workers of the two factories were paid Rs. 1,000 per month as wages for the period from July 1963 to March 1967. The company had a factory at Ranchi which consisted of three factories, namely, Jamshedpur, Jamshedpur and Ranchi. In respect of the other two factories there were disputes between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said Indoxco Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and the workmen of that factory at Patna" was without jurisdiction. The High Court also held that the union 's constitution was duly amended by the notification dated January 6. 1963 and therefore the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal 's award would cover them also. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the reference was not maintainable because the dispute raised by the Union is in respect of employees of the company where there are two factories and one at Patna and the rest of the workmen in the other establishment are situated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not committed any error in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the union.

The assessee firm was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business, inter alia, in timber at Abdullapur. The assessee contended that the firm had been dissolved on March 31, 1939 and that the business in timber was taken over by two partners of the firm, Gajjan Mal Tani Mal, who entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on the business. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was carrying on business when Act 7 of 1939 came into force and was on that account entitled to relief under section 25(3) or in the alternative under section 26(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In appeal to the Tribunal it was contended that (i) the assessee had been carrying on the timber business at the time when Act No. 7 of 1938 came into operation and was not entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (3) of that Act; (ii) the firm alone was entitled to claim relief under s 25(4); and (iii) the Tribunal erred in holding that the appellant was carrying out business after March 31 , 1939, when the assessee became effective. The High Court held that it was not necessary for the Tribunal to decide whether the assessee could be said to have carried on the work of timber business in the name of the partnership firm Gajjan and Jodha Mal. HELD: (i)(a) The assessee was constituted to carry out the business of timber, and the business at Abdulapur in the names of the partners of a firm of Lala Hakam Mal Toni Mal. [675 B] (b) The fact that the partners were partners and shareholders in the firm of the Firm Jodhas had become effective would imply that the partnership was not carried on till March 31. 1939, and that it must therefore be held that there was no other evidence to show that the partner was carrying in the business after the dissolution of the assessee firm. [650 C] (c) The High Courts were right in holding on the facts that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding the assessee 's case to be carried on by the dissolution. [643 D] (d) The finding of the High Court that the respondent was carrying business at Jodhad in 1934, and therefore, it was entitled under section 24(4), to the benefits provided in Section 25(1)(b) or 25(2) of Indian Income Tax Act, is not correct.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority Shimogi by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. The appellant produced the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal held that the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority Shmogi was competent to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Rules after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit, and directed the appellant to produce the relevant records and the Certificate of registration. On appeal by the State Transport Authority, the High Court held that there was no period of limitation under r. 119 of Mysore Motor vehicles Rules 1963 for issuing a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Trans port Authority granting the permit and that the grant was made beyond the prescribed period of Limitation under rule119 of the old Rules. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that no appeal lay under section 64 of the Act to the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal against the issue of a permit. [189E] (1) The provisions of r. 118 of the new Rules are mandatory and the Regional Authority has no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal against the grant or renewal of a stage carriages permit. It is only necessary to read section 64(1)(a) which is material for the purpose of this appeal that the procedure for appeal to the various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute. There is no dispute that section 64 has to be read with r. 178 of the rules which prescribes the procedure to appeal to various authorities appeal is abodies of the statutes. There was, therefore, a clear error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant o f the permit to the appellant. [190F G] (2) The High Courts have not been right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. He was elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in 1967. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant denied the allegations and pleaded that the respondent was guilty of any corrupt practice under section 123 (1)(b). The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was no attack on the office of the Republican Party. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the news item in the newspaper 'falls on the public and therefore the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The publication of the entire evidence in the newspapers is not mentioned at all either in the Vir Arjun of 892 893 or in the Hindustan dated 8 February 1967. [895 D] (2) The report of the Joint Secretary to the President of the country bearing the date 8 February, 1967 alleged that the supporters of the appel lant Vir Shastri attacked the office and the supporters were alleged to have chased the appellant. The evidence on behalf Of the respondent is that the meeting was not held. [889 F G] (3) The appellant 's case was that there was an assault on the Office of the Prime Minister by the appellant, and the speech of the supporters was also published in the daily newspaper. The news item was lodged by the supporters at Hapur. The High court rightly came to the conclusion that no notice was given to the appellant before the election was held. The report was not proved as to the truth of the contents therein.

The appellant purchased the property in question from one B.K. Jain, a co tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property auctioned purchased by him on July 17, 1980. The District Judge held that in view of Article 134 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree would be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree was passed and all questions relating to the delivery of posses sion of the properties shall be questions relating t o the execution of the decree and as such, Article 134 could not apply. The learned District Judge upheld the order of the District Judge holding that in spite of the settlement, the sale became absolute and the decree holder respondent having filed the application for delivery, the High Court was right in holding that the application was quite within time. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that (i) since the auction purchaser will be deemed not to be the party in the suit, he is entitled to file an application for setting aside the sale; and (ii) even though the auction purchasers will be entitled to prefer an applica tion under Order 21 Rule 95, the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134 would apply. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Article 134 does not apply to an application made under Order I Rule 95 for setting tain a decree for possession so as to apply 12 years ' period of Limitation as prescribed in Article 136 of the . [361C] 1.2 In view of the provisions of Article 135 of the , an application filed under Order 1 Rule 95 is maintainable and not barred by limitation. [362D] 1:3. The expression "as may be" occurring in clause (a) of Explanation II to Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 has been interpreted by this Court in a number of decisions to mean that the period for which possession is sought to be taken under Order 14 Rule 95 would be the period during which the suit was pending and all other matters relating to delivery of actual possession of property would be questions incidental to the main tain action. [361D] 2.1 The expression 'as may have been used in clause(a) or clause (b) of explanation II to section 47 of Civil Proce dure Code, is not restricted to applications under Order XXIII Rule 95. It is not correct that the sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92 and that apart from the provisions contained in Rules 89, 90 and 91 of Order XXI of the C.P.C., an auction sale can be challenged on grounds other than those mentioned in the said Rules. [364E F] 2:2 In the instant case, the application under order XXIII Rule 90 was made within one year of the dismissal of the application of the 4th judgment debtor for setting it aside and not from the date of the first confirmation. The High Court has rightly held that after the amendment of section 47 by Act 17 of 1976, an application to set aside sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from the time of decree irrespective of the date on which the sale was confirmed. [365F G] 2 :3.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which he used to reside. He had also a shop adjacent to the house of one P.W. 1. The appellant and his wife were living together at the time of the election. On the day previous to the election, they were returning home from the house. They saw a number of persons including the appellant coming out of the house with a view to take the photographs. The first respondent was arrested for an offence under section 120B I.P.C. and later released on bail by the High Court. The trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to various terms of imprisonment. On appeal, the High COurt held that the wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with consent of the appellant 's election agent and therefore it was an admitted fact that the first respondent had not seen the wall posters together with exhibit P 1 being pasted on the wall. The High Court also found that the appellant had not taken the photographs in question on the date prior to the filing of the present election petition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the evidence adduced by the first Respondent himself was inadmissible and that the contents of exhibit P1 being pasted near the wall could not be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contents of the wall pamphlet directly named the first respond ent as the murderer of the four victims and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to his election, it would not be necessary to do so and all that is necessary is to prove that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's prospects of the elections. [776B C] 1.2 The contents in this wall pamphlet are clear and a direct reference to the first appellant ' s speech was made by him on the day prior to election. It is not necessary to prove the same on the basis of the evidence of his witnesses, therefore, it is difficult to understand as to how this witness could have seen the walls poster together with the exhibit PI being pasted one week prior to that date. [767C D] 1:3 The contents and the wall hoardes are not material and they are merely a direct references to the second respondent 's speech. It may also be necessary for the first and the second respondents to prove their case that the poster was used by them reasonably calculated and did so in the interest of the general public. [777D] 1 :4 The contents are clear, unambiguous and admit of no doubt that the content of the contents is not such as would affect the prospectus or its contents. It has also to be proved that there was a reasonable connection between the offending poster and the personal character or conduct of the candidate. [777E F] 2:1.

The respondent No. 5, a development applicant, filed an application under section 21 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 for permission to construct a hotel on the land in question. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation rejected the plan submitted by the respondent No 5 on the sole ground that it was proposed to be used as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent filed an appeal before the Minister of State for Urban Development, who rejected the same on the ground that the property was proposed for a park or recreation ground in the revised development plan and the High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The ground for rejecting the plan is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development scheme has since been published and the plan was submitted by respondent No 2 and conditioned by the Respondent No. 2. [924C] 2.1 In granting permission to the respondent NO. 5 to construct an additional ground under reference as a recreation ground with proper internal network, the Municipal Commissioner had not considered the proposal for the preparation of a draft revised plan. The plan of the respondent no. 5 was also not considered by the High court in its judgment disposing of the review applications. [936E] 2:2 In granting sanction to the plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds., belonging to the res pondent No. 1, the Respondent NO. 2 directed sanction of the same. The respondent No . 2 directed that the said land be included in the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the draft revision of development plan had been published. [981F] 3.1 The High Court was not justified in merely relying upon a proposal for preparation of the revised plan, which had since been approved and the Plan submitted by Respondent No 2. The High court was therefore right in rejecting the review application of the appellant. [980G H; 924A] 3:2. In the instant case, the question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park or exploitation ground for the benefit of the members of the public is a matter which should be decided by the Court on its own merits. The question whether there was a proposal to revise the plan or that such a revision was under contemplation, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [977B C] 3 :3. In view of the position that in granting sanction for development plan of respondent No 1, it is not possible to decide the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3, the order granting exemption should be quashed.

The appellant union, a trade union of workmen, filed two complaints before the Industrial Court alleging that the employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act 1971 ( 'the Act ' for short). The Industrial Court held that the employer had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continued a lockout. The appellant union appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Industrial Courts have not at all considered whether the employer has imposed a lock Out or has closed down the business. It is only after considering the evidence produced before them that the Industrial court can come to a conclusion that the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or that it was bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. [678C D] 1.2 The question whether the employers have imposed a ' lockout or has close down the industrial activity is an unfair Labour practice. While examining whether the management has imposed any lockout, the Industrial Courts are not concerned with the question as to whether the closure is a device for terminating services of the workmen or whether it is bonafide and if so, what relief they are entitled to. [688D E] 1:3 The Industrial court while considering whether the appellant has imposed and continued the lock out has taken into consideration all the relevant circumstances at the time of closing the industrial undertaking. It has not at any stage of the proceedings before the employer that the management had imposed a ban on the trade union or has closure down the industry. [698E F] 1 :4 The Industrial Tribunal while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant union which does not command to itself and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, has taken a view that the appellant is willing to take back all the old workmen and in order to satisfy the court about the bonafides of the employers at the relevant time, it is necessary to find out what was the intention of the appellant at the date when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down. [708F G] 1 5. The Industrial courts have not considered whether there has been a closure of the industrial establishment or has failed to exercise their jurisdiction in accordance with law. It would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial process he can not do so on the pain that the closing down of the industry itself permanent and irrevocable. [718F H] 1 6. The question as regards the lockout is concerned, whether the workmen have imposed or had closed down their business.

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of the company were set out in cl. III of the memorandum of association and the previous assertion made by the assessee company that it was a dealer in investments and properties. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and therefore, he was not an investor. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee 's company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but also the case relating to investment in shares securities and immovable properties of the appellant company could be taxed as business profits. The High Court on reference answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law. [655 B] (ii) The test for determining whether a particular person is a dealer or an investor has been laid down by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs M/s. Doypack Systems Ltd., ; , followed. (iii) The tests laid down in the decision of this Court are: (a) that there must be a transaction between a person and another; (b) that it must be an adventure in the nature of trade or business; and (c) that the test is whether the activity carried on by one person is one which is primarily engaged in the carrying on of the other. [643 C D] (iv) The expression "business" has been defined in section 2 (1)(a) to mean any business, profession or vocation carried on with a view to carry on such trade or profession. It does not include the business of buying and selling goods or immovable properties. [641 B] In the present case, the assessee had no business connection with the sale of shares securities or immovable property of the respondent company. It was not shown that there were at least two materials on record to support the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the appellant was a "dealer" in respect of the shares securities. [651 C] (v) The High Courts have taken the view that the tests laid by this court in the present cases for determining the question of law are not satisfied.

The appellant was appointed as Subordinate Judge in 1935. He was promoted to the post of Subordinate Judge and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On April 28, 1954, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28,1954, on the grounds that (i) the charge proved was not fully established and (ii) the enquiry held by the High Court after October 1, 1953, resulted in the order suspending him from service. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry was without jurisdiction as the enquiry had been conducted after October 20, 1953; and that the Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry into the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High Courts were not competent to decide the question whether the charges proved were well founded and (2) the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion; Held, that the order passed by the Government on January 28. 1954, was a valid order under section 4(1)(a) of the Madras Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1953. The order passed on January 29, 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the government and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor of removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution. The Government could not therefore decide whether the allegations were well established or not.

The appellant, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co., a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay, died on May 13, 1945. The legal representatives of the deceased shareholder were not brought on record as parties to the proceedings before the Income tax Officer pursuant to which the income was deemed to be distributed under section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant contended that even if after the expiry of the year of account receipts which if the person earning had not died would have been treated as his income, ceased to be liable to assessment as income of the assessee, they could still be taxed as his individual income and therefore the claim of the Income Tax Officer to make an assessment under section 23(4) must fail. The Income tax officer rejected the contention and held that the appellant was not liable to pay tax on the dividend so deemed to have been distributed. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax officer. In further appeal, the Tribunal held that even though the assessment proceedings were pending before the Incometax Officer pursuant thereto, the Income 'tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the appellant as the dividends deemed to accrue to him under section 12B of Act. The High Court in reference, on a reference, held that section 24 B did not authorise the levy of tax on receipts by the legal representative of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year in which such person died and therefore, the income received by him before his death and received by his heirs and legal representatives after his death in that previous year became assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even assuming that after the expiration of the period of assessment receipts which were deemed to arise under section 2(2) of the Act, the expression "any tax which would have become payable by him under this Act if he had not die" could not be said to have supplied the machinery for taxation of income received in the year when such person was alive. HELD: (i) The expression "assessee" in section 2 (2) as substituted by the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953, with effect from April 1, 1952 means a person by whom income tax or any other every person in respect of whom any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his income or of the loss sustained by him or of any amount of refund due to him. [603 D] (ii) The word "assessee ' in section 24A is used in a wider sense than that of an assessee who is not liable under the Act. [501 E F] (iii) The Legislature did not intend to make any provision for taxation on income received or receivable by a legal representative which would, but for the death of the legal representatives, have been received by such deceased person, and therefore they are not liable for tax as income. [500 G H] (iv) The words "any other person in this Act" in sub section (2), of section 24 A are wide enough to include a Hindu Undivided Family consisting of himself and his wife or children. [525 B C] (v) The definition of "assessee " in section 12A(1) is not restricted to persons by whom the income is payable but only those who are liable to be taxed under the Indian Act. Therefore, the Legislature did intend that all assessable incomes should be treated as the personal income of a legal person and therefore it could not have supplied it.

The appellant was the Ruler of an Indian State. He was a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant claimed that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was not a "maufidar" within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Indian Constitution and that the provisions of the Act did not apply to him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts rightly held that in these circumstances it was for the appellant to establish that the villages in question had never been assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to prove that the village in question was not assessed to the land revenue. [502 D] (ii)The High Court rightly held on this point against the appellant. The question whether the villages were assessed to lands revenue or not did not arise for consideration. The expression "mauufidar ' is not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler, of a State. It is only when there is no evidence that the holder of the land was in possession of the village. [506 G] (iii)The appellant had given no evidence to establish his case that the lands were not assessed as "maafidar" and therefore he fell within the definition of the word 'proprietor ' in the Act. [500 C D] The High court rightly held, that the petitioner was an ex Ruler and that article 366 did not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the , Act. The fact that the State had given any evidence to prove the existence of the lands in question does not make it a Ruler within the purview of article 367(22).

The respondent was a Garden Curator in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of Director, Botsangpur. He submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. The said guidelines are applicable to the case of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of transfer on the following grounds: (i) The guidelines contained therein did not apply to the facts and circumstances of the case; (ii) The transfer was made in violation of the statutory provisions, (iii) The administrative instructions issued by the Government were not kept in view while ordering the transfer. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines do not require the two spouses to be posted at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees. [440E] 1.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by transfer. [ 430G] 1:3. The guidelines say that as far as possible, husband and wife must be posted to different places. The administrative authorities should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouse to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employee. [ 431F] 1 :4. The order of the Tribunal read as if it were sitting in appeal over the orders of transfer made by the senior Administrative Officer (competent authority). [439A] 1 Whether the guidelines are kept in line with the statutory rules or not is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide.
