Unless the order is vitiated by malafides or is made in contravention of any statutory provisions the Court cannot interfere with it. [ 432C D] 2. The Tribunal has completely exceeded its jurisdic tion in interfering in the order, of transfer, if any of the administrative instructions/guidelines are not followed, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. [ 433E F] 3. The High Court does not interfere with the orders passed by the Tribunal. The appeal is allowed.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with section 34, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of Jawahar and causing him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. The Trial Court convicted them under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, IPC and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court maintained the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 323 read with 34, but reduced the sentences to rigorous imprisonment for five years. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that the participation of the accused in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellant was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 149, I P.C., [630E] 2.1 The intention is to cause simple and grievous injuries and as a matter of fact the facts and circumstances of this case indicate that the appellants were guilty of the crime coming within the purview of Section 326 read with Sections 34, 1.P., C. [631F G] 2(a) The intention was to causing grievous hurt, as such, they came within the ambit of Section 323, I PC. [643B] 3.2 In the instant case, the intention of appellants was to caused simple and simple injuries to Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while granting special leave to appeal this Court by its order dated August 10, 1979 allowed bail to the appellants. [641C D] 2.(b) The participation of accused in a occurrence which resulting in the murder is proved beyond any doubt. The offence committed was punishable under Section 325 I. P. C.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 came into force on January 1, 1973. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the Banking companies Act shall apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian law for India. Section 3(27)(a) of that Act defines "special Indian Law" as including any law made by Parliament or the Legislature of a State. The appellant Bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said provisions on the ground that the words `special Indian law ' were placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament of India ' and before the words`by or under" in section 4(a) and (b). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Banking companies Acts are a special law enacted by the Indian Parliament as a piece of special legislation applicable to India. [968C] 1.2 The words `any special Indian Law ' refer to action taken under the law and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section 4 (e) and therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. [940F G] Krishna Murthy vs State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to. 1.3 The intention of the Legislature was very clear that the expression `special ' law ' refers and relates to a law made in pursuance of or by or under the special Indian laws. It will be highly unreasonable and unrealistic to think that as a corporation has been formed by or on behalf of or under a special IIII law and cannot come within its purview, it will not come within section 4.(e) Of the Act.

The petitioners, who were sugar factories in Punjab and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it was beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and cl. 5 of the Order which imposed an unreasonable restriction on their right to trade under article 19 (1) (g), inasmuch as (i) it imposes an unreasonable restrictions on their fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 14, 19(1)(g), 31 (2) and 31 (3) of the Constitution; (ii) it fixes the price arbitrarily and does not take into account the cost of production of sugar in the country; (iii) it provides for a fair and equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price; (iv) it prescribes a reasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade under Article 19(6); (v) it is discriminatory because (i), it imposes unreasonable restrictions upon the right guaranteed by article 19(5) and (vi) it contravenes articles 14 and 19(2). Held, that the impugned notifications were invalid. The impugned notification was beyond question as it contravened the provisions of article 19 of the Consti tution and was therefore void. The object of the , is to secure equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The power conferred on Parliament under section 1 (3), read with cl. (a) of article 246, is not unguided or uncanalised but subject to reasonable restrictions which may be imposed by the State in public interest. The fact that the Central Legislature has made a law imposing an unreasonable restraint on the fundamental right to freedom of trade and commerce in essential commodities does not make any difference. The Act was beyond its legislative competence and was void. It is well settled that the power conferred by section 3(1) read with el. 5 Of the Order is subject to the restrictions imposed by it. The restrictions imposed are reasonable within the meaning of article 31 (5) of India, and the impugned Notification cannot be said to contravene articles 14 or 19(i)(g). The impugned notifications are therefore invalid.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947, and its employees were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 400 per month. The Company had to pay a sum of Rs, 500 per month as bonus for the years 1957 58 to 1959 60. In 1951, the Company made an application before the Tribunal under section 19(6) of the , claiming that the workmen should be paid 75 per cent of the basic wages and dearness allowance in addition to the minimum wages prescribed by the Act. The Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index was Rs. 350 per month and that the company had not been able to prove any substantial change in the working classes cost of the living index. On appeal, the High Court held that there was a fall in the rate for working class and that it was not necessary to show that there had been any substantial increase in the cost of production. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal rightly relied on Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, for ascertaining the working Class cost of live class cost. [148 E] (ii) The Company was not prepared to pay any additional dearness allowance to its employees. It had no right to claim that it should be allowed 75 per centum of the increase in dearness allowance. [149 F G] (iii) The award made by the Tribunal was binding on the parties and therefore the date of the agreement was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change of the working, class cost or living index in the years 1954 55 to 1959 61. [150 C D] (iv) The finding given by Tribunal that the work done by the Company was a part of the cost for living index is not correct. It is true that the Tribunal wrongly relied on the information furnished by the Government, but it could not be said that the award was binding between the parties.

The appellant was the Matadheen of Sri Gavi Mutt. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the ground that it contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to him under article 19(1)(f) and (g). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the scheme had been framed as early as 1939, and that the challenge to its validity was not barred by article 19. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme was framed in 1948 and it must now be deemed to be a scheme which was finalised under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act. [254 B] (i) The scheme is valid only if it is found that any of the said provisions are inconsistent with the relevant provision of the latter Act. It does not, however, mean that the provisions of section 103(d) apply to a scheme framed under the earlier law. [255 C D] (ii) The object of the impugned scheme was to provide for the proper administration of the Mutt and its endowments. The object was to make the schemes in question operative as if they were framed under sections 63, 64 and 65 of the Act. The scheme did not come with in the purview of section 102(d). [255 D E] (iii) The impugned scheme did fall within the mischief of article 19 (1)(g) and the provisions Of section 103 (d) applied to it. [256 G] (iv) The effect of the provision merely is to make a scheme operative as though they were prepared under the provisions, of the later Act; but the effect of this provision merely was to give effect to the provisions contained in the latter enactment. [257 D E].

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised in terms of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [995B] 1.2 The High Courts erred in not granting relief to the petitioner on the basis of the judgment of this Court in State of Orissa vs Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei, ; and the decision of this court in State Of Orissa vs M.A. Mann, ; , relied upon. 1.3 The High courts erred in giving directions to regularise the services of those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31, 1976 but not later than 31st December, 1984. [996C D] 1:4 In view of the provisions of Section 23 of the Act, the appellant is entitled to get his salary and allowances including the salary for summer vacation and other service benefits. The State of Andhra Pradesh will do well to consider the cases of all those who had completed one y year or less as ad interim measure to regularise their services. [997F G] 1 5. The Government has been given a discretion to regularise such employees in terms thereof. It is not open to the Government to deny the benefit to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like 89 day appointment as here with one day break and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other services benefits.

The appellant was a member of the Panchayat Samiti and was disqualified from being a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The respondent, who was defeated by respondent No. 1, filed an Election Petition challenging the election on the ground that he was disqualified under r. 3 to 7 of the Rules. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that the allowance paid under rules 3 to7 of the rules did not convert the office of Chairman into an office of profit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the allowances paid under r 3 to the Chairman, Vice Chairman and Members for the purposes and journeys mentioned in rule 5 were in addition to the payment of consolidated monthly allowance under r, 5. [417 D] (ii) The appellant had not established that he had been disqualified for being a member for being chosen as a candidate. He was therefore not disqualified from contesting the election. [420 G H] (iii) The respondent had failed in establishing that the amount received by him for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. [416 A B] (iv) The charge of corrupt practice under r 4(1)(d) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Rules, 1965 was not made out. [414 C D] In the present case, the High Court came to a correct conclusion that the charges were proved against the respondent.

The appellant was the tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration and on that finding the trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent landlord the High Court reversed the findings of the First Appellate Court and dismissed the suit holding that the tin shed shown by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin sheds marked with letters CDGH on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommodation, were not material alterations. The High Court also held that the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the premises from the tenant for his eviction under section 13(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in interfering with the findings recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition deed marked with letter CDG H on the eastern side were material alterations as the same were temporary in nature which could be removed without causing any damage to the premises. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature and they alter, the form, front and structure of the accommodation. A Division Bench of the High Courts has to consider whether the construction have been made with the consented of the land lord and if so, whether those constructions are of such a character that they alter the accommodation or not. [975C D] 2. The question as to what material alterations should be made in the premises is a mixed question of fact and law. The courts below have recorded findings on the questions of fact. The First Appeal Court has rightly interfered with the finding of fact recorded by both the Courts below on the ques tion whether the structures are substantial or temporary. [ 975E] 3.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the passing of the ex parte order. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the appellant company against the said order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the respondent had no knowledge of the decree, even otherwise before 29 7 1975, the summons would be deemed to have been duly served and therefore, there was no service on the respondent company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code are not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on a company in the sense as to what is meant by service of summons on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. and another vs The Union of India and others it was held that the words " Principal Officer" have to be understood in the background of the provisions of the code in order to give effect to the object of the Act. [1032C D] 2.1 In order to attract the applicability of the first part of clause (a) of rule 2, the words 'Principal Officer ' must be understood as having been served on a person who is entitled to be served with summons on his behalf. The meaning of clause(b) has got to be determined in the light of the background and the provisions contained in the Code in order 5 Rule 13 C.P.C. [1132G H] 2:2 In the instant case, the respondent was not aware of the notice issued by the Company as required under the first para of clause 2 of Rule 1 of Order 9 of the Civil Procedure Code. The respondent had also no knowledge about the service of the summons as it was left at the registered office of the company. [1232G] 3.1 The meaning to be given to the words `Principal Officer` in clause(a) has been given by the Legislature in order 2.2 before 29 6 1975. The word 'Principal officer ' has got a wider connotation than that of 'Principal Officers ' in clause 2.3. [1332G, 1333A] 3:2. In view of the language of the provision contained in Order 9 Rule 13 of the C. P.C., it is not possible to accept the contention that the respondent could have been served with a notice as required by the first paragraph of clause 1 of Rule 12 of Order. [1434B] 4. The appellant company was not in charge of and responsible for the service on its registered office. It had no control over the company in relation to its business. [1534C] 5. The expression 'Principal Office ' has been defined in clause 3(b), as including any office, place or office which is deemed to be a place of residence by the company itself. In the present case, it was not the case of the Respondent that the company had no know of the service. [1634D] 6. The fact that the appellant had no personal knowledge about its service on it would not make any difference as the respondent has not been given a notice under Order 9 rule 13 of C.p.C.; nor is there anything to show that the service was duly served upon the company because it was within the meaning of section 2(a). [1635E] 7. The question whether the summons in suit was duly duly served or not would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. [1734G] 8.

The respondents were prosecuted under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for having committed an offence punishable under section 135(1) read with section 135 (2) of the Act. The Magistrate passed a preliminary order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, therefore, the final orders were bad and set aside the order of the Magistrate. In this appeal by Special Leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the preliminary order was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of the peace existed at the time when the order was passed; (2)(a) the Magistrate had not recorded any finding on this aspect of the matter also but had merely recorded his satisfaction in the preliminary report and (b) the High court erred in holding that the final decision of the magistrate was vitiated by non application of mind. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of a Magistrate is limited to the question to who was in actual possession on the date of the preliminary orders irrespective of the rights of the parties. [94C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach of an peace that he has jurisdiction to take proceedings under section145, Cr. P.C., and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub section (4) and pass a final order under sub sections (5) and (6). [94D] 3. The High Court was right in holding the preliminary issue of the final report that there is no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under subsection (5). [95F] 4. The expression "in actual possession" in section 145(5) Cr.P.C. means actual physical possession or constructive possession of any land etc. In the instant case, the respondents had full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Magistrate and they were given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence in support of their contention that the dispute was not having ended. [95G] 5. The question whether a breach has been committed by the respondents or not is a pure question of fact which can be determined only on appreciation of oral and documentary evidence. If it is found that there has been a breach, then the Magistrate has jurisdiction under section 482 Cr. It is not necessary that at the stage of passing the final Order the apprehension of the breach of a peace should continue or exist. [96H; 96A] 6. The respondents had no opportunity to adduce evidence in their defence before the Court and they could have produced their evidence in defence. They were given an opportunity to rebut the evidence adduced by them. The trial Magistrate was, therefore. justified in holding him guilty of the offence under section 138(1). [96F G] 7.

The appellant, a non resident of the United States of America, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1941 42 on the ground that it had sold its goods in British India and received prices higher than those fixed by the Government. The Income tax Officer included these sales in his assessable income for the relevant assessment years as business profits. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the Tribunal held that the appellant was not liable to pay tax on the sale price of its goods sold in British Indian and that the profits had accrued to it both in the business and in the legal sense and that therefore, the appellant could not be taxed under section 14(2)(c) of the Act. The High Court, however, held that as the appellant sold its products to the ultimate purchasers and received the prices, there can be no question of the tax payable on the sales price. Held, that the decision of the Tribunal was correct and must be upheld. The question whether a particular sale is taxable under section 3(1) or not was a mixed question of law and fact; it was open to review by the court only on the grounds that it was not supported by any evidence or that it is perverse. Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., ; , referred to. The decision in Commissioner of income tax and Excess Profits Pax vs section Sen, (1923) L.R. 59 I.A. 206, relied on. Commissioner for the purpose of determining whether a sale was taxable under s.3(1), is final and conclusive and does not depend upon any evidence, or if it is not supported either by any such evidence or if its decision is based on no evidence or is perverse, but that where there is evidence to support the conclusion, the finding is open to challenge as erroneous in law only if it was shown that the Income Tax Officer had erroneously come to the conclusion. Commissioner vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai & Co., (1924) L R. 59 1. A. 206 and Commissioner of Incometax vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai, (1931) L I. A C.

The assessee carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75465 as commission paid to the General Manager. The Income tax Officer determined a sum of Rs, 70465 as the commission paid by the assessee to the general manager. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that Rs. 37465 paid to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of the case the amount of Rs 37465 was an ex gratia payment made wholly or partly for the purposes of business and was rightly disallowed by Income tax authorities. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out wholly or solely for the purpoSe of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of the Income Tax Act has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances. [528 B] (2) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in view of the practice in similar business concerns, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner expressed the view that the rate of commission paid was not really expended wholly and exclusively for purposes of the business. [525 C D] (3) The High Court was right in taking the view, that in a case where the assessee worked in the mill at the initial stage and of the Managing Director was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of the General manager, the amount paid to him was an allowance for the commission on profits clause. [500 E] (4) The fact that the mill was old and dilapidated and it never made profit of even a lakh of rupees in the past and that the assessee was not laid out fully or exclusively within the meaning of section 10 (2)(XIv) does not mean that it is not incurred by the asses see in the character of a trader or it is a laid out for the business, of the assesses.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. He was actually represented by an officer of that Union and was actually representing his case before the Tribunal but was not present at the hearing of the case. The appellant filed a fresh petition stating that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and prayed for an order directing the Tribunal not to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. The Tribunal rejected the application for a writ of certiorari and dismissed the petition. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Labour Court was right in refusing to record a compromise in respect of the appellant as it had not been entered into in what was considered to be the best interests of the workman himself. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the Union, of which the workman is a member, as a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act, does not arise for consideration in this case. It was not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Industrial Dispute Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represented by another union, not independently of the Union which has espoused his cause. The necessary corollary to this is that the individual workman was at no stage a party in the industrial dispute independently of his Union.

The appellants were the tenants of two defendants. The respondents filed a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the appellants on the ground that they constituted a joint Hindu family, that the right to appeal survived to the surviving appellants alone and that they could have continued their appeal in view of O.XXII r. 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that it was not proved that Kedar Nath, deceased, and the other appellants constituted a Joint Hindu family that the rights to appeal survive to the remaining appellants. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The right to appeals survived to a surviving appellants only when all the respondents or defendants were negligent in not taking steps for substitution. [558 C] (ii) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellant when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as he was not an appeal against the whole decree in pursuance of the provisions of r. 4 of 0 XLI, r. 3 of the code. [559 E] (iii) The appeal by a person who is not a party to the whole suit or proceeding could not be brought before the court for setting aside the entire decree in view Of O.XLIII, r 33. [560 G] (iv) The provisions of 0. XLI, rr. 33 and 34 were intended to apply to the stage when an appeal was filed and empowered one of the plaintiffs or defendants to file an appeal. When the legal representatives of the deceased appellant and the surviving respondents were negligent, in not taken steps for substituted, the Court is not to exercise its discretion in favour of such a party.

The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by pleading that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The Rent Controller rejected the application and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the tenancy having expired by afflux of time, the landlord could not seek to break his tenancy by seeking to terminate the tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The statutory law as it now stands is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 (g) does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in that behalf. [920C] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions of the Act apply to the lease of 1952 executed in Delhi and, secondly, if it does not whether its present provision, as amended in 1929, has to be treated as a rule of justice, equity and good conscience, or whether it is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based on any well established principles of equity. [936D] 3. The provisions of sections 106 and 111 of the P.C. are mandatory in character and do not create an obligation to give notice of termination of tenancy under section 106 or section 111. [815E] 4. In the instant case, no notice whatsoever was sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux or by forfeiture following the breach by the tenant. The requirement of a notice in writing to the lessee of an intention to determine lease is not dependent upon the principles of justice equity and natural good. [981F] 5. The Court has to consider whether the provisions contained in sections 106 & 111 of P. C. are directory or not, and if it finds that there is no such provision, then the Court may hold that the notice must be treated to be a rule or principle of justice. [980G H; 921A] 6. The mandatory requirement of notice in section 106 of the is that notice must have been present at the time when the lease was sought and not on the date of the notice. It is a necessary corollary of the requirement of law that the existence of such a provision does not render it invalid merely because it does so in the absence of a written notice. [977B C] 7. The essential principles embodied in section 112(g), namely, that the breach of a condition providing for re entry and sub letting in terms of the principles embodied therein would not ipso jure extinguish the tenancy but only pro tanto extinguished the lease, are not based upon any principle of equity or good conscience. [978C D] 814 In the present case, the High Courts have held that the requirement as amended by P. O. dated September 30, 1953, was not based merely on a written statement and that it did not amount to a notice under section 112 of the Evidence Act. The presumption is rebuttable and the burden of proof lies upon the landlord to prove affirmatively that the tenant has committed breach of the conditions providing for ret entry and that he has failed to discharge the onus which lay on him.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Governor of Assam. The order of dismissal was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the Governor had no power to dismiss or remove a Government servant and that the order of termination of his services was not invalid on account of violation of article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant 's case must be judged in the light of the provisions of the unamended clause (2) and the unamended Article 311(3). [488 B] (2)(a) The amended clause (4) has been reproduced in the judgment of the High court. It is not necessary to refer to the amendment as it was made after the amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963. [488 C D] (b) The unamended clause(4) had been inserted in the original clause by the amending Act. The amended cl. (4), however, did not provide that the Government servant shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank without being given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. [486 E] (c) The amendment made by the Amending Act was prospective and could not affect the appellant ' s right to continue in service. [487 F] (d) The word "dismissed" in clause (5) of article 310 means dismissal or removal from service. The word 'dismissed ' has been defined in section 2(a) to mean dismissal or discharge from service, except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a fair opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed. [485 G] (e) The words "dismissing or removing" in cl. 5(2)(b) are not intended to convey that the word 'dismissing ' is used in the amended clause. The amendment was made with a view to give an opportunity to the Government Servant to show cause against action proposed in regard, him as stated above.

The petitioners, who were the members of a Shia community, challenged the validity of the U.P. Sunni Central Board of Waqfs Act, 1936 (U.P.) and the Uttar Pradesh Sunni Central Boards Act, 1965 (U P. Act No. 1 of 1966) on the ground that they had been registered as Shia Wakfs for purposes of performing their religious ceremonies and functions under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any customary rights in respect of the customary rights of the Shias to perform their religious rites and functions over the plots and structures thereon which had been listed as Shias Wakfs under the Notification dated 15th January, 1954 issued by the Sunni Board. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners and through them the Shia Community of Mohalla Doshipura Varanasi have established their existing customary rights to perform the religious ceremonies, practices, observances, ceremonies and function in question. [1108C] 2. The Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Shian Board is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary right of the petitioners and from the date of the notification. [1108D E] 3. The impugned Notification dated 7th January 1954 issued under Section 5(2) of 1936 Act, by the respondent No. 2, is of a general nature and does not suffer from any infirmity to warrant interference with the same. [1086E F] 4. The provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder are in pari materia with those of the Uttar U. P. Sunni State Board Act, 1966. [1019G] 5. The fact remains that there was no adjudication or decision on the petitioners ' rights on merits as a result of the final order passed by this Court in the appeal. [1008A B] 6. The respondents 5 and 6 have established the existing customary right to perform religious ceremonies in favour of the members, through the Shiam community of Mohalla, Dosipura, Varanasi. [1000B C] 7. The members of the Shia Central Wakf Board are permanently restrained by an injunction from interfering with the exercise of such rights in any manner by the petitioners or members of Shia caste and respondents 1 to 4, particularly the executive magistracy of Varanasi is directed, if action under section 144 Cr. P C., is taken against the officers of the Sunni Central Wakf Boards, notices were issued to them and they were also restrained from exercising their rights in regard to the customary ceremonies etc. [1001C D] 8. The State Government has not been impleaded as a party to the petition. It is only the State which can be impleaded as party to this petition. [1210E F; 1211A B, C] 9. The Court cannot go behind the order of this Court and take into consideration all relevant factors including the fact that there is no adjudication on merits. [1311F G] 10. The question whether a customary right in favour or through a Shias is to perform any religious ceremonies or functions over a plot or structures thereon has been decided by this court in the case of Daryao vs State of U.p., ; , not produced in the earlier litigation either before the Allahabad High Court or this Court, but only by reason of these properties having been registered under the U P. Shia Waqfs (Supplementary) Act, 1964.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business of manufacturing and selling textile goods, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1965 66 under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The assessee claimed set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computation of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional loss. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for set off was admissible only if the loss had not been determined as required under section 24(3) of the 1922 Act. In the reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under Section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1), where an assessee sustains a loss such as is referred to in sub s.(2A) and the loss cannot be wholly set off in accordance with the provisions of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following year and so on. [1166D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the benefit conferred by Section 24(2)(a) continued to remain available even after the assessment had been completed. [1105E] 3. The claim for setting off is admissible under the 1922 act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the same portion not being set off would be carried for ward to the aforesaid year and set off against capital gains for that year. [1066F] 4. The provision in Section 74(1)(b) and Section 80 together with sub section 2B are clearly intended to give effect to the provisions contained in the 1961 act and the proviso thereto. [1015G] 5. The language of Section 80 is clear and unambiguous and it is not possible to read the words "in any other assessment year" as meaning a notional or notional loss, so as to include a notional liability. [1006A B] 6. The expression "in respect of which the loss has been sustained" in sub sec tion (1) of Section 24 does not mean that the loss should be computed on the basis of the loss suffered by the assessee and the amount of capital gains determined under section 71 shall be worked out accordingly. [1000B C] 7. The proviso to Section 80(2) continues to apply even after a bare analysis of these provisions. [1001C] 8. The effect of the provision is that where in respect of any assessment year, the net result of the assessment under the head "capital gains" is a loss the loss shall be set off as if it has not been computed in pursuance of a return filed under Section 139(1) or Section 74A. [1266D E] 9. The provisions of Section 74 (1)(a), section 80 and 80 together are clearly meant to give retrospective effect to both. [1205E F] 10. The object of the 1961 provision is to provide for a notional income, which has not yet been determined in pursuance to a return under Section 140. [121F] 11. The words "as if it had not occurred" in section 80(1), and section 80 (2) are clearly used to give the benefit of the fiction created by the 1961 enactment. [122G] 12. The Legislature has provided for a special procedure for computation of the income tax. It is not permissible to read into the 1961 provisions any provision which would have been in conflict with the 1961 statute. [123A B, D] 13. The scheme of Section 75 and 80 are clear and explicit. The legislature has used the words 'in respect ' and 'in relation to 'in the assessment of income tax '

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), which post he held earlier. The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of service. In the year 1966, the respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Research & Development, on October 13, 1966. He joined the post on October 14, 1966 and was posted at the Directorate General of Inspection (Deptt.) and P.W.D. (D.S.I.). The respondent was posted as Senior Scientific officer in the D.S., and was sent to different units. On his re instatement in service, he was posted according tO the exigencies of service in any of the three units. He made a representation against the order of reversion dated October 13. 1966, but the same was rejected on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity of being heard before the reversion order was passed. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated October 14. 1966 and praying for a direction to the appellants to reinstate him in service with all his emoluments from the date of his arbitrary retirement till the date on which the order was served on him. The High Court held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years, as he had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the meaning of Rule 12 of the Defence Engineering Service Rules, and that the respondent could not claim any benefit of the said rule. The appellants filed a Letters Patent Appeal against the decision of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Tribunal is both proper and valid. [711E] 1.2 The decision of this Court in Union of India vs Col. J.N. Sinha, ; , relied on. 1.3 The question involved in the present case is not whether the respondent belonged to another unit, viz., DAQAS, but was entitled to the benefit of power so exercised in the facts and circum stances of the case. [700F] 1:4. The decision in Union Territory of Chandigarh vs Col J. N. Sinha,, ; , distinguished. 1:5. In spite of the decision in Col.J.N., Sinha, it is not open to the appellant Union of india to contend that the Government had power to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the other unit was increased, it could not be held that he was also entitled to claim the benefit. [601F] 2.1 In the instant case, the decision is both correct and valid, and there is no substance in the appeal. The order passed by the Tribunal was both proper as well as valid, but there is nothing wrong in the appellant 's action. [ 700G H] 2:2. The question is not one of fact. It is a pure question of law. There is no dispute that the service conditions of the employees belonging to three units were the same and their services were inter changeable between the three unit. The service conditions are also common, viz. the three Units, therefore, belonged to and constituted one single service. [600H; 700A] 2 :3.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant on the ground that he was guilty of publication of two pamphlet containing defamatory allegations and distributed it by him as alleged by the appellant. The trial Judge held that the appellant had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him guilty of a corrupt practice under section 123(1) (a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and directed the trial Judge to decide afresh on merits. The appellant contended that having rejected this application, it was not open to the Judge to examine these two persons as court witnesses and this was a serious irregularity which the High court should have set right by quasiting the order passed by the trial judge based on the evidence of these two witnesses. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The trial judge had rightly held that there were two newspapers in the Maharashtra Gazette, one of June 8, 1967 and the other of June 15, 1967 that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June the time limit of ten days fixed under section 21 sub section (1), of the Act began to run from that date and the petition which was filed on the 24th June was beyond time. [968 D] (2) The High Court was right in refusing to quash the order.

The petitioner company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and it entered into a contract with the Government of Uttar Pradesh for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale. The State Government issued a notification dated March 31, 1956, imposing a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged its validity on the ground that the impugned notification was ultra vires the State Legislature and was therefore void. Held, that the Validation Act is intra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, List II, Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and the Validation Acts are not ultra vires. Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer (2) and Firm Bangi Mal vs Sons (3) referred to. The impugned notification must be held to be within the saving of the Validation act. Firm B. P. P., Ltd. vs Sales tax Officer (4) and M/s. Bangi Mall vs Sales (5) referred, (6) The State Legislature was competent to enact a law imposing a sales tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the constructions of works. The Validation Act was not ultra vivos. The validity of the impugned notifications was also challenged as being beyond the legislative competence of the State legislature under Entry 54, and as there was no other entry in List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule, the Validation Ordinance was not saved by the new Act. Firm Banarsi Das vs Sales I.T.O., (1955) 1 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Court, and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of imprisonment a few directives are drifting into social purpose, and this Court has held that punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart from being deterrent. [782B] 2.1 In prison treatment must be more enlightened than the blind strategy of prison severity where all that happens is sex starvation, brutalisation, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio mining pollution, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological ' conditions and emergence at the time of release of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully ' processed into a hardened delinquent. [764C D] 2:2 In prison, treatment must, therefore, be more effective than punitive deprivation to be achieved by the court in any manner. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. [774D E] 2 :3 The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. This reflection apart, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, there blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years.

The respondent company was a limited company dealing in land. It had acquired certain lands for the purpose of construction of a factory. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded compensation to the assessee under section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government. In this appeal by certificate it was contended that the amount of compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesses and therefore, the income from the said property could not be said to have accrued to it as income during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was right in holding that the compensation received under the Land acquisition Act in Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladin & Sons. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, [1962] 1 SCR 676 was not compensation. It must not be forgotten that even if a Court was awarded enhanced compensation there is a right of appeal by the Government to the High Court and the High court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [395C D] The legal position was explained in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition officer & Anr., ; , referred to. In the present case, though the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount, it was only that amount which had accrued or deemed to accrue whether in fact paid or not. As has been stated earlier, a mere claim by the appellant after taking of possession of the land at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation, and the claimant is entitled to an additional compensation and if no such claim is made, it will be a trading loss. [397D E] The High Courts were right in the view taken by them that the award made by them was merely an offer or tender of the compensation determined by the Collector to the onwer of the property on the acquisition, the High Courts should not interfere with the amount awarded under the Act. [398E F] Harish ChandraRaj Singh vs Deputy Land Acquisi tion Officer & Anr. , ; and Hari Chandra Raj Singha vs The Dy.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondent for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by him under section 12(1) (f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The Trial Court passed a decree for eviction and other reliefs in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The appellants ' appeal was dismissed by the Additional District Judge. In second appeal the High Court held that the compromise was legal and valid and executable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under the terms and conditions of the agreement, the respondent had withdrawn the suit premises from the appellant 's tenant and submitted to a decree in his favour for eviction unconditionally. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree of eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. [882 B] (2) In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance therewith. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". [883 C D] (3) In the order recording the compromise the court said: "on a perusal of the joint compromise it was found that the same is legal and is within the purview of the plaint. Therefore, plaint verification is accepted and the case is decreed in accordance With the conditions of compromise as under: 1. The order so recorded in the judgment was in full compliance with the requirement of Order 22, Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [888 D] Nagindas Ramdas vs Dalpatram & Ors., ; , followed. (4) In view of the pleadings of the parties and in view of their respective materials in this case it cannot be said that the decree for ejectment was not passed on the basis of compromise. [89 890 A B] Nagendas Ramdas v Dalpataram & Ors. A.I.R. , approved.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling textile mills. The shares were purchased by the respondent company in its own name and the shares were sold to the respondent. The respondent claimed that the shares had been purchased for the purpose of earning profits and that the sale price of these shares was not adequate for the purposes of earning the profits. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove that the company had suffered a capital loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ . On appeal by the appellant the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the respondent had failed 'to establish that the dividend was not in fact received as claimed by the company and that it was not liable to pay any income tax. The Tribunal however, on reference, held that there was no commercial profit in the relevant accounting years. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The loss in the value of the shares in Elphinstone Mills Ltd. is a capital gain. It is difficult to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matters mentioned isolated from other relevant factors. [864 C] (2) The respondent had suffered no capital loss because it was due to the loss of the company 's share capital. The question is not whether the value has been determined on the basis of the assessment under section 23A(1). [865 D] (3) The Tribunal was right in holding that the loss incurred by the assessee was a capital one and not a revenue loss.

The respondent, a displaced person, filed an application under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, for setting aside the order of the Civil Judge. The Civil Judge held that the Civil judge was not justified in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. He also held that section 47 of the Act applied to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act and that the decision of the civil judge was final. On appeal, the District Judge set aside the orders of the High Court and remanded the case for a fresh decision. The respondent filed an appeal before the District judge against the order passed by the Civil Court modifying the order. The District judge held that in view of section 46 of the , the Civil Judges were not justified under section 15 of the . He also rejected the contention that the provisions of section 37 of the did not apply because the appellants had apparently applied under section 18 of the U.P. Consolidation of holdings Act, 1953, and that section 39 of the was applicable to arbitrations. The High Court held that there was no question of considering the effect of sections 46 and 47 of , and that it was quite clear that what was made final is the decision by the arbitrator as it emerged after appropriate proceedings, if any, had been taken under the provisions Of the . In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the decisions of the District Judges modifying the awards were appealable under section 39. [641 B] (ii) Section 37 of , provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 is not applicable to arbitration under the U P. Consolidation Of Holdings Act. [651 C] (iii) The effect of section 8 of the is that all the provisions in the except sub sections (1) and (2) apply to arbitrations as provided by section 12. Section 46 provides for appeals against orders passed by a civil court. It does not say that the provision of section 15 will apply to arbitration. [652 E] (iv) The object of section 18 is to provide for an appeal from an award under the consolidation of Holdings. The effect is that the proceedings before the arbitrator are taken under sections 46, 47 and 47. If any question arises as to title or interest in any property, it has to be decided by a competent court. [631 D] (v) Section 48 of the does not apply to awards made under the Act. It only applies to awards which have been made under section 37. The result is that if an award is passed under section 36, the provisions contained in sections 46 to 47 will apply and the decision would be final. [621 D E] In re: Attar Singh, ; , followed. (vi) Section 49 of the Consolidation Act provides for the appointment of an arbitrator by the State Government. It is not necessary that the State should appoint an arbitrator under section 48 of that Act. The object is to apply sections 15 and 39 of Chapter VII of the Code of Civil Procedure to arbitrations and to make provisions for the correction and revision of revenue records for villages under consolidation. [661 D F] (vii) Section 46 of , does not provide for appeals from orders passed under the general or special Act. Therefore, section 37 must be read with section 37 as it stood before the amendment in 1953. [678 G H] (viii) The result of section 48 is that where there is a dispute as to the title and such question has not already been determined by any competent court, the Consolidation Officer has to refer the question for determination to the Civil court which thereafter will refer it to the arbitrator.

The petitioner, diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. The respondent corporation issued a resolution for promotion to the post. The petitioner challenged the said resolution before the High Court by way of writ petition. The High Court held that the promotion which was made on the basis of the sources of recruitment and not on the ground of educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to higher posts, since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The resolution dated 15th January, 1988 passed by the respondent corporation in 1988 and the resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961 are valid and do not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [10E] 1.2 In the absence of rules or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The resolution passed by respondent Corporation in 1988 cannot be said to have been challenged before the Court. [11F] 1:3. In view of the fact that the petitioner wanted such a classification to be made, it could not be done except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers. It may be observed that it was not a case where the classification was already made which was challenged before this Court.

The petitioner, a member of the Indian Administrative Service (Judicial Branch) was appointed as an Additional District and Sessions Judge in January, 1986. He was promoted to the post of Additional District & Sessions Judge on July 1, 1987. In May, 1988 he was promoted as Additional District Judge on August 3, 1989. On September 30, 1990 he was transferred to the High Court of Kerala. The petitioner challenged his transfer order by filing a writ petition in this Court. This Court dismissed the petition holding that the Chief Justice of India had no power to review his earlier order and made a statement that he was of the view that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union of India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union Government to fill up the vacancies were maintainable. The Court also held that the failure to make the necessary arrangements for the implementation of the recommendations made by the Chief justice would not be a ground for review. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to review their earlier orders and that the decision of the Chief Justices of India should be reviewed only if there was any element of public Interest and the Writ Petition requiring a mandamus to the State Government to make a direction for filling up the vacancy were maintainable, and that this Court should not interfere with the order of transfer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Chief Justice is the final authority to decide whether or not there has been any violation of the constitutional provision. [439C] 2.1 The Chief justice of India is the Chief Judge of the High court and such other Judges of the Supreme Court as the Central Government may deem it neces sary to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. [441F] 2(2) The Chief Justices have quite often both before the Parliament and outside has stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior Courts without the name being cleared by the chief Justice of the India. [442G] 3.1 In case the Commission is not constituted, the two questions indicated above which are of vital importance to the efficient functioning of the judicial system in the country require consideration and there is an element of immediacy in the matter. The correctness of the opinion of the majority in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of the respondent No. 1 may not be considered by a larger bench. [444A B] 3(3) The decision of this Court in S P Gupta ' case is not, therefore, to be considered as final say. [443C D] 4.1 It is clear on a plain reading of these two Articles that the President of India has quite often either constitutional functionaries or having a consultationative role, having a Consultative role or the power to appoint any person as Additional Sessions Judge. The matter is not one of policy and process it becomes imperative that the role of the institution of the Judicial system in this country requires consideration and no other selection to be made.

The respondent was a Bank official. He was appointed as an Enquiry Officer on January 9, 1979 and he was appointed an Enquiry Offi cer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9.1979. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report to the Chief Execu tive Officer on May 10, 1980 recommending that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. On May 11, 1980, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of punishment and praying for quashing the said order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the enquiry was incompetent as the original order was without jurisdiction and, therefore, null and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High, Court ought not have interfered with the impugned order of penalty because (i) the respondent had submitted to the jurisdiction of the Enquiry Officer, (ii) the disciplinary authority had acted in violation of the principles of natural justice; and (iii) the High court ought not to have directed payment of all consequential benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of removal from service was quashed by the High 'Court on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High Courts for the first time in a writ peti tion. [199F] 2.1 The High court was right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment but it is not open to the appellant to contend that the order imposing punishment is bad in law. [200G] Pulin 's case concluded by this Court in Pulin vs 'Somely ' ; , followed. Pulin & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; and Pulin Chandra 's Case, referred to.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was constituted under the Delhi Development Act, 1957. The respondents were owners of certain plots in the area. The appellant applied for sanction to the plan submitted by them but the same was rejected on the ground that the building operations were allowed to be carried on there and the proposed user mentioned by them in the plan sent for sanction was not in contravention of any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the rejection of the appellant 's application. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had to establish, as it sought to, that the proposed building or the use of the site for the building by the respondents would contravene the provisions Of section 14 of the Development Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The purpose of the development scheme is to provide for the development of a particular area and not to make any provision for the same. [167 E] (2)(a) The word "development" in sub section 2(b) of Section 336 means "to develop a particular land or building". If the word " development" is used in the context of the Act, it would mean development of land and not development of any other law. [168 B C] (b) The words "or any building" in the sub section are wide enough to include any building which has been constructed for a purpose of residence or business or for carrying on any occupation or trade or business. [169 E F] (c) The scheme of the scheme is not that the only development plan is to be prepared and has not come into operation for the zone concerned, but it is proposed to be used in a different manner. If the Master Plan has come into force and sent to the Central Government for approval, parties and local authorities will have to be given an opportunity of sending their objections and suggestions and representations which have all to be duly and properly considered by the Authority concerned. [170 E F; 171 A] (d) The appellant 'could have been permitted to use the land as asked for by them. If that was so, there is no violation of section 14(2). [171 G H] (e) The High court was right in holding that it could not be said that there would be any violation of either the Master plan or any provisions of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1956.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary of Industries, Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government, of India. The appellant No 1 was a Minister of State for India and was in charge of the administration of the country. On the day of the incident the appellant was found to have been in possession of certain sums of money which were disproportionate to his known sources of income. The prosecution case against him was that he had brought Rs. 2,000 from the top drawer of the dressing table in the bedroom of the appellant no 1 and that on the night between 8th and 9th April 1949 he went to the Constitution House and saw the appellant along with two others armed with guns and a revolver. The currency notes were recovered from the bottom drawer of his dressing Table in the post office of the appel lant No. 2. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000. On appeal by the State the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. Held, that the evidence of the two witnesses was not reliable and could not be relied upon as they were interested in the success of the prosecution case. The evidence of these two witnesses did not inspire confidence and it could not have been proved orally by them. The fact that the appellant had brought those moneys from his home to the State Government and became a limb of the police as it were, was sufficient to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the appellant that he was brought to the country without any inducement or threat.

The respondent was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The trial court dismissed the plaintiff 's suit for declaration that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the judgment of the first appellate court and remitted the case back to it for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In the meantime, the Senior Superintendent of Police, Patiala, thereafter dismissed the appellant on 20.4.1976. The respondent filed a regular second appeal before the High court against the decree of the trial court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving: "HELD: "The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [826D E] The question involved in this appeal is not required to be decided on merits, since the judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine. [827F G] The High court should have examine the plaint in accordance therewith and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In view of the fact that the appellant had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order of his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that later he was again dismissed, it should have considered the correct Article of the limitation Act applicable.

The appellant company was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In the assessment year 1962 63, the Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 123(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. On further appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the transaction involved mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods sold. In reference, the High Court answered the question referred in favour of the revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Explanation to section 24(1), as it stood before its amendment by Act 2 of 1969, was not applicable to transactions which were not completed by actual delivery but only laid down that if there was a actual delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set off against the profits made by the assesses 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decision in D. (P) Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; and D. N. Mukherjee vs Commissioner Income tax (supra), held that where the speculative transactions were of such a nature as to constitute a business, the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. [184 G H] The Explanation is not relevant for the purpose of this case because it permits the set off of a loss against the assessee 's profits and gains, i any in a similar business only. [185 B C] D. K. Mukherjee & Ors. vs Income tax Officer, Calcutta , followed.

The appellant was the successful candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The first respondent filed an Election Petition challenging the validity of the appellant 's election on the ground that he had committed a corrupt practice under section 123(1) (a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The petition was dismissed by the Election Tribunal and the High Court in appeal held that the appellant had failed to prove that he was guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (1)(a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the first respondent that the word "subscribe" in the Representation Of the People (Amendment) Act, 1952, is used in its ordinary sense and not as a substantive provision. Held, that the words "to be signed " in section 36(1)(b) are wide enough to include the making of a mark. The word "sign" is used with reference to the original marks and it is clear from the form that " signatures are required " and not " subscribed". The word 'subscribe ' is not defined but it is equally clear, when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that " signature " is not the only method of signing. It is true that the use of the word 'sign ' is used and not the word ` subscribed '; but the word has been used in the ordinary way to denote the making or signing of a marks as the Act itself does in the definition of "sign". The words " signed " are used in this sense in the same sense in which they are used.

The appellants were working as Chemical Workers in the Company. On September 7, 1972, the Company sent separate communications to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Company from that date. The Company sent a letter dated September 21, 1972 to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of their services by the appellants. On October 2, 1972 the Company wrote to the Company stating that it had been informed that its letter dated Sept. 7,1972 had reached them only on September 20, 1972 and that they were not willing to resume work on or after September 18. 1972. The appellants ' union wrote to this effect on September 21. 1972 and stated that their letter dated October 2. 1972 was received by them only at the factory gate and that their names might be struck out from the rolls of Company. The company sent a separate communication to the workmen stating that they did not intend to abandon service but had also returned the cheques sent by the Company on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The Labour Commissioner, however, without giving any reasons for his refusal to give them notice of termination of services, terminated their services. On the question whether in the circumstances of the case it could be said that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the service of the company and did not want to continue in service of its workmen, HELD: (1) The letter dated August 7, 1971 was received on September 7. 1972 by the company which stated that the Company 's letter dated December 21,1972 was received only on Sept. 20,1972. [629A] (2) The appellants had no intention to abandon their service and did nothing from duty. They were no provision in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services of the appellants in the aforesaid circumstances, the impugned action on the part of the respondent company clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of appellants during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [625B C] (3) The Company 'Some of the workmen had gone on indefinite strike which ended on October 22, 1972 in response to the strike notice given by the union to the company to press its demand for re instatement of their three dismissed leaders and had not only by their letters dated September 7/27, 1972 unequivocally intimated to the respondent that they would not take any longer in service. The letter was received back by them on September 22,1972 and not earlier was ever denied or refuted by the respondent in the correspondence that passed between the parties. [613C D] (4) The company 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid. [526D] (5) The High Court was right in holding that there was no abandonment of the service on the appellants ' part and that the termination of the services could only be in terms of the appellant 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, the order of termination could only have been in terms thereof. [600E] (6) The respondent company had no right to terminate the services by giving one month 's notice or one month"s pay in lieu of notice.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees took out a loan from the Trust and executed a mortgage deed in favour of the appellant. The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee would pay off the loan to the appellant against the mortgage debt. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs. 1,000. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the sale was not in accordance with law and that the property sold was not liable to be sold. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the mortgage deed was not a valid one as the mortgagee had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees, abandonment of the execution proceedings was in law equivalent to payment to the decree holder of the money specified in the proclamation of sale for recovery.
