(2) that a judgment of a Full Bench of the Court could be ignored by a Single Judge if the Full Bench judgment was given on a reference made on a question of law arising in a matter before him, and a decision given on such a reference was binding upon the judgment debtor when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution; (3) that even though there was a judgment by a single Judge of the High court, he was not bound to follow that precedent. HELD: (1)(a) The judgment of the Full Court of Gujarat was binding on Raju J., if the learned Judge was of the view that the decision of Bhagwati, J. in Pijare Karimbhai 's case and of Nacleod, C.J., was erroneous by a Division Bench of a High Court. [465 F] (b) The Full Bench was not right in holding that a Judgment delivered by a Full bench of the Gujarat High Court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to he regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the full Bench for purposes of examining the question. [467 A] (c) The decision of the Division Bench was binding between Raju J. and Raju J, but the Full bench did not agree with the view taken by Bhagwati, j. In the circumstances there will be no order as to costs in this Court and in the High Courts. [466 B C] (d) The question whether a judgment delivered by the Full court of a Division of a Court after proper consideration of points before itself is liable for confirmation under section 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, is a question which can be regarded as relevant by Judges in that Court.

The appellant joined the Post and Telegraph Department as clerk on June 4, 1935. He was promoted to the post of Telegraph Officer in July, 1948. The Government of India by its order dated November 30, 1962, issued under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, granted absolute right to prematurely retire a government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the Government had issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule 1(2)(a) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The High Court held that Rule 2 (2) was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 2 of the Pension Rules is ultra vires Article 14 and is ultra rites Articles 14 & 16 of India [799B] 1.2 Rule 2 is ultra vivos Articles 14, 16 and 16. The object of Rule 2 being to give a right to retire an officer who has completed thirty years of service, he must be retired at anytime at the discretion of the Government under Rule2(2). The said rule gives unguided discretion to the Government to retire a Government servant at a time after having completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. [701C D] 1:3.

The assessee firm carried on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. During the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December, 1941 to 29th September, 1941, the assessee firm sold katecum in Bombay and its branch offices at Raichur and Bombay. The sales tax authorities did not set off the deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable account years ending 31 st March, 1942 and as such there could be no deficiency of profit during those periods. The assessee claimed a set off of the deficiency only for the year 1940 41. The Income Tax Officer did not allow any deduction on account of the said deficiency in the computation of the excess profits. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed that order. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accounts from October, 1940 41 was attributable to the manufacturing activity between 28th OCtober, 1940 to 31 st April, 1944 and therefore there could not be any deficiency of income during the chargeable assessment year ending 31.3.1944. The High Court also rejected the assessee 's contention that the loss in the accounting period ending 31 March, 1943 must be set off against the excess profit for the relevant chargeable accounting years ending 30th March, 1946 and as the assessee could not claim any set off under the Act, the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up the posts of Civil Judge (Junior Division) in the Kerala State Judicial Service. The applicants were not selected and they filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the Rules. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the applicants who had qualified in Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had obtained the diploma in Civil engineering (Junior division) and the Mechanical Branch were not entitled to exercise their option and then take their turn according to their rank in the common list prepared by the Public Service Com mission. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The Kerala Government or the KPSC was not directed to prepare a common list. The KP SC has stated clearly that the petitioner will be entitled to exercised his option and thereafter take his turn according ties according to his rank in that common list preparing by the Commission. [728C D] 2. The petitioner will also be entitled for a post, if he has exercised his options in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the Common List for claiming the post. [750D E] 3. The State Government or KPS is not directed by the Single Judge to prepare separate list. It may be mentioned that preparation of no common list was directed either by the single judge or by the Division Bench of the Kerala High Court. But facing difficulties, in giving effect to the directions given by the learned Single Judge and that of the Division bench, the State has not been directed to frame a common seniority list. [751E F] 4. The judgment of the learned single Judge is set aside and the K PSC is directed to consider the question whether the K.PSC or K.S.C. was entitled to make selection and prepare a separate list, one for Civil Engineering graduates and the other for Mechanical Engineering graduate on the basis of examination already conducted. [753G H] 5. The writ petitions are accordingly allowed.

The respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm on the ground that the plaintiff had no interest in the business and excluded the plaintiff from the partnership business. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was governed by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, and the plaintiff was entitled to get an order directing the defendant No. 2 to pay a sum of Rs.50 for declaration, Rs. 50 for profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. On appeal, the High Court held that the correct value of the suit is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proper valuation of the plaint was not within the pecuniary Jurisdiction of the High court, and that the court was bound to accept that the valuation given by the plaintiff as grossly inadequate was wrong. On behalf of respondent No 1 it was submitted that the Court was competent to entertain a suit being valued for purposes of court fees and jurisdiction. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The valuation put by the appellant on the plaint is arbitrary and unacceptable. [512C] In a suit of accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose.

The respondent assessee is a manufacturer of cement. The State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industries in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this notification and have commenced production after 1st April, 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in columns (3) and (4). The respondent assessee claimed exemption on the ground that the industries run by them are "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. The Assessing Authority rejected the claim on the view that the industry run by the assessee was "tractive industries". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assessing Authority. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the exemption granted under column (3), in respect of the industries mentioned in column(1) was valid and the assessee could not rely upon the said exemption. On reference, the High Court held that since the relief by way of deferment of tax is only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption and the former is not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above, the same should be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since there was no specific condition imposed in column 3 of the notification excluding "trained industries" from the exemption, the exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect to the industries specified by it is based on the words which require that the director of Industries shall grant a certificate (a) that the dealer is entitled to claim the exemption and (b) that he has not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of tax. [608C D] 1.2 The assesses in those cases had set up the industries after the explicit instructions of 12.1. It was not necessary for the rules of deferment to specifically provide that they will not be available to the Industries listed in rule 14 particularly when rule 4 has incorporated the requirement of an quali fication in accordance with the previous instruction for the said purpose. [625D] 1:3 The assesses had set out in the notification itself and all that the Directors of Industries have to do is to certify that the applicant is entitled, as a condition precedent to exemption, to the benefit of the exemption. It may be that the conditions are satisfied but they cannot say that they are fulfilled. [613E] 1 :4 The assesses 's contention that since they set up their industries after 1.4.1981 from pay able tax under rule 14(1)(i) they should have been exempted, is not correct.

The petitioners were appointed as Additional District and Sessions Judges in the Delhi Judicial Service. They were promoted to officiate as Additional Sessions Judges on the basis of selection from amongst members of the Delhi judicial Service, that is to say, the promotees. The petitioners challenged the seniority list prepared by the Full Court of the High Court on the ground that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis the promotees was not determined according to the dates on which their appointments were made and that the quota rule in the proviso to Rule 7(b) of the Rules was not applicable to them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not appointed regularly as Additional Judges, and that they had been continuously officiating as Additional judges for a number of years. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the proviso in Rule 7 of the rules was applicable only to direct recruits who were appointed to substantive vacancies in the Service; (ii) the quota prescribed under Rule 7 must necessarily be followed, and (iii) the promotees were not entitled to claim seniority over the promotees as they had not been appointed regularly. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The proviso to rule 7(a) provides for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits, and so on. [395C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners are appointed regularly that all the promotees are appointed to temporary posts in accordance with the qualifications laid down under Rule 4(1). The seniority of promotees vis avis the promotees shall be determined according the dates when their appointments are made. [397D E] 1:3. The quota rule is not applicable in the instant cases as it was not in existence at the time of appointment of the direct recruits. [398E F] 1 :4. In the matter of seniority, any distinction between direct recruits and promotees should be made on the principle of "quota" or "quotation". If a direct recruit is appointed after a member of the service has been appointed in a substantive capacity to a temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge, cannot and should not rank higher than the latter in the list of seniority. [399F G] 1 5. The seniority must be governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruitment who is appointed before a member has been promoted to a substantive vacancy in the service. If a promotee is appointed to a permanent post after a person has completed not less than ten years of service in the judicial Service as required under Rule 16(2) of Rules, the seniority rule will have to be framed according to that date and if such posts are not filled by promotion from members of Delhi Judicial Services, the senior most among them will rank lower in seniority than the former. [400H; 400A B] 1 6. The rules of recruitment to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service are governed by Rule 7 (a) which provides for recruitment to a post in the Indian Administrative Service also inter by promotion on the recommendation of the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 5(1) of that Rules. The Rules of recruitment are made by selection and after completion of a minimum of ten years judicial service, the appointments are to be made according to seniority cum merit basis. [403C D] 1 7. The direct recruits are appointed in substantive capacity as Additional district & Sessions Judges and not on the result of any competitive examination. They are appointed on the recommendations of the Third Pay Commission which is a statutory body constituted under Article 309 of the Constitution. The appointments are by promotion or appointment after a period of 10 years of continuous service to which they have been appointed. [404D E; 405A] 2:1. The proviso in r. 7(c) provides that the inter se seniority of the promotees vis the direct recruit shall be governed under the rules, of continuous officiating service in that Service.

The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The High Court in reference held that the income was assessable under section 27 of the Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood at the relevant time. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) The Income tax officer was of the view that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business could not be brought to tax on that footing. [392 B] (2) The power of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner under section 33A of the Act read with section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax, 1922 is a judicial power and it cannot be exercised in respect of an assessment made by an Association of persons. [391 C D] Commissioner of Income tax vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate Ltd., ; , referred to. (3) The income earned by the assessee was assessed to tax as income of an association or individuals of which he was a member. The income from business was liable to be brought under section 28(1)(c) of that Act read along with section 33B(2). [391 E] Commissioner off Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Colliery Co. Ltd., , referred. (4) The High Courts in India have held that where the income tax Officer assesses a firm or association of individuals, it is competent to him to assess the members individually.

The appellant filed a suit in the Madras High Court for partition of his claim for partition and separate possession of his share. The plaint was amended by adding a prayer that the court fee paid on the memorandum of appeal should be taken to be the valuation for purposes of court fees under section 7(iv)(b) of the Indian Court Fees Act, 1870. The appellant contended that the amendment made in the plaint was inconsistent with the earlier order that the proper court fee should be paid on a memorandum of appeals and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct the appellant to pay court fees on the basis of the value of Rs. 15,00,000 as the valuation of his relief for partition for the payment of court fee. Held, that the appeal must fail. The order of the Division Bench was not justified in directing the appellant 's application for amendment of the plaint and it could be reopened at this stage. The suit was governed by section 7 (iv)(a) of Act 1 of 1908 which provides that the plaintiff should first value his claim to the purpose of court Fees and it provided for the determination of the valuation. The court fee on the plaint as well as the memorandum Of appeal were in substance different from the amount claimed by the appellant. The High Court was right in directing him to pay the court fees both on the original plaint and on the Memorandum of appeal. The plaintiff 's claim for division of his suit for partition was governed under section 8(iv) (b) and it cannot be reopened in a subsequent suit.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee sought to impugn the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2. Respondent No. 1, who was a member of the Executive Council of the New Delhi Corporation, seeking to impeach the said decision by instituting an appeal before the High Court under Section 116A of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the NDMC had not raised any objection to the proposal for construction of refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor and that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged in Bye law 16.4.8 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the Municipal Council to satisfy itself that the building plans provided for adequate fire safety measures were adequate. The appellant, who had been running a workshop in New Delhi, filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the decision dated 18th February, Respondent No 1, contending that the approval given by the Chief fire Officer envisaged under Bye law 17.4 8.1 was an extra condition and the acceptance of the same was implicit in the clearance given by Respondent No 2, who did not raise any objection on the ground that either they were not in conformity with Bye law16.4 or 16. 4.8.1 or that the plans were defective for want of pedestrian walk way. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that there was no question of any specific objections to the plan on the grounds that neither the approval nor the sanction of the Chief Municipal Officer envisaged by Bye law17.4, 8.2 and 16.04.1 had been obtained. The Division Bench dismissed the Letters Patent Appeal filed by Respondent 1 and 2. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The requirement of bye laws 16.1 is an additional conditions and not an limitation on its power of approval to satisfy themselves that the construction plans provided are adequate and not the limitation prescribed by the Bye law. [608C] 2.1 The approval given to the scheme by the Executive Committee envisaged in bye law 17(4) is an extra requirement and not one of limitation on their power of approving the plan. [613D] 2:2. The approval of the Council of Municipal Corporation envisaged under bye law 16(4), is an addition or subterfuge to the sanctioned Zonal Developmental requirements in the manner indicated by Bye laws 16(1) and 16(3). [609E F] 3.1 It is not a case where the sanction given by respondent No. 2 was not in accordance with Byelaw 16. [625G] 3:2 The approval contemplated under bye laws 17.1 and 16 (4) cannot be said to have been obtained by the Municipal Corporation at the time of the grant of the licence. [656C D] 3 :3.

The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in motor business, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling motor business. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties and for accounts of the motor business and claimed that the compromise decree should be made absolute. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the cause of action in the two suits was different from the cause, of action, in the first suit and that the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had not made any mistake or misunderstanding in the compromise about his legal right inasmuch as he thought that when accounts were to be taken up to a certain date, the joint Hindu family business would be still a joint family business and that he had a right to ask for accounts from March 31, 1946. HELD : (i) The cause of actions in the second suit was different than the cause or action in both the suits. The cause or matter in the third suit was identical with the cause in the earlier suit. [103 C] (ii) The compromise was made after due deliberation and that it was not a case of mistake or misapprehension. It was not as if there had been an oversight on the part of the parties but the parties knew that the businesses might go on afterwards; but the party knew that he would go on later, and did not specifically care for providing by the compromise decrees for accounts. [104 E] (iii) The question whether a particular case was one of law or fact depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is well settled that in a suit based on a compromise the plaintiff must prove his case by leading evidence, both oral and documentary, and the court must also satisfy itself that the parties had acted bona fide and that there was no mistake or confusion in the filing of the suit. The question as to whether a party has acted mala fide or not is essentially one of fact depending upon the circumstances of the case. [106 E F] (iv) In the present case, the compromise was not made by the parties at all; it was only an attempt to get rid of the plaintiff 's claim to account for the subsequent period. The suit was therefore barred under O. II, r. 2(1) of C.P.C. [107 B] (v) The court has to consider whether the compromise is bona fide or genuine and if it does not disclose any fraud or misrepresentation on the plaintiff, it will be a nullity. If the plaintiff really intended that accounts should be taken into account, he was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it.

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of sea water and salt products. The salt works were carried on in the salt Works, that is, the salt works which were being carried on by the appellant 's Salt Works. The appellant was prosecuted under section 92 of the , for working the salt work in connection with the conversion of sea waters into salt. The trial Court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 93 of the Act and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the expression " premises" in the definition of the word " factory" in el. (k) of section 2 of the Bombay Salt Act, 1948, is not restricted in scope to buildings alone; (2) the process of converting sea water into salt did not amount to "manufacturing process " as no process for making, altering, packing, cleaning or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal was carried on. HELD : (i) The expression " factory " in el.(k) is wider than the general word " premises " and must be given its ordinary meaning. [603 D] (ii) The definition of "factory" in cl. (y) of s 2 of Bombay Salt Works, which includes salt works as such do not include any building or structure which is used for the manufacture or production of salt. [507 E] (iii) The process of conversion of the sea water to salt was carried out in the open air and not in building, and therefore the salt was not a factory within the meaning of the expression 'factory '. [613 G] (iv) The word "premises" is used in els. (p) and (q) of cl. 2 of section 3 of the Indian Factories Act, which are as follows: "The term " premises", includes any building, structure or part thereof, whether fixed or not, and also any part of a building, hut or part of any building which is intended to be used for human habitation. " The word 'premises ' in el., (y), means any building and its appurtenant thereto. [625 G] In the present case, the appellant was carrying on the manufacture and sale of sea Water. It was not shown that the salt manufactured by the respondent was a factory as defined in cl.(k).

The respondent was appointed as Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, he was promoted to the post of Director of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949. He joined the new post on November 28. 1949. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments to the Polytechnics and all of them, except the respondent, were absorbed permanently in the department of Technical education with effectfrom November 28 1949. In 1960, he joined the Engineering Department as Tailoring Instructor. He was not confirmed in the post till November 28 but was confirmed in that post by an order dated February 19, 1964. The appellant challenged his appointment on the ground that he had no legal right to be absorbed in the service of the Department. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the respondent in the Engineering department be given effect from the date on which he was initially taken over by the Director and appointed as Tailor. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had no right to the absorption in the Service of the department because the order of the Chetty 's absorption was passed in 1951 and that of the Government of Mysore, which was a concession which could not be claimed as of right, and consequently, a writ of mandamus should not issue. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person is deputed to the Department, of Technical Educational from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date when he was originally sent". [262 D] 2. In the present case, the High Court was fully justified in granting relief to the respondent. [262 E F] 3. The order of Chetty 'Some State Government dated February19, 1964 was not challenged by the appellant before the High court and it did not challenge that order.

The petitioner, a foreign parent for being appointed guardian of a child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, filed an application before the court under section 14(1) (c) of the , praying that the petitioner be appointed guardian for the child in adoption. The court held that the application was not maintainable as it had been filed by a foreign parents who were not parties to the petition. In appeal, the High Court held that since an application for appointment as guardian could, according to the principles and norms laid down by this Court, be processed only by a recognised social or child welfare agency, the court should not make an order for appointment of a foreigner as guardian unless it is satisfied that the applicant of the foreigner for adopting a child has been sponsored by such social or labour welfare agency. The High Court also held that in most cases where an application is made by a person other than foreign parents for being impleaded as a party, the Court should not direct the foreign parent to take the child to his own country with a view to its eventual adoption. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the High Courts in most of cases where applications are made by foreign parents seeking appointment of guardian of the child are pending before them, have not been constituted as a court for the purpose of making an order under section 12(1)(c) and (d) of . The Court should be satisfied that it will be for the welfare of the minor child to be taken in adoption; (ii) the foreign parents whose application is being considered, are not entitled to be given in inter country adoption; and (iii) the court has no jurisdiction to appoint a foreigner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Court has in most matters where an applicant for appointment is considered, every effort must be made by the recognised social and child welfare agencies to find placement for the minor in the court and community of the foreigners and will be able to get warmth and affection of family life as also moral and material stability and security and whether it will serve the purpose. [804C D] 2. The foreign parents, who have taken a child, are normally expected to take care of the children available with them for adoption on and if the Indian family wants to see the child study report in respect of any particular child, child study reports should also be made available to the Indian social or Child welfare agency through which such child is proposed to be made. [8804D] 3.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Ltd. was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute "Whether for the accounting year 1965 66 the quantum of bonus payable by the appellant to its workmen is 20% of the effective salaries or wages with a further direction to set on a sum of Rs. 1,46,252. The Tribunal held that for the assessment year 1965 67, the quantum was 20% and allocable surplus was worked out at Rs. 2,94,252 and directed the surplus amount of Rs, 1,47,252 to be added back as allocable. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain items from gross profits for purposes of computing the available and alloca tion of bonus. [617 D] (ii) The payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. [625 E F] (iii) The award of the Tribunal can be maintained even on the basis that the principle adopted by the Tribunal in respect of direct tax is found to be erroneous by this Court. [650 D] In the instant case, the Tribunal had rejected the claim of the Unions for depreciation and set on record its own calculation of direct taxes. It did not accept the contention of the Union that the amount of compensation was not an item which could be deducted from gross profit under the Act as claimed by the management.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954. He was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on August 1, 1955 and as a Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1957. The appellant was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner on September 10, 1969 and as Additional Commissioner of Sales Tax on October 7, 1970. On promotion as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. He continued to hold the post till November 29, 1974 when he was promoted. The Government accepted his representation and dropped the charges against him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of November 29. 1974 of the Government was not sustainable in law as the appellant had been promoted to a higher post in 1957, and that the Government had no power to retire him from service after he had attained the age of SO years or after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is set aside and the appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He will be entitled to his costs. [717C] 2.1 When there is nothing in the conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it is impossible to sustain the order. The fact that the appellant was reverted as Deputy commissioner of Commercial taxes does not make any difference. [818F G] 2:2 In the instant case, the 1969 entry noted that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant, the ultimate result of the enquiry which was that the charges should be dropped was nowhere noted in the personal file of the appel lant.

The appellants were the owners of certain transport vehicles. The Regional Transport Authority, Andhra Pradesh, issued a notification under section 68D(1) of the , authorising the State Transport Undertaking to ply the said vehicles on the routes specified in the notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme framed under section 63(1), not having been approved by the Chief Minister, the scheme could not be assailed as not in conformity with the requirements of section 68C; and (ii) the schemes were vitiated by non compliance with the requirement of section 69C. HELD: The scheme was valid. The scheme did not contain any provision for the nationalisation of transport vehicles within the meaning of section 63 of the Act. [368 E] (i). The scheme framed by the Corporation could not therefore be assailed on the ground that it was not in accordance with the provisions of section 66 C. [369 G] (ii). The schemes were invalid because they did not comply with the mandatory requirements of s 68C. [370 A B] (iii) The scheme is vitiated by noncompliance with the required conditions of section 70 C and the Rules made thereunder. [371 D E] State of Andhra Pradesh vs N. Krishna Rao, ; , followed. (iv). The Scheme framed under the Act was not a valid scheme. It was not open to the appellants to challenge it on the grounds that they were not covered by the provisions in the Act or that they had been singled out for consideration as not warranted by law. [372 F G] State Transport Corporation of Andhra vs A. V.V.S. Rao, A.I.R. 1963 S.C. 971, followed.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The appellant made certain declarations to the Commercial Tax Officer that he had issued the declaration forms duly filled in and signed by the registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the appellant 's claim for exemption on the ground that the declaration form was not a condition for claiming exemption thereunder. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant had failed to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued a declaration forms to it and that the said declaration forms were not genuine. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal holding that the mere fact that the declarations form was furnished did not make any difference as regards the nature of the declaration made by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "in writing" in section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act are wide enough and must be given a liberal construction so as to give it a complete meaning. [626 B] (ii) The expression "in the form prescribed" in the proviso to section 5 (2)(b) is not intended to cover a case where the proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove the fact that sales were for the said purpose. [625 C D] (iii) The word "in any form" used in the second proviso to s.5(2) (a)(i) of Act, is not restricted to cases where the provision is mandatory and the words "by the authority concerned" are wide in amplitude. [650 E F] (iv) The language of section 5 is plain and unambiguous. It does not require that the dealer should have a declaration form duly filled up and signed before the prescribed authority has to be furnished in the prescribed manner by the dealer who sells the goods.

The petitioners were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the provisions of sections 167(2), 167(3) and 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not complied with; (2) the under trial prisoners whose particulars were given in the list filed by Mrs. B.B. Singh, Assistant Inspector General of Prisons, Bihar, could not be released on bail because they had attained the age of 18 years on the date of the incident and therefore their detention was illegal; (3) the petitioners were entitled to have their cases considered for release on bail under section 167(1)(2); (4) the State should furnish to this court the dates on which these under trial prisoner were remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrates, so that they could satisfy themselves whether these under trials prisoners had been periodically remanded from time and again by the Magistrate; (5) the failure of the State Government to provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail and opposing remand provided that no objection was raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for such bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of it in accordance with the broad outlines set out by this Court in its judgment dated 12th February 1979; (6) the provision of section 167 (2), Cr. P.C., which provides that no objections shall be raised to a lawyer who would apprise them of his right to apply for bail, and (7) the fact that under trial Prisoners who are produced before the Magistrates are unaware of their right to obtain release on their bail is not sufficient to justify the detention of the accused in jail. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951. The respondent filed an application under section 29(2 A) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the notice was not given within the time prescribed by the Act. On appeal the Collector held that the tenancy had been terminated by the respondent and the Mamlatdar had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 34(2A) of Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1947. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amendment made by the Amending Act did not affect the rights of the landlord by subs.(2 A), and that the right to terminate a tenancy having arisen when the notice given before the Amending act came into force, the law to be applied in case of notices given before December 31. 1951 was the law existing on the date of notice. HELD : (i) The amendment did not effect any rights of landlord by sub section (2 A). The restriction imposed by subs. (2A), is on the right of the landlords to terminate the tenancy and this restriction would come into play on the day on which the landlord 's right to termination of the tenancy is perfected, namely, the day when the tenancy actually terminates in consequence of the notice issued to terminate, it. [574 D E] (ii) The words "the land held by the landlord" in sub section(2 B) are wide enough to include all lands which have been acquired before the coming into force of the Amending Acts. The word "land" is not defined in the Act and it has no meaning in any sense. It has a well known connotation. [575 E] In the present case, the notice under section 31(1) was merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the respondent to terminate tenancy and no further proceedings could be taken by the appellant in consequence thereof. The period of notice is the same before and after the amendment in the present ease. [576 G H] (iii)The word "tenant" has been defined in section 2(2) of Act, which includes a person who has been in occupation of any land for a continuous period of not less than one year immediately preceding the date on which he is deemed to have become such tenant under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1952. The words 'the landlord ' are wide in amplitude and include all persons who were in possession of land for more than one years immediately preceding that date. [577 A B] (iv)The notice under s.34(1)(b) is merely a declaratory to the effect that the tenant has terminated the tenancy, but it is always open to the landlord not to carry out his intention. The notice under sec. 34(1), is merely an declaration to that tenant of his intention to terminate his tenancy and does not affect any rights in respect of land which have accrued to him after the coming to force of this Act. [578 C D] (v)The period of the previous notice is not the date when the right is acquired by the landlords. The date of the termination of a tenancy is the date from which the tenancy stands terminated. The tenant continues in possession till the end of the period of his tenancy. Therefore, the provisions of the Act do not apply to notices already given before coming into operation of the amending Act. The amendment does not effect the rights or rights of a landlord by section 31 sub section 2 A.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan. The property of one Khadim Ali was acquired by the Custodian under section 8 of the , and he took possession of them. The petitioners filed a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the acquisition on the ground that they had been deprived of their rights in the houses, that the properties were evacuee property and that they could not be declared evacuees and their properties were the two houses in dispute, that they were evacuee and the houses were evacuee properties. The High Court held that the petitioners were entitled to declare the entire house evacuee property as evacuee property. On appeal by special leave: Held, that section 12 of the Act does not affect the petitioners ' rights under the will. It only affects the rights of an evacuee which the petitioners, on the admitted facts, are not. The act of the Custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The acts of the custodian in so respect of the houses did not affect anyone of them and it remained so in spite of the appeal. The Act does riot affect the rights under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The order of January 10, 1952, was without jurisdiction as the Custodian had no jurisdiction to declare that the entire property evacuee property was evacuee property, because, the petitioners had not filed any notice under section 7 of the . Held, further, that in view of the provisions of section 12 Of the Act, the properties could not have vested in the Custodian without due notice to the petitioners.

The assessee company was a manufacturer of yarn from raw and waste wool and yarn. The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn and (2) for weaving cloth. The department found that the two amounts mentioned above were in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents, and therefore, the amount paid to them could not be claimed by the assessee as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal held that the agreement amounted to a joint venture for distribution of profit, between the assessee company and the selling agent after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that though the agreement did not amount to a separate contract for distribution, it was a composite transaction resulting in division of net profits and therefore the amount received by the agents could not he claimed by them as deduction under Section 10(1)(xv). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal that the payments were not legally deductible under section10(2) (xv) is correct. [191B] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the payment in question was not legally deducted under section I 10(i)(iii). [192F] 3. The agreement dated October 20, 1955 by which a commission of Rs. 1,000 per year was paid to selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by the company in order to earn profits and would therefore fall within the ambit of section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax. [192G H] 4. The fact that the agents agree to share the losses which are to be excluded from the commission of the agents the agents become completely equated with the proprietors of the firm itself and therefore it is open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment is not real or that it is not incurred by assessee in the character of trader or it is a part of its business. [195A] 5. The question whether the payments made to the commission agents were expenses incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits was irrelevant and immaterial. [196B C] 6. The mere fact that an agent agreed to pay the commission does not take the case out of the ambit Of section 10. [197D] 7. The view taken by the Tribunal is correct and there is no reason to interfere with it. [198F] 8. The decision of the High Courts in the case of Dharamvir Dhir vs Commissioner of Income Tax, ; , followed.

The assessee, a public limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1962 63. The Income Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 18,950 as accumulated profits in the total income of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs, 18,0950 was not liable to be included in the accumulated profits and directed the Income Tax officer to refer the question for the opinion of the High Court. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which held that Rs.18,955 constituted a accumulated profit for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal also held that it was not open to the assessee to ask for a reference of those questions of law which arose on its submissions negatived in appeal by Appellate Tribunal. On reference, the High court answered the first question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee on the second question in negative. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the two sums of Rs 18, 950 were not liable for tax as they had been included within the accumulated profit of the company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) is used in a wide sense and includes current profits. [951 E] 2. The words "accrue profits" are used in the wider sense as including current profits and not for purposes of income tax. [954 F G] 3. The word "accurial profits" has been defined in section 4(1) to mean profits which have accrued or arisen before the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profits are those which arise after the accounting period of which income profits or gains were assessed, whereas current profits include current profits, but not "accrued profits" as in section 3(2) of that Act. [948 G H] 4. The term "accusulated profits", in section 10(1), means profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting years of which it was assessable, while "accretionary profits" means profits that have accrued before the relevant accounting year. [949 A B] 5. The definition of "accurnable profits" is not exhaustive and does not include current profit. [947 E F] 6. The question whether the provision of Rs 6,900 for dividend can be taken into account when determining the accumulated income as on March 31, 1958 is not related to the question whether accumulated profits can take in current profits or not. [946 G H; 949 A] 7. The form of reference application prescribed by rule 48 of the Income tax Rules, 1962 specifically requires the applicant to state the questions of Law which he desires to be referred to the High Courts. But in every case it is only the party applying for a refer ment who is entitled to specify the questions and to state whether the questions are of a kind specified in section I(2)(a) or (e). [948 E F; 948 A] 8. The application for reference to the Full Bench of the Tribunal under rule 48 must be considered void.

The plaintiff was the owner of certain lands in a village which formed part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan. The defendants claimed that they were tenants under the Maharaja of Burdwan and that they had been paying rent free, and that the suit lands were not Mal lands within the zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement. The trial court decreed the suits and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the defendants did not form part of a Zamindari of Burdwan, and (2) the suit properties formed part Of the Mal or assessed lands of the estate. Held, that the plaintiff was entitled to assess the income from the lands in their possession under the provisions of the Bengal Revenue Code, 1879, as it had been found by all the Courts that the defendants were trespassers. The fact that the lands formed part and parcel of the Mal and assessed lands did not make any difference. The suit properties constituted a separate and distinct estate of the plaintiff and the defendants was therefore entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their occupation. The plaintiff was not entitled to claim any assessment of the fair and just revenue on the holding in his possession. The question whether the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession was one of fact depending upon the facts found, and the finding must be based on such evidence as would satisfy the requirements of section 11 of the Act. The High Court was right in holding that the documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a Lakhe Raj grant were not proved to relate to the suit land.

The appellant was the owner of agricultural land in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ . The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur and claimed that he was an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist, but was only an agriculturist and therefore ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939. On appeal the District Judge held that the appellant was not a ' agriculturist ' within the definition of the word 'agricultural ' as contained in section 2(d) of the Act and that the suit was maintainable. The High Court on further appeal held that if an issue arises in a properly constituted civil suit which the civil court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the tenancy Act, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court would be ousted. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that the jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Tenancy act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by a competent authority under the Bombay Act, and that in view Of section 63(1) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the Civil Courts would have jurisdiction to decide the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'any issues which are required to he settled, decide, or dealt With by any authority competent to settle,, decide or dealtwith such issues under this Act" in section 64(1), is not only that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issue arise in the context of the provisions of Tenancy Act and which is required tobe settled, deciding or dealt within the same, it would be no answer to say that the issue is an incidental issue in a proper constituted civil court. [592F G] 2. The jurisdiction of Civil Court to settle , decide or dispose of any question arising under the tenancy law must be determined by competent authority and not by a mere arithmetical or clerical error. [593G] 3. In the instant case, on principle, if section 85 bars the jurisdiction, of the civil Court to decide or dealing with an issue arising under that Act and if section 8(1)(b) imposes an obligation on the civil courts to refer such issue to the competent authority, it will be no question of deciding or deal With the same in view the bar created by section 64 (1). [593H; 594A] 4. The word 'any issue which is needed to be decided, decided and dealt with, decide and dealt within by a Competent Authority under the Act, is not merely that if on assertion and denying the claim and consequent dispute an issue arose in the sense of a matter required to have been settled, determined or dealt wit nesses decided by competent authorities under the provisions Act, it is incumbent upon the Civil court to refer the issue to such competent authority. [594C D] 5. The civil court would be competent to decide and deal with the same as if the dispute was a matter requiring adjudication of the competent authori ty under the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code. If the plaintiff sued for specific perform ance, the suit would have been referred to the Competent Authority, under the Mamlatdar Act. [595D] 6. The Civil Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. It is incumbent on the Civil Judge to refer to the authority constituted under the ' Tenancy Act ' to decide whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist or not. If he does so, the competent authorities have no jurisdiction. [596E F] 7. In view of section 64 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1960, the civil Courts would be incompetent to entertain a suit.

The two undertakings of the assessee company were taken over by the Government of India under the provisions of the West Bengal Industrial Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1948. The two undertakings were owned by the assessee Company and the two undertakings had been taken over on the same terms and conditions. The assessee company was incorporated in 1944 as a limited company with effect from April 1, 1948 and its assets and liabilities were transferred to the new business of the company. In the assessment year 1958 59 (calendar year 1957) the assessee claimed exemption under section 15C of the Act. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim on the ground that the two undertaking were not formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence, namely, the business of heavy engineering. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the undertakings were not forming part of the original business and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under s 15C. The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant company that (1) the two industrial undertakings were formed by the reconstruction of a business already existing and hence, the benefit of section 15 C should be available to the assessee; (2) the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the three undertakings were forming part by the amalgamation of the appellant 's business already. HELD: (i) The two new undertakings are independent and distinct from each other. The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new industrial undertaking expands his existing business which he certainly does, would not on that score deprive him of the benefit under section15C merely because it goes to expand the general business of his main business. [776B] (ii) The new undertakings were independent and separate from the original one. The mere fact that the articles produced by the two Undertakings are used by the Boiler Division of the assesses will not weigh against holding that these are new and separate undertakings. Use of the articles by the assesses is not decisive to deny the benefit to him under section 14C merely Because it goes, to expand its general business. use of the article by the asses see is not determinative to deny him the benefit thereunder. [767E F] (iii) The fact whether an assessee has a new and distinct industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit or by transfer to a new business or by the transfer to another new business, will not prevent him from setting up new industrial undertakings and from claiming benefit under s.15C if that section is otherwise applicable. [777G H] (iv) The High court was not right in answering two questions in the negative and against the assesseee.

The inamdars were granted inam lands in the State of Madras. The inamdars had been granted permanent leases for the performance of services connected therewith. They were granted permanent lease for a period exceeding five years. The Inamdars were not lessees within the meaning of section 44 B(2)(a) (i). The inamdar was granted permanent rights to the lands under the grant. The inams were resumed by the Government and registered as O.S. No. 8 of 1954. The suit was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Madurai for disposal in accordance with law. The appellants contended that the inams were personal inams burdened with services connected with the temple and were resumable under section 44B(2) (a)(i). Held: (1) Section 44 B (2)(b)(i) allows a resumption of the inam where there has been an alienation of the Inam either before or after 1934. The lands in question are resumables under section 43 B(1) and they were resold by the alienees to any subordinate interest in the inams. [545 C D] (2) Section 45 B(3)(a)(ii) allows resumption of inam where the inamdar has made an exchange gift, sale or mortgage of the lands. The grant was not a permanent lease and the inams had been resummended under section 47 B(4)(i), but only as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of section 45 B (1). [546 C D; 516 E F] (3) Section 43 B (3)(b) allows the resumption of an inam where it has been granted before 1934. Section 44B (2(a)(iii) is attracted if the holder of the inams held before 1934, and in case of resumption on the ground that the math or temple had ceased to exist or that the charity or service in question had in any way become impossible of performance, as an endowment to the Board for appropriation to such religious, educational or charitable purposes. [511 C D]. (4) Section 47 B (4)(a), (b) and (5) are not retrospective in operation and do not authorise resumption of inams on the grounds of any alienation thereof made before 1934; but section 44 A(3) is applicable only where there had been an alienations of the land by the inamdars.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Indore Municipality levied house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or any other account whatsoever. The appellant Corporation challenged the levy of house tax under section 90(6) of the Act on the ground that it was inconsistent with sec. 73 of the 1954 Act and that it had no power to impose a tax on its own property. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the same basis for the two subsequent years. [131 E] (ii) The tax levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the footing that the resolution passed by the Municipality to levy the tax at 7% of its value was saved and therefore, the list so adopted was in force during the years in question and has to be accepted under section 76(6). [131 F G] (iii) The saving and deeming provisions in sec. 2(c) can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73 that is, if it is assessed on the net and not the gross annual rent assessed after deducting 10% Statutory allowance in the lieu of the costs of repair or any such account whatsoever.[131 G H] (iv) The appellant was entitled to levy house tax at the rate of 7% on the gross return value. [132 A B] (v) The Municipality had imposed a tax at a rate higher than that fixed by the rules made under the repealed Indore City municipal Act, 1911. The Municipal Tax is an additional charge levied for the purpose of levying house tax. The tax so levied is not liable to be deducted from the gross income of the municipality or the amount of tax leviable on such buildings or lands or both. [133 C D] (vi) The provisions of sec. 75(6)(b) can have no application if the property tax is levied in the nature of a charge on the property and not on the capital value of the property. [134 E F] (vii) The taxes imposed under the new Act are not to be treated as part of the general fund of the Municipality. The municipal tax is not an annual payment but is a charge for the benefit of the residents of the city. The Corporation was entitled only to levy a house tax and it had not been shown that the tax was in excess of the amount fixed by section 73(6), as the tax levied was not a part of its general fund. [135 G H; 135 A] (viii) The municipal taxes are an annual charge which is an increase or decrease in the annual letting values. The Municipality has to pay the tax on gross annual rental value and the amount so fixed for the period of each year is liable to revision by the Municipal Tax Officer.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, on behalf of the assessee Company, relied upon the Memorandum of Association of the company which allowed the assessee company to manufacture and sell chemicals and also on the Directors report, held that the assessee was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. On appeal by the respondent company, the Tribunal found that the business had not completely ceased to exist since the assessee 's match factory was closed and that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company had been wound up. In reference, the High Court held that there was no evidence of any profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital. The High Court also held that it was not possible to hold that there could be said to be a sale in the carrying on of the business in respect of the chemicals and other raw materials. On the question whether there could, therefore, be said that there can be said no profit other except what results therefrom from appreciation of the capital. Held: (i) The assessee company was wound up at least in so far as its match manufacture was concerned. That the business of the Company was sold as a going concern and was in fact worked by the assessee on behalf, of the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the appellant company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer. The profit and loss account showed that the price represented a payment for the entire business without a separate sale or valuation of this stock in trade for purposes of sale. (ii)The High Court was right in holding that there had been no profit another than what resulted from appreciation in capital. There was, therefore. no question of any profits other than those which arose out of appreciation of revenue. Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Doughty & Co., , referred to.
